# byoa: the full docs

> byoa, short for "bring your own agent", is the simplest way to let your users bring their own AI subscription to power the agents in your app.

This file has the full text of byoa's docs, for LLMs: the docs pages (https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs), SPEC.md, the agent skill and the to-do example, from https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa (branch main). The index is https://byoa.rippling.computer/llms.txt.

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs

# byoa docs

**byoa, short for "bring your own agent", is the simplest way to let your users bring their own AI subscription to power the agents in your app.**

## The future of AI-native apps

AI-native apps are the future. But an app that buys its AI at API prices must pass that cost on to its users. So it must choose: a frontier model, and a high price for each user, or a cheap model, and a worse agent. AI subscriptions solve this. We bet on a future where everyone has a $20 AI plan, or the same in another form, and that plan powers every app they use. In that future, every app is AI-native, so nobody says "AI-native app" anymore.

AI is like electricity, and an AI subscription is like a portable battery pack. Battery packs come in different sizes, and one pack powers all the appliances in your home. This is the economy we bet on. We build byoa to make it come sooner, so that every developer can build on it.

Diagram: Where the power comes from and who pays for it. Today: the AI labs sell tokens to each app through its API key, and each app, such as a notes app, a mail app and your app, pays per token and puts that cost in its price. With byoa: each user owns one battery, their own AI plan, and it plugs into every app they use. Your app passes on only the cost of the sandbox.

## What byoa does

Each user powers the agent features of your app with their own AI subscription: they sign in to it one time. Today byoa supports Claude (in Claude Code), ChatGPT (in Codex), Grok (in Grok Build) and OpenCode Go (beta), and more are coming soon. When your app has work for the AI, byoa runs that user's own Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build in a sandbox, with the user's tools, and streams the result back. The user's plan pays for the AI. Your app pays only for the sandbox.

Diagram: Who brings what. Your app brings the product, the sandbox account, and one call: agents.run. Each user brings their AI plan, such as Claude, ChatGPT or Grok, and their tools, such as Notion or Gmail. byoa puts them together in a new sandbox for each job: it runs the user's own Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build with their tools, and streams the result back to your app. The user's plan pays for the AI. Your app pays only for the sandbox.

byoa is an open-source library (Apache 2.0). It runs inside your app's own backend. It is not a hosted service. Start with [Getting started](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/getting-started.md). To learn the parts first, read the [Overview](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/concepts.md). To see which plans work, read [Supported AI subscriptions](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/subscriptions.md).

## What your users pay

Your app passes its AI costs on to its users, in its price. So the real question is what each user pays for the same agent:

- **Without byoa,** your app buys the AI at API prices. A frontier model gives a good agent and a high price. A cheap open-weight model gives a low price and a worse agent.
- **With byoa,** each user brings the AI, on a plan that they already pay for and that powers every app they use. Your app passes on only the cost of the sandbox.

Diagram: What each user pays a month for small agent tasks, when your app passes its AI costs on. With your API key, frontier models cost each user a lot, and cheaper models cost less for a weaker agent. With byoa, the user's own plan pays for a frontier model, and your app passes on only the sandbox. The numbers come from the cost tables in the FAQ.

For 100 tasks for each user, a month:

| How your app gets the AI | Each user pays a month |
|---|---|
| Your API key: Claude Opus 5.5 (frontier) | $49.00 |
| Your API key: GPT-6.2 Sol (frontier) | $24.50 |
| Your API key: Kimi K3 (frontier, open-weight) | $43.50 |
| Your API key: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (smaller, open-weight) | $2.97 |
| byoa on E2B: the user's own plan, with a frontier model | $1.38 and their plan |
| byoa on Daytona: the user's own plan, with a frontier model | $1.38 and their plan |
| byoa on Instabox: the user's own plan, with a frontier model | $0.14 and their plan |
| byoa on Sprites: the user's own plan, with a frontier model | $1.37 and their plan |

These are estimates for a small agent task, from the [FAQ](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/faq.md#what-does-an-ai-job-cost-with-byoa-and-with-an-api-key). byoa does not make tokens cheaper: it moves them to the user's plan. The plan has limits, and a user who runs many long tasks reaches them.

## Why and when you need byoa

You want your app to have an AI agent that does real work for each user: it reads and changes the user's data, calls the user's tools, and writes files. To build this yourself, you need many parts:

- an agent loop as good as Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build, and its updates;
- a sandbox for each user, which starts, pauses and ends at the right times;
- a sign-in to each user's AI plan, and safe storage of that login;
- an OAuth connection to each of the user's MCP tools, with the tokens kept out of the agent's reach.

And with your own API key, your app buys every token at API prices, and your users pay for them in your price. byoa gives you all of these parts as one library, and the user's own plan pays for the AI.

Diagram: Your backend, before and after. Build it yourself: your app, an agent loop, sandbox control, AI sign-in and login storage, and MCP OAuth and token storage, and an AI bill per token, at API prices. With byoa: your app and byoa, one npm install, and no AI bill, because the user's plan pays.

Use byoa when:

- your users already pay for Claude, ChatGPT, Grok or OpenCode Go, and you do not want to pay for their AI or sell them AI credits;
- your app's AI work is agent work, with many steps, tools and files, not one chat answer;
- you want Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build as your agent, not a loop of your own;
- you want each user's tools, such as Notion or Gmail, in each job, after one connection.

You do not need byoa when:

- your app needs only one model call at a time, such as a summary or a chat reply: an API key costs less there ([FAQ](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/faq.md#what-does-an-ai-job-cost-with-byoa-and-with-an-api-key));
- your agent needs no shell and no files, so an agent loop of your own can run it without a sandbox, such as on AWS Lambda, and a cheap model is good enough for it;
- your app pays for the AI itself and does not want the user's plan;
- your users do not have an AI plan, or use the agent only a little: a few tasks on a cheap model at API prices cost them less than a $20 plan.

These pages are the Markdown files in [docs/](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/tree/main/docs) of the repository. The site at https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs shows the same pages, and serves each page as Markdown for LLMs (add `.md` to its address) and all of them in [llms-full.txt](https://byoa.rippling.computer/llms-full.txt).

- [Sign users in](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md): the sign-in on the lab's own page, where the login stays, one job step by step, jobs at the same time with one login, the OpenCode Go key, and sign-out

- [Test your app](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/testing.md): test your app with the fake harness, the local sandbox and the memory store, and run byoa's own tests

## Plans and rules

- [Supported AI subscriptions](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/subscriptions.md): which Claude, ChatGPT, Grok and OpenCode Go (beta) plans your users can bring, and whether their accounts can get banned
- [Lab rules](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/lab-rules.md): what Anthropic's, OpenAI's, xAI's and OpenCode's terms allow, and what byoa and each app must do
- [FAQ](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/faq.md): what byoa is, whether a user's AI account can get banned, many agents at once, memory between jobs, models, and what a job costs with byoa and with an API key

## Reference

- [API reference](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/api.md): every import, method, option and event of byoa: `createAgents`, `agents.run`, the sandbox and store adapters, and the events that a job streams

# How byoa works

**Your app brings the product. Each user brings the agent.** You build the app and pick the sandbox. Each user brings their plan and their tools. byoa runs inside your backend and runs each job in that user's own sandbox.

Think of the user's AI subscription as a battery pack, and of your app as an appliance. The user brings the battery. byoa is the plug: it connects the user's plan, and the user's tools, to the agent features of your app. Your app supplies only the place where the agent runs, the sandbox.

## Who brings what

Diagram: You build the app and import byoa. You pay only for the sandbox. Each user signs in with their own Claude, ChatGPT or Grok plan, which pays for the AI, and connects their tools once. Your app code calls agents.run. byoa is a library inside your app's backend, and keeps AI logins and MCP grants in your database. Below your backend's edge, byoa drives three things that run outside it: a new sandbox for each job at E2B, Daytona, Instabox or Sprites on your account, where the user's own Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build runs; the AI labs, whose model calls the user's own plan pays; and the user's MCP servers, which get the real token from byoa's proxy.

```text
DEVELOPER · YOU                                           END USER
┌────────────────────────────────────┐                    ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
│ builds the app                     │                    │ uses the app                       │
│ picks the sandbox provider         │                    │ pays for the AI with a plan:       │
│ owns the database                  │                    │    Claude     ChatGPT     Grok     │
│ pays only for the sandbox          │                    │ has MCP tools and skills           │
└──────────────────┬─────────────────┘                    └──────────────────┬─────────────────┘
                   │ imports byoa             signs in on the lab's own page │
                   │                             connects each MCP tool once │
                   ▼                                                         ▼
┌─ YOUR APP'S BACKEND · you run it ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  your app code                                            your database                      │
│        │ agents.run(userId, task)                               ▲ AI logins, MCP grants      │
│        ▼                                                        │                            │
│ ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┻━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓ │
│ ┃ byoa · open source, Apache 2.0                                                           ┃ │
│ ┃   AI login · harness            skills · AGENTS.md            MCP OAuth · proxy          ┃ │
│ ┃              │                                                           │               ┃ │
└─╂┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄│┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄ ▲ your backend · outside it ▼ ┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄│┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄╂─┘
  ┃              │ create · run · destroy                         real token │               ┃
  ┃              ▼                                                           ▼               ┃
  ┃ ┌─ SANDBOX ────────────────┐  ┌─ AI LABS ────────────────┐  ┌─ MCP SERVERS ────────────┐ ┃
  ┃ │    E2B,    Daytona,      │  │ Anthropic · OpenAI · xAI │  │ Notion · Gmail · …       │ ┃
  ┃ │    Instabox,    Sprites, │  │                          │  │                          │ ┃
  ┃ │ on your account          ├─▶│ model calls, paid by     │  │ the user's own accounts  │ ┃
  ┃ │ runs the user's own      │  │ the user's own plan      │  │                          │ ┃
  ┃ │ Claude Code, Codex or    │  │                          │  │                          │ ┃
  ┃ │ Grok Build               │  │                          │  │                          │ ┃
  ┃ └──────────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────────┘ ┃
  ┃                                                                                          ┃
  ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛
```

- **You, the developer**, build the app, pick the sandbox provider (E2B, Daytona, Instabox or Sprites, on your own account) and own the database. You import byoa into your app's backend.
- **The end user** uses your app. They have a Claude, ChatGPT or Grok plan, and accounts in tools such as Notion or Gmail. They sign in on the lab's own page one time, and connect each MCP tool one time.
- **byoa** is a library in your backend. It keeps the user's AI login and MCP grants in your database, encrypted with your key. For each job, it gets a sandbox at your provider and runs the user's own, unmodified Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build there.
- **The AI labs** (Anthropic, OpenAI) get the model calls. The user's own plan pays for them, not your API bill.
- **The MCP servers** get the real token from byoa's proxy in your backend, never from the sandbox.

## The problem

To make an app AI-native, you run a big lab's harness (Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build) in a sandbox, with the user's own AI plan. For each app, you must build the same connection layer again:

- the user's AI login, through the real CLI;
- the user's MCP connections and their OAuth tokens, with one refresh owner;
- the user's skills and AGENTS.md;
- the harness install and its updates;
- the code that connects all of this to one sandbox provider.

byoa is that layer, as a library, so you do not build it again for each app.

## What byoa is, and what it is not

- byoa **is** a library. It runs inside your app's own backend (Node, Bun or Convex). Cloudflare Workers support is planned.
- byoa **stores tokens in your own database**, through a store adapter.
- byoa **is not** a hosted service. We do not run a server, and we never see your users' tokens.

| | Version 1 | Later |
|---|---|---|
| Agents | Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build | Gemini or Antigravity, maybe |
| User plans | Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, OpenCode Go key (beta) | |
| Sandboxes | E2B, Daytona, Instabox, Sprites (Fly.io) | other providers |
| Backends | Node, Convex actions | Cloudflare Workers |
| Token stores | Convex, Postgres, or your own with get, put, delete and compare-and-set | |

## How a job runs

Your app calls `agents.run(userId, task)`. byoa takes the user's sandbox, loads the user's setup, and runs the user's own harness on the user's own plan. The [sandbox lifecycle](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/sandbox-lifecycle.md) has every step and every decision.

Diagram: One job, from agents.run to the end event

1. Your app calls agents.run. `agents.run(userId, { harness, task, mcp, setup })`.
2. Take the user's sandbox. By default, resume the user's kept sandbox (a conversation has one of its own), or create it for the first job. With `sandboxPer 'job'`, create a new one.
3. Load the setup. The pinned harness, the skills, AGENTS.md, and an MCP config that points to your proxy with a job token.
4. Copy the AI login in. From your database, decrypted in your backend. Login files: login files in.
5. Run the harness. Text, tool calls and permission requests stream back as events. MCP calls go through the proxy.
6. close() This is the end. End the job token, save the login back if the CLI changed it, remove it from the sandbox, then pause or destroy the sandbox. Login files: files removed.

The user's AI login and MCP grants stay in your database between jobs. A kept sandbox keeps the files that the app wrote there and the installed harness, but no login. A job of a conversation also continues the harness's session of the earlier jobs, and keeps the job folder ([what carries over](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/sandbox-lifecycle.md#what-carries-over-between-jobs)).

## Real tokens never go into the sandbox

The agent in the sandbox gets a short-lived job token, for one job and one user. The proxy in your backend adds the real MCP token to each request.

Diagram: How an MCP call from the sandbox gets the real token

1. The harness calls an MCP tool. Its MCP config points to your proxy, at `<proxyUrl>/<name>`, with the job token. It has no real MCP token.
2. Question: Is the job token good for this server? If yes: go on to step 3.
   - If no: Refuse the call. This is the end. The job ended, or the job did not get this server.
3. Add the real token. From your database, encrypted with your key. byoa refreshes it when it is due, with one refresh owner.
4. Send the request on to the MCP server. This is the end. The answer goes back to the harness. The real token does not.

[MCP tools and the proxy](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/mcp.md) has the details, and [AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md) says where the user's AI login is at each step.

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/getting-started

# Getting started

New to byoa? Read the [Introduction](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/index.md) first. In short: byoa is a library in your app's backend. Each user signs in to their own Claude, ChatGPT or Grok plan one time, and connects each MCP tool one time. When your app has work for the AI, byoa runs that user's own Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build in a sandbox, with the user's tools, and streams the events back to your app. The user's plan pays for the AI, and your app pays for the sandbox.

This page takes you from `npm install` to a first agent job: one `agents` object, two routes, a sign-in and a job. A new app needs fewer than 50 lines of its own code for this. The [to-do example](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/tree/main/examples/todo), a chat with the agent, uses byoa in 49.

## Install

Install byoa from npm. Its package is `@madeyexz/byoa`, because npm does not allow the name `byoa`:

```sh
npm install @madeyexz/byoa
bun add @madeyexz/byoa
```

Also install the sandbox SDK that your app uses: `e2b` for E2B, `@daytona/sdk` for Daytona. Instabox, Sprites and the local sandbox need none. byoa needs Node 22.18 or later, or Bun. To use the newest commit on `main` before it is released, install from GitHub: `npm install github:madeyexz/byoa`.

## Get a sandbox API key

Your app pays for the sandboxes, so your app needs its own account and API key at one sandbox provider. Make an account, make a key, and put the key in your backend's environment. Do not send the key to the browser.

- **E2B**: [sign up](https://console.e2b.dev/sign-up), then copy a key from [API keys](https://console.e2b.dev/?tab=keys). byoa reads `E2B_API_KEY`. The free plan gives $100 of credit one time and runs 10 sandboxes at a time; a paused sandbox does not count. A sandbox runs for 1 hour at most before it must pause, so one job can take at most 1 hour ([billing and limits](https://e2b.dev/docs/billing)).
- **Daytona**: [sign up](https://app.daytona.io), then make a key in [API keys](https://app.daytona.io/dashboard/keys). byoa reads `DAYTONA_API_KEY`. A new account gets $200 of compute ([pricing](https://www.daytona.io/pricing)). On Tier 1 and 2, a sandbox can reach only [allowed domains](https://www.daytona.io/docs/en/network-limits).
- **Instabox**: [sign up](https://dashboard.instabox.sh), then make a key in [API keys](https://dashboard.instabox.sh/dashboard/api-keys). byoa reads `INSTABOX_API_KEY`. The free plan has 1 sandbox in all, also when it is stopped, so it is enough for 1 user's kept sandbox or 1 job ([limits](https://instabox.sh/docs/account/limits)).
- **Sprites** (Fly.io): [sign up](https://fly.io/app/sign-up?s=sprites), then make a Sprites token of your organization ([how](https://docs.fly.io/sprites/cli/authentication)). byoa reads `SPRITES_TOKEN`. A new account gets $1 of credit with no card; the Free plan gives $5 of usage a month and has 3 Sprites ([pricing](https://fly.io/sprites)).

```sh
export E2B_API_KEY=e2b_...
```

- With the variable set, `e2b()`, `daytona()`, `instabox()` and `sprites()` read the key themselves. To give the key from somewhere else, such as your secret store, pass it: `e2b({ apiKey })`.
- A Daytona key needs `write:sandboxes` and `delete:sandboxes`, and for `cliLogin` also `read:volumes`, `write:volumes` and `delete:volumes`. An Instabox key needs `machines:write` and `machines:delete`.
- For development and tests, `localSandbox()` needs no key. It isolates nothing. See [Testing](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/testing.md).

You need no AI key. Each user signs in to their own Claude, ChatGPT or Grok plan, and that plan pays for the AI. To compare the providers, see [Sandbox providers](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/providers.md).

## Make one `agents` object

Make one `agents` object in your backend: once for each process, or once in each Convex action.

```ts
import { createAgents } from '@madeyexz/byoa'
import { e2b } from '@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/e2b'
import { postgresStore } from '@madeyexz/byoa/store/postgres'

const agents = createAgents({
  app: 'myapp',                                    // one app's AI logins are only this app's
  sandbox: e2b(),                                  // reads E2B_API_KEY
  store: postgresStore({ query: (sql, args) => pool.query(sql, args) }),
  encryptionKey,                                   // openssl rand -base64 32; grants and AI logins are encrypted with it
  proxyUrl: 'https://myapp.example.com/byoa/mcp',  // serve agents.proxy here
  oauth: { redirectUrl: 'https://myapp.example.com/byoa/callback' },
})
```

- **`app`**: lower-case letters, digits and `-`, at most 24. It names the app's sandboxes and login volumes.
- **`sandbox`**: the [sandbox provider](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/providers.md). To change the provider, change this one line.
- **`store`**: your own database, through a [store adapter](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/stores.md). For Postgres, run `POSTGRES_SCHEMA` once.
- **`encryptionKey`**: 32 random bytes as base64. Keep it the same between restarts, and keep it secret.
- **`proxyUrl`**: a public HTTPS URL. The sandbox must reach it. In development, use a tunnel such as `cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:3000`.

The default E2B template is named `byoa`, and a new E2B account does not have it. Build it one time with `buildE2BTemplate()`, or pass `e2b({ template: 'base' })`. See [Sandbox providers](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/providers.md#e2b).

## Serve two routes

byoa's handlers are fetch handlers (`Request` → `Response`). On Node, wrap your app's handler with `toNodeListener` from `@madeyexz/byoa/node`.

```ts
if (url.pathname.startsWith('/byoa/mcp/')) return agents.proxy(req)  // the MCP proxy: no app session check here
if (url.pathname === '/byoa/callback') {                               // the MCP server's sign-in page sends the browser here
  const p = url.searchParams
  await agents.finishMcp({ state: p.get('state') ?? '', code: p.get('code') ?? undefined, error: p.get('error') ?? undefined })
  return Response.redirect(`${publicUrl}/`, 302)
}
```

- The proxy checks the job token itself. Do not put your app's session check in front of it: the harness in the sandbox has no app session.
- Every other route reads the user from your app's own session. The `userId` you give byoa is your app's stable user id. Never take it from a header or a body that the browser controls.

## Sign the user in to their plan

The sign-in runs the unmodified CLI in a sandbox. The user signs in on the lab's own page. byoa gives your app only that page's URL and, for Codex and Grok Build, a code. See [AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md) for each step.

```ts
const claude = await agents.connectLogin(userId, 'claude')  // { url }: Anthropic's own sign-in page
await agents.finishLogin(userId, 'claude', { code })        // the code that page shows
const codex = await agents.connectLogin(userId, 'codex')    // { url, code }: OpenAI's page and the code to enter
await agents.finishLogin(userId, 'codex', { waitMs: 20_000 })  // call again while the state is 'pending'
await agents.cancelLogin(userId, 'codex')                     // the user closed the sign-in: its sandbox ends now
const grok = await agents.connectLogin(userId, 'grok')      // { url, code }: xAI's page and the code; finish as for Codex
```

The sign-in's sandbox lives only while your sign-in UI checks in: each `finishLogin` call keeps it for 2 more minutes. For Claude Code, call `finishLogin(userId, 'claude')` with no code about every 30 seconds while the user is on Anthropic's page.

A user with an OpenCode Go plan (beta) gives a key instead: `agents.connectKey(userId, 'opencode-go', key)`. See [AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md#opencode-go-a-key-not-a-sign-in-beta).

## Connect an MCP tool, one time

```ts
const mcp = await agents.connectMcp(userId, 'https://mcp.notion.com/mcp', { name: 'notion' })
// mcp.signInUrl: the server's sign-in page; your redirectUrl route then calls agents.finishMcp({ state, code })
```

Every later job of this user can have this server. Your app's own data needs no MCP server: give its tools to `createAgents` as functions. See [MCP tools and the proxy](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/mcp.md).

## Run a job

```ts
for await (const event of agents.run(userId, { harness: 'claude', task, mcp: ['notion'], setup: { agentsMd, skills } })) {
  // start, text, tool_call, tool_result, permission, error, end: the same events for every harness
}
```

`run` does not throw when a job fails. It gives `error` events, then always one `end` event. See [Running agents](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/running-agents.md) for the events, what the agent may do, and jobs at the same time.

## Let a coding agent do it

[skills/byoa](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/tree/main/skills/byoa) is a skill in the [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io) format. It teaches a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Amp and others) to add byoa to an app: the install, `createAgents` with a store and a sandbox adapter, the sign-in, the MCP connections and their routes, `agents.run` and its events, and the lab rules. Its `metadata.version` is the `version` in byoa's package.json next to it.

The npm package has the skill in it (from 1.1.0). After you install byoa, link the skill of the installed version into your app's repository for Claude Code, Codex, Amp, Cursor and others, so it always matches the package:

```sh
npx skills experimental_sync -y
```

`experimental_sync` is a preview command of the [skills](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills) CLI. Without it, or with byoa 1.0.0, install the skill of one release from its tag (here 1.1.0; use the tag of your version), or the skill of `main`:

- one release: `npx skills add madeyexz/byoa@v1.1.0 --skill byoa`
- `main`: `npx skills add madeyexz/byoa`, or for Amp `amp skill add madeyexz/byoa/skills/byoa`

For LLMs, the site also serves the docs as [llms.txt](https://byoa.rippling.computer/llms.txt) (an index) and [llms-full.txt](https://byoa.rippling.computer/llms-full.txt) (the docs, SPEC.md, the example and the skill in one file), and each docs page as Markdown (add `.md` to its address).

## Next

- Read the [Overview](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/concepts.md) to learn who holds what, and where.
- Try the [live demo](https://byoa.rippling.computer/demo): sign in with your own Claude, ChatGPT or Grok plan, and your own agent triages a sample inbox.
- Run the [to-do example](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/tree/main/examples/todo): an AI-native to-do list, with tests that use the fake harness.
- Test your app with no plan and no sandbox: [Testing](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/testing.md).
- Follow the [Lab rules](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/lab-rules.md). Every app on byoa must.

# Sandbox lifecycle

This page shows every sandbox byoa creates, from creation to removal, with the default `storedLogin()`. A sandbox has the user's login files only while a sign-in, a job or a sign-out runs. When your backend dies during a job, a watcher in the sandbox removes them.

byoa creates four kinds of sandbox:

- a **sign-in sandbox** for each sign-in, which byoa never keeps. It ends at `cancelLogin`, or 2 minutes after your app's last `finishLogin` check-in, 15 minutes at most ([AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md#sign-in) shows its steps);
- a **job sandbox**: by default one kept sandbox for each user, harness and `sandboxKey` (a conversation is a key of its own), paused between jobs; or, with `sandboxPer: 'job'`, a new one for each job;
- a **sign-out sandbox**, for 5 minutes, where the CLI signs out ([AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md#sign-out));
- a **models sandbox** for each `agents.listModels` call, where the CLI lists the models of the user's plan. byoa destroys it after the list, 10 minutes at most.

## The job sandbox

Diagram: A job sandbox, from the start of a job to its end

Kept for the user (default): `sandboxPer: 'user'`: byoa keeps one sandbox for each slot, pauses it after a job and resumes it for the next.

1. Pick the user's slot. One for each user, harness and `sandboxKey` (an empty key when none; a conversation's id is its key). `usersandbox/<user>/<provider>/<h>/<key>`. Login files: no login files.
2. Question: Does another job run in this slot? If no: go on to step 3.
   - If yes: Wait in line. The jobs run in the order they came. `onWait` gets `{ for: 'sandbox', ahead }`. Time limit: no limit, unless waitMs.
3. Question: Does the slot have a sandbox? If yes: go on to step 4. If no: see "Create a new kept sandbox" below.
4. Resume it. Time limit: job + 1 min.
5. Question: Does the provider still have it? If yes: go on to step 6.
   - If no: Create a new kept sandbox. Also when it was gone (SandboxGoneError). Time limit: job + 1 min. Then go on to step 6.
6. Prepare the work folder. `~/work`: nothing of an earlier job stays. In a conversation, the agent's files stay and only byoa's own files are new; in a new sandbox, byoa writes the conversation's stored transcript back.
7. Question: Is the user signed in? a stored login exists. If yes: go on to step 8.
   - If no: Stop with LoginError. This is the end. The state becomes 'signed-out'. close() still runs.
8. Check the MCP servers, install the pinned harness.
9. Copy the login in. Takes the login lease, decrypts the files, writes them, chmod 600, and writes a loan record. If a dead job's loan record is there, it first saves what that job's CLI left. Starts the watcher. Time limit: waits in line for the lease; lease: job + 5 min; watcher: job + 45 s. Login files: login files in.
10. The harness runs. The CLI may refresh its login and write its files again. byoa saves a change about every 60 s. Login files: login files in.
   - If backend dies: Warning: If your backend dies here. close() never runs. The watcher removes the files at job + 45 s. See below.
11. close(): save back, remove the files, give the lease back. Ends the job token. Saves the files only if they changed, with compare-and-set. Removes the loan record. In a conversation, keeps the session id and a copy of its transcript, encrypted. Login files: files removed.
12. Question: Did byoa remove the files? any error here counts as no. If yes: go on to step 13.
   - If no: Destroy it, forget its id. This is the end. The next job of this slot creates a new one.
13. Pause it for the next job. This is the end. E2B: pause. Daytona, Instabox: stop. Sprites: sleep.

New for each job: `sandboxPer: 'job'`: byoa creates a sandbox for one job and destroys it after.

1. Create a new sandbox, not kept. A new work folder. Time limit: job + 1 min. Login files: no login files.
2. Question: Is the user signed in? a stored login exists. If yes: go on to step 3.
   - If no: Stop with LoginError. This is the end. The state becomes 'signed-out'. close() still runs.
3. Check the MCP servers, install the pinned harness.
4. Copy the login in. Takes the login lease, decrypts the files, writes them, chmod 600. Starts the watcher. Time limit: waits in line for the lease; lease: job + 5 min; watcher: job + 45 s. Login files: login files in.
5. The harness runs. The CLI may refresh its login and write its files again. byoa saves a change about every 60 s. Login files: login files in.
   - If backend dies: Warning: If your backend dies here. close() never runs. The watcher removes the files at job + 45 s, and the provider deletes the sandbox at job + 1 min.
6. close(): save back, remove the files, give the lease back. Ends the job token. Saves the files only if they changed, with compare-and-set. Removes the loan record. Login files: files removed.
7. Destroy the sandbox. This is the end.

"Job" is `jobTimeoutMs`, 30 minutes by default. byoa gives each job sandbox job + 1 minute.

- **One kept sandbox per user (the default).** The first job of a user and harness creates it. After each job, byoa pauses it, and the next job resumes it, so files that the app wrote there and the installed harness stay. Each job gets a new job folder (`s.work`) with its own setup. One job of a slot runs at a time; the others wait in line and run in the order they came, with no time limit unless you set `waitMs`. When the provider no longer has the sandbox, the next job creates a new one.
- **Many kept sandboxes per user.** Give each job a `sandboxKey`, such as a project or a conversation. Each key has its own kept sandbox and its own lease. See [Running agents](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/running-agents.md#jobs-at-the-same-time) for the ways to run one user's jobs at the same time.
- **A conversation.** Give each job of a chat the same `conversation` id. The conversation has its own kept sandbox, and the agent continues its own session there. See [What carries over between jobs](#what-carries-over-between-jobs).
- **A new sandbox for each job.** Set `sandboxPer: 'job'` in `createAgents`. Use it when nothing may stay between jobs.

In all three, the user's AI login and MCP grants stay in your database. No real MCP token goes into the sandbox, a job token is refused after its job, and no copy of the AI login stays in the sandbox between jobs.

## What carries over between jobs

"Resume" can mean two things. byoa does both:

- **Resume the sandbox.** byoa starts the user's paused sandbox again for the next job. The files outside `~/work` and the installed harness are still there. This happens in every kept sandbox.
- **Resume the conversation.** Only for a job that names a `conversation`. The harness continues its own session, so the agent knows the earlier messages and what it did. Each CLI does this its own way: Claude Code `--session-id`, then `--resume`; Codex's app server keeps the thread, then resumes it (`thread/resume`); Grok Build's agent mode names a session, then resumes it (`session/resume`). While a job runs, it also takes more messages (`job.send`, see [Running agents](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/running-agents.md#more-messages-while-a-job-runs-steering)).

| | A job with no `conversation` | A job of a `conversation` |
|---|---|---|
| The agent's memory of earlier jobs | none: each job is a new session | the harness's session of the earlier jobs |
| `~/work` (the job folder) | emptied at the start of each job | kept; only byoa's files (skills, AGENTS.md, the MCP config, the task) are new |
| Files outside `~/work`, the installed harness | kept in a kept sandbox | kept: the conversation has its own kept sandbox |
| The AI login | never kept in the sandbox: a copy for each job | the same |
| When the provider lost the sandbox | a new sandbox | a new sandbox, with the stored copy of the transcript, so the agent still remembers; `~/work` and the other files are gone |

After each job of a conversation, byoa keeps the harness's session id and a copy of its session files (the transcript), encrypted in your store, when they are at most `transcriptBytes` (default 700 000 bytes). A longer transcript lives only in the sandbox: when the provider loses that sandbox, the next job says so (an `error` with code `conversation`) and starts a new session. With `sandboxPer: 'job'`, each job of a conversation gets a new sandbox and resumes only from the stored copy.

## When your backend dies during a job

`close()` never runs. byoa still loses little, and no login stays in the sandbox:

Diagram: A job whose backend dies, with the default storedLogin

1. The job runs. About every 60 s, byoa saves what the CLI changed in its login (a checkpoint), with compare-and-set. The loan record `ailoginloan/<user>/<h>/<sandbox>` names the stored version this sandbox has. Login files: login files in.
2. Warning: Your backend dies. The checkpoints stop. The CLI may still refresh its login in the sandbox.
3. The watcher removes the login files. The watcher started when the login was copied in. It removes the files only if no later job replaced its marker. Time limit: job + 45 s. Login files: files removed.
4. The provider pauses or ends the sandbox. Kept: E2B pauses it at job + 1 min; Daytona stops it. New for each job: the provider deletes it. See the table below. Time limit: job + 1 min.
5. The slot and the login lease run out. So the user's next job does not wait forever. Time limit: job + 5 min.
6. Question: Does the next job in this kept sandbox find the dead job's loan record? Only with `sandboxPer: 'user'`. If yes: go on to step 7.
   - If no: Copy the stored login in, as for any job. This is the end.
7. Save what the dead job's CLI left, then copy the login in. This is the end. Only when the stored login has not changed since the loan, and the files are the same account's login and not older. Else the stored login stays. Login files: login files in.

- A refresh that the CLI made more than about a minute before your backend died is already saved. Only a refresh in the last minute before the watcher ran can be lost; then the user may have to sign in again.
- byoa saves files from a sandbox only when they are the same account's login and not older than the stored one, because the agent of a job can change any file.
- A job's waiting place in line also runs out about 30 s after its backend dies, so the jobs after it go on.
- The slot's lease: until its harness starts, a job renews it every minute, so a job that waits long for the login keeps its sandbox; from the harness's start it lasts the job timeout + 5 minutes. So the lease of a dead job runs out at most the job timeout + 5 minutes after its backend died.
- The job's time starts when it has the login, not when it resumed the sandbox: then byoa sets the sandbox's time again (E2B, Sprites, and Daytona for a sandbox of one job) and starts the watcher. So a job that waited in line for the login still gets its whole time, and the watcher still runs before the provider pauses the sandbox.

## How each provider pauses and times out

| | E2B | Daytona | Instabox | Sprites |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| After a job, a kept sandbox is | paused, with no process of the job kept | stopped | stopped (not Instabox's pause) | asleep, with no process of the job kept |
| A kept sandbox whose time ends (your backend died) | pauses at job + 1 min | stops after job + 1 min with no activity | has no time limit; pauses itself after 30 min with no activity (default) | held awake until job + 1 min, then sleeps |
| A sandbox that is not kept (sign-in, sign-out, models, new for each job) | killed at its time | deleted when it stops, at the latest after its time | deleted after its time, whatever its state | at its time, ends its processes and deletes its files; the next `create` deletes it |
| A sign-in with no check-in | ends 2 min after the last `finishLogin` | ends 2 min after the last `finishLogin` (whole minutes) | ends after 15 min: Instabox cannot change a sandbox's time after it starts | ends 2 min after the last `finishLogin` |
| Resume after it paused itself | byoa ends any old process first | started again; no old process runs | byoa resumes, stops and starts it, so no old process runs | byoa ends any old process first |
| A paused kept sandbox stays | with no time limit | until archived, after 7 days stopped | with no time limit | with no time limit |
| Volumes for `cliLogin` | yes, when volumes are on for your team | one shared volume, a subpath for each login | none: use `storedLogin()` | none: use `storedLogin()` |

## Removal

- `agents.signOut(user, h)` deletes the user's kept sandboxes for that harness, then signs out ([AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md#sign-out)).
- `agents.deleteSandbox(user, { harness?, sandboxKey? })` on its own destroys each matching kept sandbox. A job in it ends. The login, the MCP grants and the conversations' stored transcripts stay.
- `agents.deleteConversation(user, conversation?)` deletes a conversation (or all of the user's): its stored session and transcript, and its kept sandbox. Call it when the user deletes a chat, and with no id when you delete the user. When you delete a user, call `agents.deleteSandbox(userId)`; when you delete a project that had a key, `agents.deleteSandbox(userId, { sandboxKey: projectId })`.
- Nothing else removes a paused kept sandbox.

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/mcp

# MCP tools and the proxy

The user connects each MCP tool one time, and every agent run that your app gives it has it. The real tokens stay in your database. The agent in the sandbox gets only a job token for your proxy.

## Connect a server, one time for each user

```ts
// A server with its own sign-in (MCP authorization, OAuth 2.1 with PKCE)
const c = await agents.connectMcp(userId, 'https://mcp.notion.com/mcp', { name: 'notion' })
if (!c.connected) return Response.json({ signInUrl: c.signInUrl })  // send the browser there; it comes back to /byoa/callback

// A server that takes a token the user pasted
await agents.connectMcp(userId, 'https://mcp.example.com/mcp', { name: 'tasks', bearer: token })

await agents.listMcp(userId)            // [{ name, url }]
await agents.removeMcp(userId, 'notion')
```

- `name`: lower-case letters, digits and `-`, at most 32. A job asks for servers by this name.
- The URL must be `https://` (or `http://` on localhost). With `bearer`, byoa checks the token with one MCP `initialize`, and throws if the server refuses it.
- byoa uses Client ID Metadata Documents when the server supports them (serve `agents.clientMetadata()` at `oauth.clientMetadataUrl`), and Dynamic Client Registration only when it does not.
- The server's sign-in page sends the browser to your `oauth.redirectUrl` route, which calls `agents.finishMcp({ state, code, error })`. It finds the user from the stored `state`, so that route needs no session. A sign-in that does not finish in 15 minutes runs out; call `connectMcp` again.
- byoa refreshes each grant itself, with one refresh owner: your backend. Two jobs that need a refresh at the same time cause one refresh request: the refresh holds a lease in the store, and renews it while the authorization server answers. byoa asks the user to connect again only when the authorization server refuses the refresh token (a 4xx answer); a 5xx, a 429 or no answer fails that request only. Do not refresh or read the tokens in your app's code.

## The proxy and job tokens

Serve `agents.proxy` at `proxyUrl` and at every path below it (`<proxyUrl>/<name>`). It is a fetch handler. For each job, byoa writes an MCP config in the sandbox that points to the proxy, with a job token for that one job and one user.

- The proxy checks the job token, adds the user's real token, and sends the request on to the MCP server.
- It refuses a job token after the job ends, and for a server that the job did not get.
- Do not put your app's session check in front of it. Each of its answers has the header `x-byoa-proxy: 1`.
- No real MCP token is in the sandbox's environment, files or processes at any time. A test checks this after each job with a real MCP call ([V5](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/SPEC.md#verification)).

The same proxy is also the relay of a job on the user's OpenCode Go key (beta), at `<proxyUrl>/_plan/opencode-go/…`: it checks the job token, adds the user's key, and sends only the model requests on to OpenCode. So do not filter the paths below `proxyUrl`. See [AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md#opencode-go-a-key-not-a-sign-in-beta).

A job gets only the servers that your app names in its `mcp`. A server in `mcp` that the user has not connected gives an `error` event with code `mcp`, and the job runs without it.

## When the proxy is down

Before the harness starts, byoa checks from the job's sandbox that each MCP server of the job answers through `agents.proxy`. When the sandbox cannot reach the proxy (a wrong `proxyUrl`, a tunnel that ended, a firewall), the job does not start: `run` gives an `error` event with code `mcp` and ends with `ok: false`, and `session` throws `ProxyError`. A server that does not answer gives an `error` event with code `mcp`, and the job runs. Without this check, a harness that cannot reach a server leaves its tools out and still ends well.

## Your app's own tools

Give your app's own tools to `createAgents` as functions (`tools`): MCP server name → tool name → `{ description, input, run }`. `input` is the JSON Schema of the arguments. A job gets them by the server's name in `mcp`, as it gets a connected server. The harness calls them through `agents.proxy`, which checks the job token and calls `run(args, { user, job })` in your backend, for the user of that job. So you write no MCP server, keep no token for it, and connect nothing for each user. What `run` returns goes to the agent (a string as it is, other values as JSON); when it throws, the agent gets the message as a failed call. byoa does not check the arguments against `input`: check them in `run`.

```ts
const agents = createAgents({
  ...options,
  tools: {
    todos: {
      add_todo: {
        description: 'Add one to-do.',
        input: { type: 'object', properties: { title: { type: 'string' } }, required: ['title'] },
        run: ({ title }, { user }) => db.addTodo(user, String(title)),
      },
      list_todos: { description: "List the user's to-dos.", run: (_args, { user }) => db.todos(user) },
    },
  },
})
agents.run(userId, { harness: 'codex', task, mcp: ['todos'] })
```

## Move a grant into byoa

To move an MCP grant that the user already made elsewhere into byoa, call `agents.importMcp(userId, { name, url, oauth })` with the MCP SDK's state (`client`, `tokens`, `at`). Delete the old copy, so that the grant keeps one refresh owner.

## Call a service's other API with the user's grant

Some MCP servers have an API next to the MCP endpoint that is not MCP, such as an export. Your backend calls it with the user's grant through `agents.fetchWithGrant(userId, 'tasks', 'https://mcp.example.com/export')`: byoa adds the current token, refreshed by the one refresh owner, and gives you the response. By default, it sends the token only to the origin of that grant's MCP server. It does not follow redirects, and never gives you the token.

When the service's API is on another origin than its MCP server, name that origin in your own configuration, for the MCP server's origin. Only grants of that MCP server can go there, and only to that exact origin:

```ts
const agents = createAgents({
  ...options,
  // Margins' MCP server is on margin.rippling.computer; its export is on its Convex site
  grantOrigins: { 'https://margin.rippling.computer': ['https://helpful-tern-930.convex.site'] },
})
const r = await agents.fetchWithGrant(userId, 'margins', 'https://helpful-tern-930.convex.site/ext/export')
```

The MCP server, the sandbox and the user cannot add an origin. Each one is an exact origin: https, no path, no wildcard.

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/security

# Security

This page is [SECURITY.md](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/security.md) of the repository.

byoa handles your users' AI logins and their MCP tokens. A bug in byoa can give an attacker access to a user's Notion, Gmail or AI plan. Please tell us about each security problem that you find.

## Report a problem

- Do not open a public issue, pull request or discussion.
- Use GitHub's private report: go to the **Security** tab of this repository and click **Report a vulnerability**.
- Tell us what the problem is, how to make it occur, and what an attacker can get.
- Do not put a real user's tokens or data in the report. Use test accounts.

We will reply within 7 days. We will tell you when we fix the problem, and we will give you credit if you want it.

## Supported versions

We fix security problems in the latest release on npm (`@madeyexz/byoa`).

## Where secrets are kept

This is how byoa must keep each secret (see [SPEC.md](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/SPEC.md)). If byoa does not do this, it is a security problem.

| Secret | Where it is | Where it must never be |
|---|---|---|
| The user's Claude or ChatGPT login | By default in the app's own database, encrypted with a key that the app gives (R1.4), or as an option in a volume of that one user (R1.5); in a sandbox only while a sign-in, a job or a sign-out runs | In a sandbox between jobs, in another app, or with us |
| MCP grants (access and refresh tokens) | In the app's own database, encrypted with a key that the app gives (R2.4) | In the sandbox (R3.3), in logs, or with us |
| Job token | In the sandbox's `mcp.json`, for one job and one user (R3.1) | Valid after the job ends (R3.4) |
| A conversation's transcript (the harness's own session files) | In the conversation's kept sandbox, and a copy in the app's own database, encrypted with a key that the app gives (R5.9) | In the store without encryption, or in another user's sandbox |

The real MCP token goes only from the app's backend to the MCP server, through the proxy (R3.2). byoa is not a hosted service, so we never get your users' tokens.

## What we count as a security problem

For example:

- A real MCP token is in the sandbox's environment, files or processes (V5).
- The proxy accepts a job token after its job ends (V6), or for a different user.
- byoa keeps a copy of a user's AI login in a sandbox between jobs, stores it without encryption, or one app can use another app's login.
- Two refreshes at the same time revoke a grant, or byoa sends a refresh request from a place other than the app's backend (R2.3).
- byoa stores a grant or a conversation's transcript without encryption, or writes a token to a log.
- byoa runs a `claude` or `codex` binary that is not the published one (V11).

## What is not ours

Report these to their owners:

- Bugs in a sandbox provider (E2B, Daytona, Instabox, Sprites), in Claude Code or Codex, or in an MCP server.
- Bugs in an app that uses byoa, for example a leaked encryption key or a database that is open to the internet. The app must keep its encryption key secret and keep the proxy in its own backend.

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login

# AI login

A user's AI login stays encrypted in your app's database, and is in a sandbox only while a sign-in, a job or a sign-out runs. This page shows how byoa signs a user in to Claude Code, Codex and Grok Build, keeps the CLI's own login files, and uses them for each job. An OpenCode Go plan (beta) has no sign-in: the user gives a key, which never goes into the sandbox ([below](#opencode-go-a-key-not-a-sign-in-beta)).

| The login tokens are in | They are never in |
|---|---|
| the sign-in sandbox, until byoa destroys it | what byoa returns to your app |
| your app's database, encrypted | the job's environment variables |
| a job's sandbox, only while the job runs | a kept sandbox between jobs |
| | the state, lease, line and loan entries in the store |

This is for the default login, `storedLogin()`. With `cliLogin`, the tokens stay in the user's volume instead of the database. byoa never uses the tokens itself and never calls the labs' token endpoints. The unmodified CLI is the only client that sends them to the lab.

## Sign-in

Your app calls `agents.connectLogin(user, harness)`. byoa starts a new sandbox, installs the pinned CLI and runs its own sign-in. The user signs in on the lab's page. byoa gives your app only that page's address and, for Codex and Grok Build, a code.

The sign-in sandbox lives only while your sign-in UI checks in. Each `finishLogin` call keeps it for 2 more minutes. A sign-in lasts 15 minutes at most, as long as Codex's device code (Grok's code lasts at least 9 minutes).

| | Claude Code | Codex | Grok Build |
|---|---|---|---|
| The CLI's sign-in | `claude auth login` | `codex login --device-auth` | `grok login --device-auth` |
| What your app shows | a link on claude.com | a link on auth.openai.com, and a one-time code | a link on accounts.x.ai, and a one-time code |
| What the user does | signs in; Anthropic's page shows a code | enters the code on OpenAI's page | enters the code on xAI's page |
| How your app finishes | `finishLogin(user, 'claude', { code })` with that code; byoa types it into the CLI and waits up to 60 s | `finishLogin(user, 'codex', { waitMs })`, again until the state is no longer `pending` | the same as Codex, with `'grok'` |
| How your app checks in | `finishLogin(user, 'claude')` with no code, about every 30 s while the user is on Anthropic's page; it answers `pending` | each `finishLogin` call; keep `waitMs` short, such as 20 s | the same as Codex |
| When the user closes the sign-in | `cancelLogin(user, 'claude')` | `cancelLogin(user, 'codex')` | `cancelLogin(user, 'grok')` |
| The files the CLI writes | in `~/.claude` (`CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`): `.credentials.json` (the tokens) and `.claude.json` (the account: email, organization, plan) | in `~/.codex` (`CODEX_HOME`): `auth.json` (access token, refresh token, last refresh time) | in `~/.grok` (`GROK_HOME`): `auth.json` (the tokens and the time they end) |

Claude Code also writes a copy of `.claude.json` in `backups/` at each start. byoa removes it and does not store it.

Diagram: The sign-in sandbox, from connectLogin to the signed-in state

1. Remove an unfinished earlier sign-in. `connectLogin(user, h)` destroys this user's earlier sign-in sandbox for the harness, if one waits. Login files: no login files.
2. Create the sign-in sandbox. storedLogin: no volume. cliLogin: the user's volume at `~/.claude`, `~/.codex` or `~/.grok`. Time limit: 15 min at most.
3. Install the pinned CLI and start its sign-in. `claude auth login`, `codex login --device-auth` or `grok login --device-auth`, in the background.
4. Question: Is the lab's page shown within 30 s? If yes: go on to step 5.
   - If no: Destroy it, and throw an error. This is the end. Also when the CLI exits at once.
5. The user signs in on the lab's page. Your app shows the link, and the code of Codex or Grok Build. From now on, the sandbox lives only while your app checks in. Time limit: 2 min after the last check-in.
6. Your app calls finishLogin. Claude Code: with the code from Anthropic's page, byoa types it in; with no code, the call only checks in. Each call keeps the sandbox 2 more minutes. Time limit: waits: Claude with a code 60 s, else waitMs (default 0)
7. Question: Has the CLI ended? If yes: go on to step 8.
   - If no: Answer 'pending'. The sandbox keeps running. Time limit: until 15 min. Then call again: back to step 6.
8. Question: Did the CLI write its token file? Login files: login files in. If yes: go on to step 9.
   - If no: Destroy it, and return the CLI's error. This is the end. For example, a wrong code.
9. Keep the login. storedLogin: byoa encrypts the files into `ailogin/<user>/<h>`. cliLogin: they stay in the volume.
10. Destroy the sandbox. The state is 'signed-in'. This is the end. `login/<user>/<h>`. Login files: no login files.

- **The user closes the sign-in.** Call `agents.cancelLogin(user, harness)`. byoa destroys the sign-in sandbox at once, also when `connectLogin` is still starting it: that `connectLogin` then destroys its sandbox and throws "the sign-in was cancelled". Nothing happens when no sign-in runs. `signOut` and a new `connectLogin` for the same user and harness also end an unfinished sign-in, so one user and harness has one sign-in at most.
- **A `signOut` or `cancelLogin` while `finishLogin` saves the login wins.** `finishLogin` saves the login and the state only while its sign-in is still the one in progress; otherwise it answers the state with the error "the sign-in was cancelled". With `storedLogin()`, a login that `finishLogin` saved just before the cancel is put back as it was (a backend that dies in between may leave it); with `cliLogin`, the login that the CLI wrote stays in the volume. A sign-in sandbox that the provider could not destroy stays named in the sign-in's entry, so the next `cancelLogin` or `signOut` destroys it. `finishLogin` right after `connectLogin`, while its sandbox still starts, answers `pending`.
- **Your app stops calling `finishLogin`** (the user left, or your backend died). On E2B, Daytona and Sprites, the sandbox ends 2 minutes after the last check-in, with any login files in it. Instabox cannot change a sandbox's time after it starts, so there an unfinished sign-in ends after 15 minutes, unless you call `cancelLogin`.
- `finishLogin` after the sandbox is gone, or after 15 minutes, answers "the sign-in ran out; start it again".
- The to-do example's `page.html` checks in, and sends `cancelLogin` when the user closes the sign-in or the page.
- The state (`agents.loginState(user, h)`) is `signed-in`, `signed-out` or `expired`, with no token in it. With `storedLogin()`, it is `signed-out` whenever no login is stored.

## Where the login stays between jobs

| | In your app's database (the default, `storedLogin()`) | In a volume of the user (`cliLogin`) |
|---|---|---|
| How it gets there | byoa reads the CLI's files from the sign-in sandbox and encrypts them together with AES-256-GCM, with your `encryptionKey` or the key you give `storedLogin`. The entry's name is part of the encryption, so the entry cannot be moved to another user. | The sign-in sandbox mounts the user's volume at `~/.claude` or `~/.codex`, and the CLI writes its files there. |
| Where it is | one entry for each user and harness, `ailogin/<user>/<harness>`, as `v1.<iv>.<ciphertext>`. It is the only copy between jobs. | the volume `byoa-<app>-<harness>-<first 24 hex of sha256(user)>`, with the files as the CLI wrote them |
| In a job | byoa copies the files in and takes them out again (below). | Every job sandbox of that user and harness mounts the same volume. byoa never reads or copies the files. The store keeps only the state. |
| Providers | all | providers with volumes: E2B (when volumes are on for your team) and Daytona, not Instabox or Sprites |

To keep the logins in a table of their own, with a key of their own, so that you can give them their own access rules and backups, see [Stores and Convex](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/stores.md#a-table-of-its-own-for-the-ai-logins). To use the volume, pass `login: cliLogin` (from `@madeyexz/byoa`).

The labs' published terms limit where these tokens may be stored. Each app checks them: see [Lab rules](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/lab-rules.md).

## One job, step by step

This is a job with the default `storedLogin()`. First byoa checks that the store has the user's login. If it does not, the job stops with `LoginError` (in `run`, an `error` event with code `signed-out`) and the state becomes `signed-out`. `close()` runs steps 4 to 7, also when the job failed.

1. **Take the lease.** Two sandboxes must not refresh one login at the same time, because the CLIs rotate their refresh tokens. byoa writes the lease `ailoginlease/<user>/<harness>` with compare-and-set. By default, the jobs of one user and harness share the lease while the login is not due for a refresh (see [Jobs at the same time](#jobs-at-the-same-time-the-shared-login)). When a job must wait, it waits in line, in the order the jobs came (`ailoginline/<user>/<harness>`), and `onWait` gets `{ for: 'login', ahead }`. It waits with no time limit, unless you set `storedLogin({ waitMs })`. The lease ends by itself after the job timeout + 5 minutes, so a lost backend does not lock it.
2. **Copy the login in.** byoa decrypts the entry in your backend and writes the files into the job's sandbox, `chmod 600`. It remembers which version of the entry it read, and writes a loan record for this sandbox (`ailoginloan/<user>/<harness>/<sandbox>`). It also starts a watcher in the sandbox: at the job timeout + 45 s, the watcher removes the login files, before the provider pauses the sandbox at the job timeout + 1 minute. `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` or `CODEX_HOME` points the CLI at the files: a folder path, not a token.
3. **The CLI runs, and may refresh.** The unmodified CLI uses its tokens to reach the lab. When its access token is due, it refreshes it and writes its own files again. About every 60 s, byoa saves what the CLI changed (a checkpoint), as in step 4.
4. **Save back what changed.** If the files changed, byoa encrypts them and writes them over the entry, only if the entry is still the version from step 2 (compare-and-set). If the user signed in again meanwhile, the newer entry stays. byoa saves files from a sandbox only when they are the same account's login and not older than the stored one, because the agent can change any file.
5. **Remove the files.** byoa deletes the login files, Claude's backups and the loan record. If it cannot delete the files, it destroys the sandbox instead of keeping it.
6. **Give the lease back.** The next job of this user and harness can take it. This also happens when step 4 or 5 fails.
7. **Pause or destroy the sandbox.** With `sandboxPer: 'user'` (the default), byoa pauses the user's kept sandbox for the next job, with no login in it. With `'job'`, it destroys the sandbox.

With `cliLogin` there is no lease and no copy. The volume is mounted in the job's sandbox, the CLI refreshes the files in place, and byoa saves nothing back and removes nothing.

When your backend dies during step 3, `close()` never runs. The watcher, the checkpoints and the loan record then keep the login safe and up to date: [Sandbox lifecycle](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/sandbox-lifecycle.md#when-your-backend-dies-during-a-job) shows how.

## Jobs at the same time: the shared login

By default, the jobs of one user and harness share the login, for Claude Code, Codex and Grok Build. Each job gets its own copy in its own sandbox (a `sandboxKey` for each job, or `sandboxPer: 'job'`), and the jobs run at the same time. Jobs in one sandbox still run one after the other: see [Running agents](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/running-agents.md#jobs-at-the-same-time).

Diagram: How a job takes the shared login

1. Question: Will the CLI refresh the login before this job could end? Within the lease time, the job timeout + 5 min. If no: go on to step 2.
   - If yes, or not known: Hold the login alone. The job marks that it waits, so no new job joins. When the sharing jobs end, it takes the lease alone. The CLI refreshes, step 4 saves the new login, and the jobs after it share again. Time limit: lease: { alone: { id, until } }, after want.
2. Share the login. This is the end. The job adds itself to the lease's shared list and gets its own copy of the login. More jobs can join. Time limit: lease: { shared: { job1: until, job2: until } }.

- To answer the question, byoa reads only the time the access token ends from the login files, and no token: `expiresAt` in Claude Code's `.credentials.json`, the token's `exp` in Codex's `auth.json`, `expires_at` in Grok Build's `auth.json`. The CLIs refresh about 5 minutes before their access token ends. Claude Code's token lasts 8 hours, Codex's 10 days, Grok Build's 6 hours. When Codex's `auth.json` has no such time, byoa uses 8 days after the last refresh. When byoa cannot tell, the answer is yes.
- If two sharing jobs both save a change, the first save wins (step 4).
- One risk stays: the CLIs also refresh when the lab answers 401 to a token that has not run out. If two sandboxes get that answer at the same time, both refresh, one refresh fails, and the user may have to sign in again.
- To hold the login one job at a time instead, pass `login: storedLogin({ parallel: false })`.

## OpenCode Go: a key, not a sign-in (beta)

**Beta.** No real OpenCode Go key has run this yet. byoa's tests use a stand-in for OpenCode's API, with the real Claude Code and Codex, locally and on E2B. The real check ([V20](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/SPEC.md#verification)) has not run.

OpenCode Go is OpenCode's subscription. byoa uses it as a plan, not a harness: it does not run the `opencode` CLI. It gives open models and others, such as Kimi, GLM, DeepSeek, Qwen and MiniMax, and the job still runs the unmodified `claude` or `codex`.

There is no sign-in page. The user creates an API key in [OpenCode's Console](https://opencode.ai/console) (`oc_sk_…`), and your app gives it to byoa one time:

```ts
const r = await agents.connectKey(userId, 'opencode-go', key)   // { state: 'signed-in' }; or 'no-plan', or an error
const models = await agents.listModels(userId, 'opencode-go')    // the plan's models, from OpenCode's API: no sandbox
agents.run(userId, { harness: 'codex', plan: 'opencode-go', model: 'kimi-k3.1-pro', task })
```

Diagram: A job on the user's OpenCode Go key

1. Your app gives byoa the key, one time. `connectKey(user, 'opencode-go', key)`. byoa checks the key with OpenCode and keeps it encrypted in your store, as it keeps MCP grants.
2. A job runs with plan 'opencode-go'. The unmodified Claude Code or Codex, with a Go model, and a config folder with no lab login. Claude Code gets `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`; Codex gets a model provider for this job only.
3. The harness sends its model requests to your proxy. To `<proxyUrl>/_plan/opencode-go/…`, with the job token. Only the model APIs go through, and only during the job.
4. The proxy adds the key and sends them on to OpenCode. This is the end. With the harness's own user agent and session id, as OpenCode asks. The key never goes into the sandbox.

- **A model of the plan.** A job with a plan needs a Go model: `model` in `run`, or `createAgents({ models: { 'opencode-go': { model } } })`. `listModels(userId, 'opencode-go')` lists them from OpenCode's API with the user's key, with no sandbox. The free models (`…-free`) are not in the list: OpenCode serves them only to its own client.
- **States.** `loginState(userId, 'opencode-go')` is `signed-in`; `expired` when OpenCode refuses the key (401: a wrong, revoked or expired key; the user makes a new one); or `no-plan` when the key's workspace has no Go plan (403). A job that gets one of these from OpenCode gives an `error` event with that code. When OpenCode answers 429 and its usage meter says that a limit is used up, the job's error is `usage-limit`, with the meter's `resetsAt` ([When the plan is used up](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/running-agents.md#when-the-plan-is-used-up)). `signOut(userId, 'opencode-go')` deletes the key.
- **Jobs at the same time.** A key does not rotate, so a user's jobs with it run at the same time, with no lease.
- **Terms.** OpenCode's terms say the user uses its services "only for your own internal use, and not on behalf of or for the benefit of any third party". A job with the user's own key for the user's own task is arguably that, but it is not clearly allowed. Ask OpenCode (help@anoma.ly) before your app offers it. See [Lab rules](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/lab-rules.md).

Sources: [OpenCode Go](https://opencode.ai/docs/console/go), [OpenCode Terms of Use](https://opencode.ai/legal/terms-of-service).

## Sign-out

`agents.signOut(user, harness)` deletes the user's kept sandboxes for this harness, signs out with the CLI so that the lab can revoke the login, and deletes the login.

Diagram: Sign-out, with the default storedLogin

1. Destroy the user's kept sandboxes for this harness. `signOut(user, h)` calls `deleteSandbox(user, { harness: h })`. A job in one of them ends. Login files: no login files.
2. Question: Is a login stored? `ailogin/<user>/<h>`. If yes: go on to step 3.
   - If no: Skip the CLI sign-out. Then go on to step 5.
3. Sign out with the CLI in a new sandbox. Takes the login lease alone, writes the files in, and runs `claude auth logout`, `codex logout` or `grok logout`, so that the lab can revoke the login. If this fails, byoa goes on. Time limit: 5 min; not kept; waits in line for the lease. Login files: login files in.
4. Destroy it, give the lease back. Login files: no login files.
5. Delete the stored login. The state is 'signed-out'. This is the end. `ailogin/<user>/<h>` is deleted.

With `cliLogin`, sign-out also destroys an unfinished sign-in sandbox, signs out in a sandbox that mounts the user's volume, and deletes the volume.

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/agent-tools

# Give your agent tools

The agent in each job is the user's own Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build. You decide what it can do in that job: which tools it can call, what it knows, and what it may do in its sandbox. This page shows each way, and which one to choose.

| The agent needs | Give it | Where it runs | Who connects it |
|---|---|---|---|
| your app's own data and actions (to-dos, mail, documents) | [your app's tools](#your-apps-own-tools), as functions in `createAgents({ tools })` | in your backend | nobody: the job token says which user |
| a service where the user has an account (Notion, Gmail) | [the user's MCP server](#the-users-mcp-servers), with `connectMcp` once | at the service | the user, one time |
| to know how to do a task, or your app's rules | [skills and AGENTS.md](#skills-and-agentsmd), in `setup` | files in the sandbox | nobody |
| skills and MCP servers as one package | [a plugin](#plugins) (Agent Plugins 1.0), in `plugins` | files, and the user's servers | the user, for each server |
| a shell, files, packages and the network | [the sandbox itself](#what-the-agent-can-do-in-its-sandbox), with `access: 'full'` | in the sandbox | nobody |

Name the tools of each job in its `mcp`. A job gets only the servers that you name, and none by default.

## Which one to choose

Diagram: Which way gives the agent an ability

1. Question: Is it your app's own data or action? If no: go on to step 2.
   - If yes: Your app's own tools. This is the end. `tools: { todos: { add_todo: { description, input, run } } }`, and `mcp: ['todos']` in the job.
2. Question: Does the user have an account at a service with an MCP server? If no: go on to step 3.
   - If yes: The user's MCP server. This is the end. `connectMcp(user, url, { name })` once, and `mcp: ['notion']` in each job.
3. Question: Is it knowledge, a how-to or a rule, not an action? If no: go on to step 4.
   - If yes: A skill or AGENTS.md. This is the end. `setup: { agentsMd, skills }`. The harness reads them from the job folder.
4. Question: Does it need a shell, files, packages or the open network? If no: go on to step 5.
   - If yes: The sandbox, with access: 'full'. This is the end. The default. The agent installs and runs what it needs in its own sandbox.
5. Write it as one of your app's tools. This is the end. An API that your backend can call becomes a function in `tools`. The agent then calls it through the proxy, and your backend keeps every key.

Keep secrets out of the sandbox. A key that a tool needs stays in your backend, in the tool's `run` or in the user's grant. Never put a token in `setup`, the task, the environment or a file: the agent can read everything in its sandbox.

## Your app's own tools

Give your app's tools to `createAgents` as functions: MCP server name → tool name → `{ description, input, run }`. A job gets a group by its name in `mcp`, as it gets a connected server. You write no MCP server, keep no token for it, and connect nothing for each user.

```ts
const agents = createAgents({
  ...options,
  tools: {
    todos: {
      add_todo: {
        description: 'Add one to-do.',
        input: { type: 'object', properties: { title: { type: 'string' } }, required: ['title'] },
        run: ({ title }, { user }) => db.addTodo(user, String(title)),
      },
      list_todos: { description: "List the user's to-dos.", run: (_args, { user }) => db.todos(user) },
    },
  },
})
agents.run(userId, { harness: 'codex', task, mcp: ['todos'] })
```

Diagram: A call to one of your app's tools

1. The agent calls todos.add_todo. The harness sends an MCP `tools/call` to `<proxyUrl>/todos`, with the job token.
2. Question: Is the job token good, and did the job get todos? If yes: go on to step 3.
   - If no: Refuse the call. This is the end. The job ended, or its mcp did not name todos.
3. run(args, { user, job }) in your backend. `user` is the job's user, from the token. Never take the user from the arguments.
4. Question: Did run throw? If no: go on to step 5.
   - If yes: The agent gets a failed call. This is the end. With the error's message. The agent can try again or tell the user.
5. The agent gets the result. This is the end. A string as it is, and any other value as JSON.

- `input` is the JSON Schema of the arguments, which the harness shows to the model. byoa does not check the arguments against it: check them in `run`.
- Write a `description` that says when to use the tool. The model reads it to choose.
- Names: a server is lower-case letters, digits and `-`, at most 32; a tool is letters, digits, `_` and `-`, at most 64.
- Give a job only the groups it needs. A to-do job gets `todos`, not your billing tools.

## The user's MCP servers

The user connects a service one time, and each job that you give it can use it. The real token stays in your database, and the proxy adds it to each call. [MCP tools and the proxy](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/mcp.md) has the sign-in routes and the details.

```ts
const c = await agents.connectMcp(userId, 'https://mcp.notion.com/mcp', { name: 'notion' })
if (!c.connected) return Response.json({ signInUrl: c.signInUrl })  // the browser comes back to your redirectUrl route
agents.run(userId, { harness: 'claude', task, mcp: ['notion', 'todos'] })
```

Diagram: A call to the user's MCP server

1. The agent calls notion.search. To `<proxyUrl>/notion`, with the job token. The sandbox has no Notion token.
2. Question: Is the job token good, and did the job get notion? If yes: go on to step 3.
   - If no: Refuse the call. This is the end.
3. Take the user's grant. From your database, decrypted in your backend. byoa refreshes it first when it is due, with one refresh owner.
4. Send the call on to Notion's MCP server. This is the end. With the real token. The answer goes back to the agent; the token does not.

A server in `mcp` that the user has not connected gives an `error` event with code `mcp`, and the job runs without it. Before the harness starts, byoa checks from the sandbox that each server answers through the proxy ([When the proxy is down](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/mcp.md#when-the-proxy-is-down)).

## Skills and AGENTS.md

A skill teaches the agent how to do one kind of task, in the [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io) format: a folder with a `SKILL.md` and any files it needs. AGENTS.md has the rules for every task of the job, such as your app's voice or what the agent must not do.

```ts
agents.run(userId, {
  harness: 'claude', task, mcp: ['todos'],
  setup: {
    agentsMd: 'You are the to-do assistant of Acme. Change only the to-dos that the user asks about.',
    skills: [{ name: 'weekly-review', files: { 'SKILL.md': weeklyReviewSkill } }],
  },
})
```

byoa writes them into a new job folder, where each harness reads them:

```text
~/work                          the job folder, new for each job
├── AGENTS.md                   setup.agentsMd
├── CLAUDE.md                   the same text, for Claude Code
├── .claude/skills/<name>/      the skills, for Claude Code
├── .agents/skills/<name>/      the skills, for Codex and Grok Build
├── .codex/config.toml          Codex's MCP config: each server at the proxy, with the job token
├── .grok/config.toml           Grok Build's MCP config: the same (it reads the folder with --trust)
└── .byoa/
    ├── mcp.json                Claude Code's MCP config: the same
    └── task.md                 the task
```

## Plugins

A plugin in the Agent Plugins 1.0 format is a folder with `plugin.json`, `skills/<name>/` and `mcp.json`. Read it with `readPlugin(readPluginDir(dir))` (`readPluginDir` from `@madeyexz/byoa/node`), and give it to a job in `plugins`:

```ts
import { readPlugin } from '@madeyexz/byoa'
import { readPluginDir } from '@madeyexz/byoa/node'

const plugin = readPlugin(readPluginDir('./plugins/research'))
agents.run(userId, { harness: 'codex', task, plugins: [plugin] })
```

- The job gets the plugin's skills, and each of its MCP servers through the user's grant of the same name. So the user connects each server with `connectMcp` under that name; byoa never gives the plugin's URL to the harness, only the proxy's.
- Only Streamable HTTP servers load. A stdio server would run inside the sandbox with no proxy, so byoa skips it and lists it in `plugin.skipped`.

## What the agent can do in its sandbox

With `access: 'full'` (the default), the agent has every tool of its harness, with no approval: a shell, file changes and the network. So it can install a package, run a script, clone a repository or call a public API, in a sandbox that is the job's alone.

- **Files stay in a kept sandbox.** With the default `sandboxPer: 'user'`, files that the agent writes outside `~/work` are there in the user's next job. The job folder `~/work` is new each time. With `sandboxPer: 'job'`, nothing stays. See [Sandbox lifecycle](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/sandbox-lifecycle.md).
- **Results come back as events.** The agent's answer is the `end` event's `result`, and its tool calls are `tool_call` and `tool_result` events. To get a file out, give the agent a tool that saves it, such as `save_report` in your `tools`, or open the job with `agents.session` and read the file yourself with `s.sandbox.run`.
- **Limit it with `access: 'read-only'`** when the agent needs only its MCP tools, such as in a mail client. It can then call the job's MCP tools and read files, but not change a file or reach the network by itself. See [Running agents](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/running-agents.md#what-the-agent-may-do).

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/running-agents

# Running agents

Your app runs a job with `agents.run`. byoa takes the user's sandbox, loads the user's setup, runs the user's own harness on the user's own plan, and streams its events. To continue a chat, give its jobs one `conversation` id. For a program of your own around the harness, use `agents.session`; for a harness outside byoa's sandboxes, `agents.jobToken`.

## Run a job and stream its events

```ts
for await (const ev of agents.run(userId, {
  harness: 'claude',                   // 'claude' | 'codex' | 'grok' | 'fake'
  task,                                // the user's request
```
