```ts
  mcp: ['notion', 'todos'],            // the servers this job gets; default none
  setup: { agentsMd, skills },         // AGENTS.md (and CLAUDE.md for Claude Code); skills: [{ name, files: { 'SKILL.md': '...' } }]
})) {
  // ev.type: 'start' | 'text' | 'tool_call' | 'tool_result' | 'permission' | 'error' | 'turn' | 'end'
}
```

- The events are the same for every harness. The schema is in the [API reference](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/api.md#events-one-schema-for-every-harness).
- `run` does not throw when a job fails. It gives `error` events (`code`: `signed-out`, `expired`, `no-plan`, `usage-limit`, `rate-limited`, `harness`, `sandbox`, `mcp` or `conversation`), and always ends with one `end` event (`ok`, `result`, `usage`, and in a conversation `session`). On `signed-out` or `expired`, show the sign-in again (for `plan: 'opencode-go'`, ask for a new key). On `no-plan`, tell the user that the key's workspace has no OpenCode Go plan. On `usage-limit` and `rate-limited`, see [When the plan is used up](#when-the-plan-is-used-up).
- byoa writes skills where each harness reads them (`.claude/skills/`, `.agents/skills/`), AGENTS.md (and CLAUDE.md for Claude Code) from one source, and the MCP config in each harness's own format. `plugins` adds the skills and MCP servers of an Agent Plugins package (`readPlugin(readPluginDir(dir))`).
- byoa installs the pinned version of each harness in each sandbox, so a new pin reaches every user at their next job.
- If the client goes away, stop the loop (or call `return()` on the generator). byoa still ends the job token, takes the login out, and pauses or destroys the sandbox.

## When the plan is used up

Each plan has limits: Claude's and ChatGPT's 5-hour and weekly limits, Grok's plan limit, OpenCode Go's 5-hour, weekly and monthly limits. When the user's plan is used up, the job ends with an `error` of code `usage-limit`. Its `resetsAt` (ms since 1970) is when the plan resets, when the tool says: Claude Code and Codex say it, and for OpenCode Go byoa asks OpenCode's usage meter; Grok Build does not say it. `message` is the tool's own words.

```ts
if (ev.type === 'error' && ev.code === 'usage-limit') {
  show(ev.resetsAt ? `Your plan is used up. It resets at ${new Date(ev.resetsAt).toLocaleString()}.` : ev.message)
}
```

byoa keeps the used-up plan in the store, for that user and harness (with `plan: 'opencode-go'`, for that user and plan, with both harnesses), until `resetsAt`, or for 15 minutes when the tool did not say. Until then, a job of that user and harness ends at once with the same error, and starts no sandbox. To check before a job, with no sandbox:

```ts
const limit = await agents.usageLimit(userId, 'codex')   // undefined, or { message, resetsAt?, until }
if (limit) return show(`Your plan is used up until ${new Date(limit.until).toLocaleString()}.`)
```

A new sign-in (`finishLogin` that says `signed-in`), a new key (`connectKey`), `signOut`, and a job that works end it. One user's plan is one user's: an app that runs every visitor on one user's login (such as byoa's own help agent) gets one check for all of them.

`rate-limited` is a refusal for now: too many requests, or the lab is overloaded. byoa keeps nothing; try again in a moment. A login that the lab refuses is `expired`, as before.

byoa reads each CLI's own code first, and its words only when the code is missing: Claude Code's API error and its `rate_limit_event`, Codex's `codexErrorInfo` and its rate limits, Grok Build's `error_kind`. These checks use output in the shape that each pinned binary writes; no check has run a real plan out.

## What the agent may do

By default (`access: 'full'`), the agent has every tool of its harness, with no approval: a shell, file changes and the network. This is for a sandbox that is the job's alone. An app whose agent must only use its MCP tools, such as a to-do list or a mail client, gives the job `access: 'read-only'`:

```ts
agents.run(userId, { harness: 'codex', task, mcp: ['mail'], setup: { skills }, access: 'read-only' })
```

The agent can then call the job's MCP tools and read files, so the harness can still read its skills and AGENTS.md. It cannot change a file or reach the network by itself. byoa only sets each CLI's own options: Codex runs in its own sandbox with a read-only permission profile, which also denies its commands Codex's home folder (CODEX_HOME), where its login is, Claude Code gets only its tools that read, and Grok Build gets rules that deny its shell, file changes and web fetch (and its web search finds nothing); each tool a CLI refuses is a `permission` event or an error for the model. Apart from Codex's home folder, `read-only` does not hide files: the agent can read each file that its user can read, also Claude Code's and Grok Build's login files. Use it always with `localSandbox()` on a user's own computer, where the sandbox isolates nothing.

## Sandbox modes

| | Where a job runs | Jobs of one user and harness at the same time |
|---|---|---|
| `sandboxPer: 'user'` (the default) | the user's one kept sandbox for that harness, paused between jobs | one; the others wait in line, in the order they came |
| a `sandboxKey` for each job | one kept sandbox for each key, such as a project or a conversation, each with its own lease | one for each key |
| a `conversation` for each job | one kept sandbox for each conversation, whose `~/work` stays | one for each conversation |
| `sandboxPer: 'job'` | a new sandbox, destroyed after the job | all of them |

```ts
agents.run(userId, { harness: 'claude', task, sandboxKey: projectId })  // one kept sandbox for each project
const agents = createAgents({ ...options, sandboxPer: 'job' })          // a new sandbox for each job; default 'user'
```

A job waits in line with no time limit. To make it fail after a time, set `createAgents({ waitMs })`, for example on a short-lived backend such as a Convex action. [Sandbox lifecycle](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/sandbox-lifecycle.md) shows each step of each mode, and what each provider does.

## Conversations

A job with a `conversation` id continues the harness's own session of the earlier jobs with that id, so the agent knows what the user said and what it did. Use your chat thread's id:

```ts
// the second job knows what the first was told
const chat = {
  harness: 'claude', conversation: chatId,
} as const
agents.run(userId, { ...chat, task: 'My name is Ann.' })
agents.run(userId, { ...chat, task: 'What is my name?' })
```

- The first job's `start` event has `resumed: false`, the next ones `resumed: true`. The `end` event has `session`, the harness's own session id.
- The conversation has its own kept sandbox (its id is the `sandboxKey`; give no other one), so its jobs run one at a time, and its `~/work` stays from job to job: the agent finds the files it wrote. byoa replaces only its own files there.
- byoa keeps a copy of the transcript, encrypted in your store, so the conversation goes on when the provider loses the sandbox. A transcript longer than `createAgents({ transcriptBytes })` (default 700 000 bytes) is not kept; then a lost sandbox loses the conversation, and the next job gives an `error` with code `conversation` and starts again.
- `agents.deleteConversation(userId, chatId)` deletes it, with its sandbox. [Sandbox lifecycle](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/sandbox-lifecycle.md#what-carries-over-between-jobs) has what carries over between jobs.
- The harness must be the same for each job of a conversation: each harness has its own sessions.

### More messages while a job runs (steering)

`run` returns a `Job`. `job.send(message)` gives the running agent one more message, with each harness:

```ts
const job = agents.run(userId, { harness: 'codex', task, conversation: chatId })
for await (const ev of job) {
  if (ev.type === 'turn') show(ev.result)     // one turn ended; the agent now reads the next message
  if (ev.type === 'end') show(ev.result)      // the turn that answered the last message
}
// from another request of the user, while the job runs:
await job.send('Also add the dates.')         // true; false once the job ended
```

Codex and Grok Build take a message that comes during a turn into that turn: the agent reads it at its next step, and answers both in the same turn. Claude Code takes it when the turn ends, as the next turn. A message that comes after a turn ended starts the next turn. byoa uses only each CLI's own protocol, through a small driver script in the sandbox: Claude Code's stream-json input, Codex's app server (`turn/steer`) and Grok Build's Agent Client Protocol (`x.ai/interject`). Once the job ended, `send` returns false: send the message as the next job of the conversation.

## Jobs at the same time

Your app chooses how one user's agents run. It can mix the three ways:

```ts
// 1. A queue: jobs of one sandbox run one after the other, in the order they came
agents.run(userId, { harness: 'claude', task, onWait: ({ for: what, ahead }) => show(`${ahead} jobs before yours (${what})`) })

// 2. Several messages to one agent, which reads them all and decides the order itself
agents.run(userId, { harness: 'codex', task: ['water the plants', 'call mom', 'plan the week'] })

// 3. Several sandboxes at once: a sandbox key for each agent (or sandboxPer: 'job')
const jobs = projects.map((p) => agents.run(userId, { harness: 'codex', task, sandboxKey: p.id }))  // read each stream; they run together
```

- **A queue.** `onWait` gets `{ for, ahead }` each time the number of jobs ahead changes. `for` is `'sandbox'` while the job waits for its sandbox, and `'login'` while it waits for the AI login.
- **Several messages.** byoa gives the agent all of them in one task, with a line that tells it to read them all first and then decide the order. It is one job, in one sandbox.
- **Several sandboxes.** Jobs of one user in different sandboxes run at the same time with one sign-in, for every harness. They share the login while it is not due for a refresh. One risk stays, and `storedLogin({ parallel: false })` turns sharing off: see [AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md#jobs-at-the-same-time-the-shared-login).

## Models and effort

`run(userId, { harness, task, model, effort })` runs the harness with that model and effort, with each CLI's own flags: Claude Code's `--model` (an alias such as `opus`, or a full name) and `--effort` (`low` to `max`), Codex's `-m` and `model_reasoning_effort`, Grok Build's `-m` and `--reasoning-effort`. Without them, a job gets the harness's default from `createAgents({ models })`, else the CLI's own.

```ts
const agents = createAgents({ ...options, models: { claude: { model: 'opus' }, codex: { effort: 'high' } } })

const models = await agents.listModels(userId, 'codex')   // [{ id: 'gpt-6.2-sol', isDefault: true, efforts: ['low', ...] }, ...]
agents.run(userId, { harness: 'codex', task, model: models[0].id, effort: 'high' })
```

`agents.listModels(userId, harness)` lists the models that the user's plan can use, as the CLI lists them with the user's login: `[{ id, name, description, isDefault, efforts, resolved? }]`. `id` is what `model` takes, and `efforts` what `effort` takes; `resolved` (Claude Code) is the full name of an alias. Each call starts a sandbox, so keep the list for a while. It throws `LoginError` when the harness is not signed in. With `session`, `s.args` has the flags for the job's model and effort, for your own command line.

A job on the user's OpenCode Go key (beta) passes `plan: 'opencode-go'` and a Go model; `listModels(userId, 'opencode-go')` lists them with no sandbox. See [AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md#opencode-go-a-key-not-a-sign-in-beta).

## A program of your own around the harness

An app that runs its own program around the unmodified harness (for example its own server, which starts `claude`, `codex` or `grok` itself) opens the job with `agents.session` instead. It gets the same sandbox, login, pinned harness and job token, and runs its own command:

```ts
const s = await agents.session(userId, { harness: 'claude', mcp: ['notion'] })
try {
  // s.bin: the pinned claude binary; s.env: its login folder, the job token and its MCP start timeout; s.mcp: [{ name, url }] at the proxy
  await s.sandbox.run(`my-server --claude ${s.bin}`, { cwd: s.work, env: s.env })
} finally { await s.close() }  // ends the job token, takes the AI login out, and pauses the user's sandbox
```

`session` throws `LoginError` when the harness is not signed in, and `ProxyError` when the sandbox cannot reach the proxy.

## A harness outside byoa's sandboxes

A program outside byoa's sandboxes, such as a harness on the user's own computer, gets a job token with no sandbox: `const t = await agents.jobToken(userId, { mcp: ['notion'] })` gives `t.token` and `t.mcp` (the proxy URLs), with the same rules as a job's token, until `t.close()`. Send `t.token` as `Authorization: Bearer` to each `t.mcp[].url`.

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/providers

# Sandbox providers

Each sandbox provider is one adapter with one interface. Version 1 has E2B, Daytona, Instabox and Sprites (Fly.io), and a local sandbox for development and tests. To change the provider, change the adapter that you give `createAgents`:

```ts
import { e2b } from '@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/e2b'
const agents = createAgents({ ...options, sandbox: e2b({ apiKey }) })   // or daytona({ apiKey }), instabox({ apiKey }), sprites({ token })
```

`e2b()`, `daytona()` and `instabox()` read their API key from `E2B_API_KEY`, `DAYTONA_API_KEY` or `INSTABOX_API_KEY` when you give none, and `sprites()` reads its token from `SPRITES_TOKEN`. The sandbox must reach your `proxyUrl`. [Sandbox lifecycle](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/sandbox-lifecycle.md#how-each-provider-pauses-and-times-out) compares how each provider pauses and times out.

| | E2B | Daytona | Instabox | Sprites | Local |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Import | `@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/e2b` | `@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/daytona` | `@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/instabox` | `@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/sprites` | `@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/local` |
| Package to install | `e2b` | `@daytona/sdk` | none | none | none |
| Between jobs, a kept sandbox is | paused | stopped | stopped | asleep (Sprites' own pause) | a folder |
| Volumes for `cliLogin` | yes, when volumes are on for your team | one shared volume, a subpath for each login | none: use `storedLogin()` | none: use `storedLogin()` | folders |
| A sign-in with no check-in ends | 2 min after the last `finishLogin` | 2 min after the last `finishLogin` | after 15 min (no keepAlive) | 2 min after the last `finishLogin` | 2 min after the last `finishLogin` |
| Network | every public domain | Tier 1 and 2: allowed domains only | every public domain | every public domain | this computer |

## E2B

Use `e2b({ apiKey?, template?, timeoutMs? })`. It needs the `e2b` package.

- The default template is named `byoa`, and a new E2B account does not have it: the first job then fails with `404: template 'byoa' not found`. Build it one time for each pin change with `buildE2BTemplate()`, or pass `e2b({ template: 'base' })`. Any template with Node 20 or later works: byoa then installs the pinned harness in each new sandbox (about 10 seconds).
- `pause` ends the sandbox's processes, then takes a full snapshot, with the memory: the next job's resume takes about 0.3 seconds, and node and the harness start warm. When E2B refuses it, because it still saves the sandbox's previous snapshot, byoa takes a snapshot of the files only; the next resume then boots the sandbox again and reads its disk cold, which can add 10 to 20 seconds. E2B keeps a paused sandbox with no time limit, and charges no compute for it.
- A kept sandbox that times out (a crash, a lost network) is paused, not killed. When byoa resumes a sandbox that paused itself, it ends any old process first.

## Daytona

Use `daytona({ apiKey?, client?, snapshot?, volume?, timeoutMs? })`. It needs `@daytona/sdk`.

- `pause` stops the sandbox, and `resume` starts it, also from archived (more slowly). A kept sandbox is not ephemeral and has no time to live; Daytona archives it after 7 days stopped. A sandbox for one job is ephemeral: Daytona deletes it when it stops, and at the latest after its time.
- Daytona allows 100 volumes for each organization, so with `cliLogin` the adapter keeps every user's AI login in its own subpath of one shared volume (`byoa` by default). A sandbox mounts only that user's subpath.
- On Daytona Tier 1 and Tier 2, a sandbox can reach only [allowed domains](https://www.daytona.io/docs/en/network-limits), so serve `agents.proxy` on one of them (for example `*.convex.site`), or use Tier 3 or higher. `*.workers.dev` is on Daytona's list but does not work: a Worker's address has two labels below it (`<worker>.<account>.workers.dev`), and Daytona does not resolve those.

## Instabox

Use `instabox({ apiKey?, apiUrl?, template?, snapshot?, timeoutMs? })`. It calls Instabox's HTTP API itself, so it needs no package.

- Each sandbox starts from the `agent-browser` template (Node 22, user `user`, home `/data/home`), or from a snapshot that you name (`snapshot`).
- byoa stops the user's sandbox after each job (not Instabox's pause), so the next job starts it again with its files and no process of the last one. A sandbox that paused itself (idle for 30 minutes, or at the plan's longest run) is booted again. A sandbox for one job is deleted after it, and at the latest at its `timeoutMs`.
- byoa gives a sandbox none of your account's Vault items or org Secrets, and leaves its commands out of Instabox's command history, which would otherwise keep their output (and so the AI login that byoa reads back).
- Instabox has no volumes, so `cliLogin` does not work there; the default stored login does. Instabox sandboxes reach every public domain, so a tunnel works for `proxyUrl`.
- On the free plan, a workspace has one sandbox in all, also when it is stopped (so one user with one kept sandbox, or one job), and three starts a minute (byoa waits when Instabox answers 429). A run starts with 2 hours before Instabox pauses the sandbox, and grows to 8 hours at most while the sandbox is in use ([limits](https://instabox.sh/docs/account/limits)).

## Sprites

Use `sprites({ token?, apiUrl?, init?, timeoutMs? })`. A [Sprite](https://fly.io/sprites) is a Linux VM of Fly.io with a disk that stays. The adapter calls the Sprites API itself, so it needs no package. Make a Sprites token of your Fly.io organization ([how](https://docs.fly.io/sprites/cli/authentication)), and set it as `SPRITES_TOKEN`.

- Each Sprite has Ubuntu, Node, git and the labs' CLIs; user `sprite`, home `/home/sprite`. byoa still installs its pinned harness (about 5 seconds). Sprites has no templates: to add what your jobs need, such as a clone of a repository, pass a shell command as `init`, which runs once in each new Sprite, with the network and sudo.
- A Sprite sleeps by itself about 30 seconds after nothing runs in it, also when a process of byoa still has work, such as the watcher that takes the AI login out (R1.4). So the adapter holds each Sprite awake until its time, with the Tasks API in the Sprite: a sandbox's `timeoutMs`, `setTimeout` and `keepAlive` work as on E2B. At its time, a kept Sprite sleeps with its files; one that is not kept stops its processes and deletes its home folder, and the next `create` deletes it at Sprites.
- `pause` ends the job's processes and lets the Sprite sleep, so the next job wakes it in about a second, with its files. When byoa resumes a Sprite whose time ran out (your backend died during a job), it ends any old process first.
- A Sprite's user has some Linux capabilities, such as `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`. byoa runs each command with none, so the agent has no more power than an ordinary user, and Codex's own sandbox, which `access: 'read-only'` uses, works.
- Sprites has no volumes, so `cliLogin` does not work there; the default stored login does. Sprites reach every public domain by default, so a tunnel works for `proxyUrl`.
- byoa names its Sprites `byoa-` and 20 hex characters, and gives each the job's labels as `key=value`. A Sprites [connector](https://docs.fly.io/sprites/concepts/connectors) can give your app's Sprites an API without its key in them: limit the connector to the label `byoa-app=<your app>`. Do not use a connector for the user's AI login: byoa's stored login keeps it in your database, for each user (see [AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md)).
- From some hosts (seen from Convex), a call to the Sprites API sometimes hangs for 11 seconds or more. The adapter gives each call 8 seconds, and a command's connection 6 seconds to open, then tries again; a command runs only when its connection is open, so it never runs twice.
- On the Free plan, an organization has 3 Sprites; Pay As You Go removes that limit. Plans set how many run at once (10 or more) and how many start a minute ([pricing](https://fly.io/sprites)).

## The local sandbox

`localSandbox({ root?, volumes?, env? })` is folders on this computer. It isolates nothing: use it only for development and tests, and with `access: 'read-only'` for a harness on a user's own computer. On macOS, the Codex sign-in works in it; the Claude Code sign-in needs Linux.

## Write an adapter

An adapter implements one interface ([src/sandbox/types.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/src/sandbox/types.ts)): create (with volumes), resume, run a command, write a file, pause, destroy, delete a volume, and optionally read a file, set a running sandbox's time again (`Sandbox.setTimeout`), `capabilities`, and keepAlive (a new end time for a sandbox that is not kept: byoa uses it to end a sign-in 2 minutes after the app's last check-in).

```ts
interface SandboxProvider {
  readonly name: string
  readonly capabilities?: { volumes: boolean }  // optional; false: create refuses a volume, and createAgents refuses cliLogin
  create(opts?: { volumes?: { name: string; path: string }[]; labels?: Record<string, string>; timeoutMs?: number; keep?: boolean }): Promise<Sandbox>
  resume(id: string, opts?: { timeoutMs?: number }): Promise<Sandbox>  // starts a paused one; throws SandboxGoneError when it is gone
  destroy(id: string): Promise<void>                                   // by id, running or paused
  deleteVolume(name: string): Promise<void>
  keepAlive?(id: string, ms: number): Promise<void>  // optional: a sandbox that is not kept ends ms from now (the sign-in's check-ins)
}
```

- `keep: true` is a sandbox that byoa keeps for the user. When it times out, the provider must pause it instead of deleting it, and no process of that job may run when it resumes.
- A provider with no volumes refuses `create` with volumes, and says `capabilities: { volumes: false }`.
- `run` resolves for a non-zero exit code, and with exit code 137 for a command that runs out of its `timeoutMs`; it does not throw.
- `Sandbox.readFile(path)` (optional) reads a file through the provider's file API, or gives null. byoa reads the login files and a conversation's transcript with it; without it, byoa reads them as base64 on a command's output, which a provider may keep in its command history.
- `Sandbox.setTimeout(ms)` (optional) sets the provider's time of a running sandbox again, `ms` from now, as `timeoutMs` at create: then a kept sandbox pauses, and another one ends. byoa calls it when a job has the user's AI login, so the time the job waited in line for the login does not count.
- `test/helpers/conformance.ts` in byoa's repository checks what byoa needs of an adapter: run it on yours, as `test/fake.test.ts` does for the local one.
- The [API reference](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/api.md#sandbox-adapter) has the `Sandbox` interface.

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/stores

# Stores and Convex

byoa keeps its state in your own database, through a store adapter: MCP grants, AI logins (by default), login states, sandbox slots and leases, and conversations (the harness's session id and a copy of its transcript). Grants, AI logins and conversations are encrypted with your `encryptionKey`.

## The store adapter

A store is four methods. byoa ships one for Postgres, one for Convex and one in memory for tests. For another database, write your own.

```ts
interface Entry { value: string; version: string }
interface Store {
  get(key: string): Promise<Entry | null>
  put(key: string, value: string): Promise<void>                        // writes whatever is there
  delete(key: string): Promise<void>
  cas(key: string, version: string | null, value: string): Promise<boolean>  // null: only if no entry; true if it wrote
}
```

The version must change on every write, and a key that is deleted and written again must never get an earlier version back. Each call must take effect at one instant, and `get` must answer the latest write: do not send it to a read replica or a cache, or a job that came later can take a sandbox or a login first, and an index can lose an entry. Do not send a write again after an error (a retry wrapper): the first one may have written. The one refresh owner of each grant, the login lease and the sandbox slots depend on `cas`. The to-do example's `sqliteStore` in [examples/todo/todos.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/examples/todo/todos.ts) is one in 19 lines.

## The keys byoa writes

Every key is in one file, [src/keys.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/src/keys.ts). The values marked sealed are encrypted with your `encryptionKey`, with the key as associated data; the others hold no secret. `<user>` and the sandbox key are URL-encoded.

| Key | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `grant/<user>/<name>` | sealed: one MCP grant |
| `grants/<user>` | the names and URLs of the user's grants |
| `lease/<user>/<name>` | the lease of the one refresh of a grant |
| `mcpflow/<state>` | sealed: an MCP sign-in that has not come back yet |
| `job/<hash>`, `jobid/<job>` | a job token, by its hash, and its hash by the job id |
| `login/<user>/<h>`, `loginjob/<user>/<h>` | the state of a lab login; a sign-in that runs now |
| `ailogin/<user>/<h>` | sealed: the CLI's own login files |
| `ailoginlease/…`, `ailoginline/…`, `ailoginloan/…` | who holds the login, the jobs that wait for it, and the sandboxes that have a copy |
| `aikey/<user>/<plan>`, `aikeystate/<user>/<plan>` | sealed: a plan's key; its state |
| `usersandbox/<user>/<provider>/<h>/<key>` (and `…/line`) | a kept sandbox: its id and the lease of its job; the jobs that wait for it |
| `usersandboxes/<user>/<provider>` | the user's kept sandboxes |
| `conversation/<user>/<h>/<id>` | sealed: a conversation's session id and its transcript (at most `transcriptBytes`) |
| `conversations/<user>` | the user's conversations |

A conversation's transcript can be large: with the default `transcriptBytes` (700 000) one entry stays below a Convex document's 1 MiB. Postgres has no such limit.

## Postgres

```ts
import { postgresStore, POSTGRES_SCHEMA } from '@madeyexz/byoa/store/postgres'

await pool.query(POSTGRES_SCHEMA)  // once; or postgresSchema('my_table')
const store = postgresStore({ query: (sql, args) => pool.query(sql, args) })
```

## Convex

In a Convex app, byoa's state is one table and four internal functions in your deployment (`@madeyexz/byoa/store/convex`). Call byoa from actions and HTTP actions, which can make network calls; serve `agents.proxy` from an HTTP action.

```ts
// convex/schema.ts
import { convexTable } from '@madeyexz/byoa/store/convex'
export default defineSchema({ ...yourTables, byoa: convexTable() })

// convex/byoa.ts
import { convexFunctions } from '@madeyexz/byoa/store/convex'
export const { get, put, remove, cas } = convexFunctions()

// in an action or HTTP action
import { convexStore } from '@madeyexz/byoa/store/convex'
const agents = createAgents({ ...options, store: convexStore(ctx, internal.byoa) })
```

A Convex action has a time limit, and a job waits in line with no limit by default, so set `waitMs` shorter than the action's limit. On Daytona Tier 1 and 2, `*.convex.site` is an allowed domain for the proxy.

## A table of its own for the AI logins

To keep the logins in a table of their own, with a key of their own, so that you can give them their own access rules and backups:

```ts
import { createAgents, storedLogin } from '@madeyexz/byoa'

// Convex: convex/schema.ts has  byoaLogin: convexTable(),  and convex/byoaLogin.ts has
//   export const { get, put, remove, cas } = convexFunctions('byoaLogin')
const loginStore = convexStore(ctx, internal.byoaLogin)
// Postgres: run postgresSchema('byoa_ai_login') once
const loginStore = postgresStore({ query, table: 'byoa_ai_login' })

const agents = createAgents({ ...options, login: storedLogin({ store: loginStore, encryptionKey: loginKey }) })
```

To keep each login in a volume of that user and app instead, behind the sandbox adapter, pass `login: cliLogin` (from `@madeyexz/byoa`). Your database then never holds the login. This needs a provider with volumes; see [AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md#where-the-login-stays-between-jobs).

## Tests

Use `memoryStore()` from `@madeyexz/byoa`. See [Testing](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/testing.md).

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/testing

# Testing

## Test your app without a plan or a sandbox

Use `harness: 'fake'`, `localSandbox()` from `@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/local` and `memoryStore()` from `@madeyexz/byoa`. The fake harness runs no model and needs no login. It reads the same MCP config Claude Code would, and calls MCP tools through the real proxy: each task line `call <server>.<tool> <json>` is one call. So a test proves your app's routes, grants and proxy end to end.

```ts
import { createAgents, memoryStore } from '@madeyexz/byoa'
import { localSandbox } from '@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/local'

// serve agents.proxy at http://127.0.0.1:3000/byoa/mcp, as in Getting started
const agents = createAgents({
  app: 'myapp-test', sandbox: localSandbox(), store: memoryStore(), encryptionKey,
  proxyUrl: 'http://127.0.0.1:3000/byoa/mcp', oauth: { redirectUrl: 'http://127.0.0.1:3000/byoa/callback' },
  tools: { todos: todoTools },
})
for await (const ev of agents.run('u1', { harness: 'fake', task: 'call todos.add_todo {"title":"milk"}', mcp: ['todos'] })) {
  if (ev.type === 'end') assert.ok(ev.ok)
}
```

- The fake harness shows the task's first line as one `text` event and skips the other lines. The last call's output is the `end` event's `result`.
- In a `conversation`, the fake harness keeps each task in a session file and says how many earlier messages it remembers (`fake harness remembers 1 earlier messages: <first line>`), so you test your app's conversations with no model.
- With the local sandbox, `proxyUrl` can be `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/byoa/mcp`.
- Copy [examples/todo/todo.test.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/examples/todo/todo.test.ts). Do not offer `fake` to end users in production.

## Test byoa itself

- `npm test` runs V10, V12, the fake-harness tests and the unit tests. `npm run test:v11` runs V11; it downloads about 600 MB. CI runs both on every commit.
- `npm test` never starts a paid sandbox, also when the providers' keys are set: each paid check needs its own flag. `npm run test:daytona` checks the Daytona adapter against Daytona and runs V8 there. It needs `DAYTONA_API_KEY`, and with `BYOA_DAYTONA_VOLUMES=1` also checks its volumes; that needs a key with the volume permissions. `npm run test:v4` runs V4 ([test/v4.test.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/test/v4.test.ts)) with `E2B_API_KEY` and `DAYTONA_API_KEY`; it needs `cloudflared` to give the proxy a public URL. On a Daytona org on Tier 1 or 2, also set `BYOA_V4_RELAY` to a relay on an allowed domain, such as [test/relay](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/test/relay/convex/http.ts) deployed to a temporary Convex project.
- `npm run test:e2b` checks the E2B adapter against E2B and runs V8 there (a user's jobs in one paused and resumed sandbox, and `sandboxPer: 'job'`). It needs `E2B_API_KEY`, and with `BYOA_E2B_VOLUMES=1` also checks volumes, for an E2B team with volumes turned on.
- `npm run test:instabox` does the same on Instabox. It needs `INSTABOX_API_KEY`. `npm run test:sprites` does the same on Sprites, and also checks that a Sprite stays awake until its time, so the login's watcher runs, and sleeps after it. It needs `SPRITES_TOKEN`. `BYOA_V4_PROVIDERS=e2b,instabox` runs V4 on E2B and Instabox.
- Each of these adapter tests first runs the conformance check, [test/helpers/conformance.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/test/helpers/conformance.ts); `npm test` runs it on the local sandbox.
- `node scripts/v21.ts` runs V21 (conversations and steering with real logins on E2B) in steps, because a person signs in: `login claude|codex|grok`, then `check`, then `cleanup`, which signs out and deletes the sandboxes. It needs `E2B_API_KEY`.

- `spec/tla/check.sh` runs V22: TLC checks the TLA+ models of the job lifecycle, the login lease, the sign-in, the store and its adapters, steering, the MCP grant's refresh, job tokens, plan keys, the usage-limit hold and the hosted demo ([spec/tla](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/spec/tla/README.md)). It needs Java 11 or later, and downloads TLC the first time. `TLA_SET=fast spec/tla/check.sh` runs the fast set (about 15 minutes); the whole set takes hours. No CI runs them: run them by hand when a protocol or its model changes.

The checks V1 to V22 are in [SPEC.md](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/SPEC.md#verification).

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/subscriptions

# Supported AI subscriptions

Your users bring an AI subscription that they already pay for. byoa runs it in the lab's own, unmodified CLI: Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build.

| Subscription | Plans that work | Can the user's account get banned? |
|---|---|---|
| [Claude](https://claude.com/pricing), in Claude Code | Pro, Max, Ultra, Team and Enterprise. Not Free. | It can. Anthropic's terms forbid apps to store Claude logins, and Anthropic may act without notice. |
| [ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/codex/pricing), in Codex | Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu. Not Free or Go. | It can. OpenAI's terms want the login kept where the user controls it, and paid or hosted apps must apply to be partners. |
| [Grok](https://x.ai/grok), in Grok Build | SuperGrok and X Premium+ | Unclear. xAI's terms forbid sharing an account and "unauthorized automated" access, and say nothing about apps that run Grok Build for their users. |
| [OpenCode Go](https://opencode.ai/docs/console/go) **(beta)**, in Claude Code or Codex | Go, Go Plus and Go Teams | It can. OpenCode's terms say "only for your own internal use". |

Why, and what to do before you launch: [Can my user's AI account get banned?](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/faq.md#can-my-users-ai-account-get-banned)

- **Claude, ChatGPT and Grok:** the user signs in on the lab's own page. See [AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md).
- **OpenCode Go (beta):** the user gives a key from OpenCode's Console, and the key never goes into the sandbox. No real Go key has run it yet. See [AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md#opencode-go-a-key-not-a-sign-in-beta).
- **Prices and limits:** the labs change them often, so read their own pages, linked in the table.

## What every plan has in common

- **The user's plan limits apply.** A job uses the same allowance as the user's own chats and coding: the five-hour and weekly limits are shared. When the user is at a limit, the CLI refuses, and the job ends with an `error` event.
- **One plan for each harness.** A user can sign in to each of them, and each job names its harness: `harness: 'claude'`, `'codex'` or `'grok'`. A job on the user's OpenCode Go key also names `plan: 'opencode-go'`.
- **The login belongs to your app.** A login that a user made in your app is only for your app. Another app on byoa needs its own sign-in. See [Lab rules](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/lab-rules.md).
- **The labs' terms apply.** The labs restrict where an app may store the login, and OpenAI asks paid or hosted apps to apply to be partners. Read [the FAQ](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/faq.md#can-my-users-ai-account-get-banned) before you launch.

## What byoa does not support

- **API keys.** byoa signs in only with a plan. The one key it takes is the user's OpenCode Go key, which is a plan's key. An app that wants to pay for the AI with its own API key does not need byoa for the login.
- **Other labs' plans,** such as Gemini or Kimi memberships. byoa runs only Claude Code, Codex and Grok Build in version 1. Gemini or Antigravity may come later. OpenCode is also an agent itself (the `opencode` CLI), but byoa does not run it in version 1: an OpenCode Go plan runs in Claude Code or Codex.
- **Sharing one login between apps.** The labs do not allow it, and byoa keeps each app's logins apart (`app` in `createAgents`).

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/lab-rules

# Lab rules

byoa runs the labs' own CLIs on each user's own plan, so byoa and every app on it follow the labs' published rules. This page has the rules from [SPEC.md](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/SPEC.md#lab-rules), and what each app must do.

## Rules we follow

- We run the real, unmodified `claude`, `codex` and `grok` binaries. We never pretend to be another client. A test checks the hash of the installed binaries against the published packages (V11).
- The user signs in through Anthropic's, OpenAI's or xAI's own sign-in page.
- One app's AI login is used only by that app.
- For OpenCode Go (beta), byoa uses only the user's own key, with OpenCode's documented API and the harness's own user agent, never OpenCode's Console CLI sign-in. OpenCode's terms do not clearly allow an app to run it for its users, so each app asks OpenCode first.
- The labs' terms restrict where an AI login may be stored. byoa keeps it in your database by default, so each app checks those terms and signs its own agreements with the labs.

## What the labs' terms say

byoa follows the labs' published rules as read on 2026-11-22:

- Anthropic ([legal and compliance](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/legal-and-compliance)) allows an end user to sign in to the unmodified Claude Code binary with their own plan, including where a platform hosts Claude Code. It forbids third parties to "collect, store, or intermediate Claude.ai credentials or session tokens", unless Anthropic agrees otherwise.
- OpenAI ([Sign in with ChatGPT Terms](https://openai.com/policies/sign-in-with-chatgpt-terms/), effective 2026-11-04) requires that "any persistent storage of Authentication Tokens must be local and under the user's control, not in a remote or managed environment", and that the plan is used "only for the application they connected". Paid or remotely hosted apps must [apply](https://openai.com/form/sign-in-with-chatgpt-interest/) to be partners.
- OpenCode ([Terms of Use](https://opencode.ai/legal/terms-of-service), effective 2026-11-08, read on 2026-11-25) says that the user "will only use the Services for your own internal use, and not on behalf of or for the benefit of any third party", and forbids using "multiple accounts to circumvent usage limits". Its [Go docs](https://opencode.ai/docs/console/go) say Go "is designed for OpenCode and other coding agents that produce similar types of requests", and ask each client to send "its own user agent" and "a stable session ID". OpenCode documents a Go key in Claude Code and in Codex. Whether an app may run a user's key for that user's own tasks is arguable, not clearly allowed: the work is the user's own, but the app gains from it too. Ian Hsiao accepted this for version 1 on 2026-11-25. There is no "Sign in with OpenCode" for apps; the user creates the key in OpenCode's Console.
- xAI (read on 2026-11-25) publishes Grok Build (`@xai-official/grok`, Apache-2.0) for SuperGrok and X Premium+ subscribers, with a device-code sign-in and a headless mode for scripts. Its [terms of service](https://x.ai/legal/terms-of-service) (2026-10-27) say "You may not share your account credentials or make your account available to anyone else", and its [acceptable use policy](https://x.ai/legal/acceptable-use-policy) forbids "Accessing the Services through unauthorized automated or non-human means". Neither says anything about an app that runs Grok Build for its own users, or that stores their login. Ian Hsiao accepted this when he added Grok Build to version 1; we have not asked xAI.

So byoa MUST:

- run only unmodified `claude`, `codex` and `grok` binaries, and never pretend to be another client (Codex's app server names byoa as its client: `clientInfo.name` is `byoa`);
- send the user to the lab's own sign-in page;
- not share one AI login between apps;
- for OpenCode Go, use only the user's own key, with OpenCode's documented API and the harness's own user agent, and never OpenCode's Console CLI sign-in, which has OpenCode's own client ID.

The labs' terms above restrict where these tokens may be stored. byoa keeps the AI login in the app's database by default (R1.4), and ships a per-user volume as an option (R1.5). Each app checks the labs' terms for its own use.

Each app is responsible for its own agreements with the labs. An app that offers OpenCode Go asks OpenCode (help@anoma.ly) before it ships it. We plan to sign agreements for our own apps when they have traction.

Our hosted mail demo (https://byoa.rippling.computer/demo, `examples/mail/convex`) is a hosted service for strangers: it keeps each visitor's Claude, ChatGPT or Grok login, encrypted, in its Convex deployment, for at most one hour after the visitor's last request, and then signs it out with the CLI and deletes it; sooner when the visitor clicks Sign out or Delete my data. That is the storage that Anthropic's and OpenAI's terms above restrict. Ian Hsiao accepted this on 2026-11-26, before we have an agreement with Anthropic or OpenAI. The demo's page tells visitors that the job uses their own plan and how long their login stays.

Our help agent, the chat in the corner of each page of https://byoa.rippling.computer (`site/help.html`, backend in [madeyexz/byoa-help](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa-help)), is the one place where we do not follow "each user uses their own plan": every visitor's question runs on Ian Hsiao's own ChatGPT plan, in Codex, signed in once with `codex login --device-auth` and kept, encrypted, in its Convex deployment. OpenAI's [Codex app-server docs](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/app-server) say "App-server authentication has never been permitted for commercial or hosted services", and its Terms of Use forbid making an account "available to anyone else". Ian Hsiao accepted that risk to his own account on 2026-11-26. The chat says that it runs on the maintainer's plan, and limits keep its use small. An app on byoa must not do this.

## What your app must do

Every app on byoa must follow these rules. If a request breaks one, stop and tell the developer.

- Run only the unmodified `claude`, `codex` and `grok` binaries that byoa installs (pinned, and checked in byoa's own tests). Do not patch them, wrap them to change what they send, or set headers or a user agent to pretend to be another client.
- Send the user to the lab's own sign-in page, from `connectLogin`. Do not embed, proxy or copy that page, and never ask the user for a password or an API key in place of it. The one key byoa takes is an OpenCode Go key, with `connectKey`, which OpenCode's Console makes for this.
- For OpenCode Go, never use OpenCode's Console CLI sign-in (`npx @opencode/console`): it has OpenCode's own client ID. OpenCode's terms say "only for your own internal use, and not on behalf of or for the benefit of any third party", so it is not clearly allowed for an app: tell the developer to ask OpenCode (help@anoma.ly) first.
- Never read, export or call the labs' APIs with the user's AI tokens. The CLI is the only client that uses them. Do not call the labs' token endpoints.
- One app's AI login is only for that app. Give each app its own `app` name and its own store. Never share a login between apps.
- Real MCP tokens never go into the sandbox. Give a job its servers with `mcp: [...]`. Never put a grant's token in `setup`, the task, environment variables or files.
- The labs' terms restrict where AI logins may be stored. Anthropic says third parties may not "collect, store, or intermediate Claude.ai credentials or session tokens" without its agreement. OpenAI says stored tokens must be "local and under the user's control", and paid or hosted apps must apply to be partners. xAI's terms forbid sharing an account and "unauthorized automated" access, and say nothing about an app that runs Grok Build for its users. byoa's default keeps the login in the app's database; `cliLogin` keeps it in a per-user volume. Each app checks the terms and makes its own agreements: https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/SPEC.md#lab-rules

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/faq

# FAQ

## What is byoa?

byoa, short for "bring your own agent", is the simplest way to let your users bring their own AI subscription to power the agents in your app. Each user signs in to their own AI plan one time: Claude (in Claude Code), ChatGPT (in Codex), Grok (in Grok Build) or OpenCode Go (beta). When your app has work for the AI, byoa runs that user's own Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build in a sandbox on your E2B, Daytona or Instabox account, with the user's tools, and streams the result back. The user's plan pays for the AI. Your app pays only for the sandbox.

byoa is an open-source library (Apache 2.0), the npm package `@madeyexz/byoa`. It runs inside your app's own backend, on Node or Bun. It is not a hosted service. See [Why and when you need byoa](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/index.md#why-and-when-you-need-byoa) and [Getting started](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/getting-started.md).

## Can my user's AI account get banned?

It can. byoa cannot promise that it will not, because the labs decide, and their terms allow parts of what byoa does but not all of it. byoa is built to stay inside the parts that the labs allow:

- **It runs the labs' own CLIs, unmodified.** The agent is the real Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build, installed from the labs' own npm packages, and a test checks the binaries against those packages (V11). byoa never pretends to be another client, and never calls the labs' APIs with the user's tokens.
- **The user signs in on the lab's own page,** with the CLI's own sign-in. byoa never sees a password.
- **Each user uses their own plan, for their own work,** and one app's login is only for that app.

Anthropic's [Claude Code legal and compliance page](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/legal-and-compliance) allows "an end user signing in to the unmodified Claude Code binary with their own Claude subscription, including where a platform hosts Claude Code". But the same page also says:

- developers "may not collect, store, or intermediate Claude.ai credentials or session tokens". byoa's default login stores the CLI's login files, encrypted, in your app's database ([AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md)).
- "Advertised usage limits for Pro, Max, and Ultra plans assume ordinary, individual usage of Claude Code". An app that runs many jobs for one user can go beyond that.
- Anthropic "reserves the right to take measures to enforce these restrictions and may do so without prior notice."

OpenAI's [Sign in with ChatGPT Terms](https://openai.com/policies/sign-in-with-chatgpt-terms/) say that stored tokens "must be local and under the user's control, not in a remote or managed environment", and that paid or remotely hosted apps must [apply to be partners](https://openai.com/form/sign-in-with-chatgpt-interest/).

xAI's [terms of service](https://x.ai/legal/terms-of-service) say "You may not share your account credentials or make your account available to anyone else", and its [acceptable use policy](https://x.ai/legal/acceptable-use-policy) forbids "Accessing the Services through unauthorized automated or non-human means". Neither says anything about an app that runs Grok Build for its users, or that stores their login. So for Grok, the answer is unclear.

OpenCode's [Terms of Use](https://opencode.ai/legal/terms-of-service) say the user uses its services "only for your own internal use, and not on behalf of or for the benefit of any third party". So an OpenCode Go key (beta) in your app is arguable, not clearly allowed ([AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md#opencode-go-a-key-not-a-sign-in-beta)).

So, before you launch:

- Read the [Lab rules](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/lab-rules.md), and decide where the logins stay: the default stored login, or `cliLogin` in a volume of each user.
- Apply to OpenAI's partner program if your app is paid or hosted, and ask Anthropic for an agreement if you store Claude logins. If you offer OpenCode Go, ask OpenCode (help@anoma.ly) first.
- Keep each user's jobs to the user's own requests, at a pace that a person would use.
- Tell your users that the jobs use their own plan and its limits.

## What happens when the user's plan runs out?

The job ends with an `error` of code `usage-limit`, and `resetsAt` when the tool says when the plan resets (Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode Go say it; Grok Build does not). byoa keeps this until the reset, or for 15 minutes when it does not know the time. Until then, a job of that user and harness ends at once and starts no sandbox, so a used-up plan does not cost you a sandbox for each try. `agents.usageLimit(userId, harness)` tells you before a job. A refusal for now, such as a lab that is overloaded, is `rate-limited`: try again in a moment. See [When the plan is used up](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/running-agents.md#when-the-plan-is-used-up).

## Can one user run many agents at the same time?

Yes, with one sign-in, for Claude Code, Codex and Grok Build. Give each agent its own sandbox: a `sandboxKey` for each, or `sandboxPer: 'job'`. The jobs then share the user's login while it is not due for a refresh. Jobs in one sandbox wait in line instead, and one job can also carry several messages to one agent. See [Running agents](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/running-agents.md#jobs-at-the-same-time).

All these jobs use the same plan, so they reach the plan's limits sooner. One risk stays with a shared login: when the lab answers 401 to two sandboxes at the same time, both CLIs refresh, one refresh fails, and the user may have to sign in again. `storedLogin({ parallel: false })` turns sharing off ([AI login](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/ai-login.md#jobs-at-the-same-time-the-shared-login)). Jobs on an OpenCode Go key have no such risk: a key does not rotate.

## Does the agent remember earlier jobs?

Only in a conversation. A job with a `conversation` id continues the harness's own session of the earlier jobs with that id, in the conversation's own kept sandbox, and its job folder (`~/work`) stays. A job with no `conversation` starts a new session, and its job folder is new. byoa keeps a copy of each conversation's transcript, encrypted in your database, so the agent still remembers when the provider loses the sandbox. A running job of each harness also takes more messages (`job.send`): Codex and Grok Build into the turn that runs, Claude Code after it. See [Running agents](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/running-agents.md#conversations) and [what carries over between jobs](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/sandbox-lifecycle.md#what-carries-over-between-jobs).

## Which model does a job use?

The model and effort that you give `run`, else the harness's default from `createAgents({ models })`, else the CLI's own default. `agents.listModels(userId, harness)` lists the models that the user's plan can use, and the efforts of each, as the CLI lists them with the user's login. Pick from that list, because each plan has its own models. A job on an OpenCode Go key (beta) needs a Go model: `agents.listModels(userId, 'opencode-go')` lists them from OpenCode's API, with no sandbox. See [Running agents](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/running-agents.md#models-and-effort).

## What does an AI job cost with byoa, and with an API key?

Your app passes its AI costs on to its users, in its price, so the question is what each user pays. With an API key, your app buys every token at API prices. With byoa, the user's own plan pays for the model, and your app passes on only the sandbox. For 100 small tasks a month, that takes each user's cost from $24.50 to $49 with a frontier model, or from $3 with a cheap open-weight model and a worse agent, down to $1.38 on E2B, and a frontier agent on the plan they already pay for.

### One small task

Take a small task in an AI-native app, such as "add these three to-dos and sort them by date". The agent makes about 20 model calls. Each call sends the conversation so far, so the inputs add up to about 500,000 tokens, of which about 90% are cache hits. The agent writes about 10,000 tokens, with its reasoning. The job takes about 5 minutes of sandbox time, from start to `close()`.

These are estimates. To get your own numbers, read the `usage` of each job's `end` event (`input`, `output`, `cached`, and `costUsd` when the CLI reports it).

**The model, at API prices** (per million tokens, from the labs' price pages on 25 November 2026):

| Model | Kind | 50,000 uncached input | 450,000 cached input | 10,000 output | One task |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Opus 5.5 ($4.00 in, $0.20 cached, $20.00 out) | frontier | $0.200 | $0.090 | $0.200 | **$0.490** |
| GPT-6.2 Sol ($2.00 in, $0.10 cached, $10.00 out) | frontier | $0.100 | $0.045 | $0.100 | **$0.245** |
| Kimi K3 ($3.00 in, $0.30 cached, $15.00 out) | frontier, open-weight | $0.150 | $0.135 | $0.150 | **$0.435** |
| DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ($0.30 in, $0.006 cached, $1.20 out) | smaller, open-weight | $0.015 | $0.0027 | $0.012 | **$0.0297** |

**The sandbox,** 2 vCPU and 4 GiB of memory, for 5 minutes (prices per hour, billed by the second, only while it runs):

| Provider | 2 vCPU | 4 GiB | One hour | One task (5 minutes) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E2B ($0.0504 a vCPU, $0.0162 a GiB) | $0.1008 | $0.0648 | $0.1656 | **$0.0138** |
| Daytona (the same rates) | $0.1008 | $0.0648 | $0.1656 | **$0.0138** |
| Instabox ($0.004 a vCPU, $0.00225 a GiB) | $0.008 | $0.009 | $0.017 | **$0.0014** |
| Sprites ($0.0385 a CPU, $0.021875 a GB, for what the job uses) | $0.077 | $0.0875 | $0.1645 | **$0.0137** |

Claude Opus 5.5 has a cache write price too ($5.00), which this leaves out. DeepSeek's prices are its weekday peak prices; at other times they are half.

Sources: [Claude pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing), [OpenAI API pricing](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing), [Kimi API pricing](https://platform.kimi.ai/docs/pricing/chat), [DeepSeek API pricing](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/quick_start/pricing/), [E2B pricing](https://e2b.dev/pricing), [Daytona pricing](https://www.daytona.io/pricing), [Instabox pricing](https://instabox.sh/pricing), [Sprites pricing](https://fly.io/sprites).

### For a month

What each user pays a month for 100 such tasks, when your app passes its costs on:

| | Model at API prices | Sandbox with byoa |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Opus 5.5 | $49.00 | |
| GPT-6.2 Sol | $24.50 | |
| Kimi K3 | $43.50 | |
| DeepSeek V4.1 Flash | $2.97 | |
| E2B or Daytona | | $1.38 |
| Instabox | | $0.14 |
| Sprites | | $1.37 at most |

The user already pays for their own plan, such as $20 a month for Claude Pro or ChatGPT Plus, and the task uses its allowance.

To try other numbers of tasks:

Diagram: What each user pays a month for small agent tasks, when your app passes its AI costs on. With your API key, frontier models cost each user a lot, and cheaper models cost less for a weaker agent. With byoa, the user's own plan pays for a frontier model, and your app passes on only the sandbox. The numbers come from the cost tables in the FAQ.

For 100 tasks for each user, a month:

| How your app gets the AI | Each user pays a month |
|---|---|
| Your API key: Claude Opus 5.5 (frontier) | $49.00 |
| Your API key: GPT-6.2 Sol (frontier) | $24.50 |
| Your API key: Kimi K3 (frontier, open-weight) | $43.50 |
| Your API key: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (smaller, open-weight) | $2.97 |
| byoa on E2B: the user's own plan, with a frontier model | $1.38 and their plan |
| byoa on Daytona: the user's own plan, with a frontier model | $1.38 and their plan |
| byoa on Instabox: the user's own plan, with a frontier model | $0.14 and their plan |
| byoa on Sprites: the user's own plan, with a frontier model | $1.37 and their plan |

### What the numbers leave out

- **Plan fees at the provider.** E2B's Pro plan is $150 a month, and Instabox's Pro plan is $20 a month with $20 of usage in it. Daytona has no plan fee, and Sprites' Free plan has none (it gives $5 of usage a month). Sprites bills the CPU and memory that a job uses, not what it could use, so a job that mostly waits for the model costs less than the table says.
- **A kept sandbox between jobs.** A paused or stopped sandbox costs no compute. It can cost a little for its disk: Daytona bills disk past the first 5 GiB.
- **The sign-in sandbox,** once for each user and harness, for a few minutes.
- **An agent with no sandbox.** An agent that only calls your app's own API, with no shell and no files, can run as an agent loop of your own, such as on AWS Lambda, with no sandbox. Then an API key costs only the tokens. byoa needs a sandbox, because Claude Code, Codex and Grok Build need a shell.
- **The user's plan has limits.** A user who runs many long tasks reaches the five-hour or weekly limit of their plan, and the jobs stop until it resets.

### When an API key costs the user less

- **The user has no plan.** Then they must buy one, such as $20 a month, before your agent works.
- **The user runs only a few tasks.** 10 small tasks on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash cost $0.30 at API prices, much less than a plan. A plan pays off when the user uses it in many apps, or uses your agent a lot.
- **The user runs many long tasks.** They reach the limits of their plan.

### What your app gets

Your costs do not grow with each user's tokens. You do not have to choose between a good agent and a low price. Your app has no per-user token bill, no usage metering or credits to sell, and no API key for the model to keep secret.

---

Source: https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/api

# API reference

This page is the agent skill's API reference, [skills/byoa/reference/api.md](https://byoa.rippling.computer/docs/api.md), so a coding agent and you read the same text.

This is the API of byoa 1.1.0 (`@madeyexz/byoa` on npm). The source of truth is `src/agents.ts`, `src/index.ts` and the files they import.

## Imports

| Import | What it gives |
|---|---|
| `@madeyexz/byoa` | `createAgents`, `LoginError`, `ProxyError`, `SandboxGoneError`, `memoryStore`, `storedLogin`, `cliLogin`, `readPlugin`, `JOB_TOKEN_ENV`, `PINS`, `clientMetadataDocument`, `PLANS`; types `Agents` (what `createAgents` returns), `AgentsOptions`, `RunOptions`, `Job` (what `run` returns), `RunHarness`, `ConnectResult`, `Session`, `SessionOptions`, `JobToken`, `Store`, `Entry`, `Sandbox`, `SandboxProvider`, `Capabilities`, `AgentEvent`, `Usage`, `AppTools`, `AppTool`, `Access`, `Setup`, `Skill`, `Plugin`, `LoginState`, `LoginStart`, `LoginResult`, `PlanName`, `PlanState` |
| `@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/e2b` | `e2b({ apiKey?, template?, timeoutMs? })`, `buildE2BTemplate(name?, { apiKey?, pins? })`, `e2bTemplate(pins?)`. Needs the `e2b` package. |
| `@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/daytona` | `daytona({ apiKey?, client?, snapshot?, volume?, timeoutMs? })`. Needs `@daytona/sdk`. |
| `@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/instabox` | `instabox({ apiKey?, apiUrl?, template?, snapshot?, timeoutMs? })`. Needs no package. No volumes: use `storedLogin()`, not `cliLogin`. |
| `@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/sprites` | `sprites({ token?, apiUrl?, init?, timeoutMs? })`: Sprites of Fly.io. Needs no package. `init`: a shell command that runs once in each new Sprite. No volumes: use `storedLogin()`, not `cliLogin`. |
| `@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/local` | `localSandbox({ root?, volumes?, env? })`: folders on this computer, for tests and development only. On macOS, the Codex sign-in works in it; the Claude Code sign-in needs Linux. |
| `@madeyexz/byoa/store/postgres` | `postgresStore({ query, table? })`, `postgresSchema(table?)`, `POSTGRES_SCHEMA` |
| `@madeyexz/byoa/store/convex` | `convexTable()`, `convexFunctions(table?)`, `convexStore(ctx, fns)`. Needs `convex`. |
| `@madeyexz/byoa/node` | `toNodeListener(handler)` (a fetch handler as a `node:http` listener), `readPluginDir(dir)` |
| `@madeyexz/byoa/verify` | `verifyHarness(sandbox, harness, bin, pins?)`: checks the installed binary against the published npm package |

`@madeyexz/byoa` still exports `harnessFiles`, `ensureHarness`, `PACKAGES` and `LOGIN_FILES`, which byoa's own tests use. They are deprecated, and version 2.0 removes them: do not use them in an app.

## createAgents(options)

```ts
interface AgentsOptions {
  app: string                 // lower-case letters, digits, -; at most 24. Names the app's sandboxes and login volumes.
  sandbox: SandboxProvider
  store: Store
  encryptionKey: string       // 32 random bytes as base64. Encrypts MCP grants and, by default, AI logins.
  proxyUrl: string            // public URL where the app serves agents.proxy; each server is at <proxyUrl>/<name>
  oauth: { redirectUrl: string; clientMetadataUrl?: string; clientName?: string }
  pins?: { claude?: string; codex?: string; grok?: string }   // default PINS; a harness left out gets its PINS version
  login?: (deps) => LoginDriver              // default storedLogin(); or cliLogin
  jobTimeoutMs?: number                      // default 30 minutes
  sandboxPer?: 'user' | 'job'                // default 'user': kept sandboxes, paused between jobs
  waitMs?: number                            // sandboxPer 'user': how long a job waits in line for its sandbox; default no limit
  models?: { claude?: ModelChoice; codex?: ModelChoice; grok?: ModelChoice; 'opencode-go'?: ModelChoice }  // each harness's default: { model?, effort? }; 'opencode-go': jobs with that plan
  grantOrigins?: Record<string, string[]>    // more exact origins for fetchWithGrant, by MCP server origin
  tools?: AppTools                           // the app's own tools: MCP server name → tool name → { description?, input?, run }
  transcriptBytes?: number                   // the most bytes of a conversation's transcript kept in the store; default 700 000; 0: none
}
```

- `oauth.redirectUrl`: the app's route that calls `finishMcp`.
- `oauth.clientMetadataUrl`: an HTTPS URL where the app serves `agents.clientMetadata()` (a Client ID Metadata Document). Without it, byoa uses only Dynamic Client Registration.
- `oauth.clientName`: the name the MCP server shows on its consent page. Default: `app`.
- `sandboxPer`: `'user'` (the default): the first job of a user and harness creates the user's sandbox; byoa pauses it after each job (E2B pause, Daytona and Instabox stop, Sprites sleep) and resumes it for the next, with a new job folder. One job of a user and harness at a time; the others wait in line, in the order they came. A job's `sandboxKey` (in `run` and `session`) gives the user one kept sandbox, with its own lease, for each key. A sandbox the provider no longer has is replaced by a new one. `'job'`: a new sandbox for each job, destroyed after it. With the default `storedLogin()`, a user's jobs in different sandboxes run at the same time with one login, for every harness.
- `models`: the model and effort a job of each harness gets when it names none. Default: the CLI's own. See `listModels`.
- `transcriptBytes`: after each job of a conversation, byoa keeps a copy of the harness's session files (its transcript), encrypted in the store, when they are at most this large, so the conversation goes on when the provider loses its sandbox. Default 700 000 bytes, below a Convex document's 1 MiB. A larger transcript lives only in the conversation's sandbox.

- `tools`: the app's own tools, as functions in the backend. `{ todos: { add_todo: { description, input, run } } }` is an MCP server `todos` with one tool. `input`: the JSON Schema of the arguments (an object schema; default: no arguments). `run(args, { user, job })` runs for the user of the job; what it returns goes to the agent (a string as it is, other values as JSON), and what it throws goes to the agent as a failed call. byoa does not check the arguments against `input`. A job gets the server by its name in `mcp`; the proxy serves it at `<proxyUrl>/<name>`. Server names: lower-case letters, digits and -, at most 32; tool names: letters, digits, _ and -, at most 64. `listMcp` does not list them, and `connectMcp` refuses their names.

It returns an object with the methods below.

## AI login

| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| `connectLogin(user, 'claude' \| 'codex' \| 'grok')` | `{ harness, url, code? }`. `url`: the lab's own sign-in page. `code`: Codex and Grok, the code to enter on OpenAI's or xAI's page. |
| `finishLogin(user, h, { code?, waitMs? })` | `{ state: 'signed-in' \| 'signed-out' \| 'expired' \| 'pending', error? }`. Claude: pass `code` (the code Anthropic's page shows); with no code, it only checks in and says `pending`. Codex and Grok: no code; `waitMs` waits that long; call again while `pending` (also right after `connectLogin`, while its sandbox starts). After a `cancelLogin` or `signOut` meanwhile, no login it saved stays (`storedLogin()`; with `cliLogin` the volume keeps what the CLI wrote) and it answers the state with `error: 'the sign-in was cancelled'`. Each call keeps the sign-in's sandbox alive for 2 more minutes; with no call for 2 minutes it ends (on E2B and Daytona; Instabox ends it after 15 minutes). A sign-in lasts 15 minutes at most. |
| `cancelLogin(user, h)` | `void`. Ends a sign-in that has not finished, and its sandbox, at once, also one that `connectLogin` still starts (that call then throws "the sign-in was cancelled"). Call it when the user closes the sign-in. |
| `loginState(user, h)` | `'signed-in' \| 'signed-out' \| 'expired'`. With `h` `'opencode-go'`, also `'no-plan'`. A used-up plan is still `'signed-in'`: see `usageLimit`. |
| `usageLimit(user, h)` | `{ message, resetsAt?, until } \| undefined`, with no sandbox. Defined while the user's plan of `h` (a harness, or `'opencode-go'`) is used up, as a job found it: `message` is the tool's words, `resetsAt` (ms since 1970) when the plan resets, when the tool said, `until` when byoa runs this user's jobs of `h` again (`resetsAt`, else 15 minutes after the error). Until then `run` ends at once with a `usage-limit` error and starts no sandbox. A new sign-in (`finishLogin` with `'signed-in'`), `connectKey` with `'signed-in'`, `signOut` and a job that works end it. |
| `signOut(user, h)` | `void`. Also deletes the user's sandbox for `h`, and cancels a sign-in that has not finished. With `h` `'opencode-go'`: deletes the user's key only; the proxy refuses the requests of jobs that still run with it. |
| `connectKey(user, 'opencode-go', key)` | `{ state, error? }`. Beta: OpenCode Go is not yet checked with a real Go key. Keeps the user's OpenCode Console API key (`oc_sk_…`), encrypted in the store, after it checks the key with OpenCode's usage meter: `'signed-in'`; `'no-plan'` (kept: its workspace has no Go plan yet; jobs work once it has one); or, when OpenCode refuses the key (401: wrong, revoked or expired), the state before and an `error`, and the key is not kept. Throws on another answer. |
| `deleteSandbox(user, { harness?, sandboxKey? }?)` | `void`. Deletes the user's kept sandboxes of this app at this provider: all of them (when the app deletes the user), or those of one harness or one sandbox key (when it deletes a project). The login, the grants and the conversations' stored transcripts stay. |
| `deleteConversation(user, conversation?)` | `void`. Deletes a conversation (or, with no id, all of the user's): its session ids and stored transcripts, and its kept sandbox. The next job with that id starts a new conversation. Call it when the user deletes a chat, and when the app deletes the user. |

Login drivers:

- `storedLogin({ store?, encryptionKey?, waitMs?, parallel? })` (default): the CLI's own login files, encrypted in the store. `store` and `encryptionKey` default to the app's. During a job byoa saves a refresh every minute or so; when the backend dies during a job, a watcher in the sandbox removes the files before the provider pauses it, and the next job in that sandbox saves a login that the dead job's CLI refreshed. It saves files from a sandbox only of the same account and not older than the stored login. `waitMs`: how long a job waits in line for the login (default no limit). `parallel` (default true): the jobs of one user and harness share the login, each with a copy in its own sandbox, while the CLI will not refresh it before the job's time runs out (byoa reads the time the access token ends from the login files: the CLIs refresh 5 minutes before it; Codex's token lasts 10 days, Claude Code's 8 hours, Grok's 6 hours). When it is due for a refresh, one job holds it alone: it waits for the other jobs, and the jobs after it wait for it. The risk that stays: the CLIs also refresh when the lab answers 401 to a token that has not run out; two sandboxes that get that answer at the same time both refresh, one fails, and the user may have to sign in again. `parallel: false`: one job of a user and harness holds the login at a time.
- `cliLogin`: the login stays in a volume of the user, mounted through the sandbox adapter. Needs a provider with volumes.

## MCP connections

| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| `connectMcp(user, url, { name, bearer? })` | `{ name, connected: true }` or `{ name, connected: false, signInUrl }`. Send the browser to `signInUrl`. |
| `finishMcp({ state, code?, error? })` | `{ user, name }`. Call it in the `oauth.redirectUrl` route with the query parameters. |
| `listMcp(user)` | `[{ name, url }]` |
| `removeMcp(user, name)` | `void` |
| `importMcp(user, { name, url, oauth })` | `{ name }`. Moves a grant made elsewhere into byoa; `oauth` is the MCP SDK's state (`client`, `tokens`, `at`). Delete the old copy, so the grant keeps one refresh owner. |
| `fetchWithGrant(user, name, url, init?)` | `Response`. A request with the grant's current token, only to the origin of the grant's MCP server (and `grantOrigins` for it). No redirects. The app never gets the token. |
| `clientMetadata()` | The Client ID Metadata Document to serve at `oauth.clientMetadataUrl`. |

`name`: lower-case letters, digits and -, at most 32. `url`: `https://`, or `http://` on localhost.

## The proxy

`agents.proxy` is a fetch handler (`Request` → `Response`). Serve it at `proxyUrl` and every path below it (`<proxyUrl>/<name>`). It checks the job token, adds the user's real token, and sends the request to the MCP server; for the app's own `tools`, it calls the tool's `run`. It refuses a job token after the job ends. Do not put the app's session check in front of it. Each of its MCP answers has the header `x-byoa-proxy: 1`.

It is also the relay of a job with `plan: 'opencode-go'`, at `<proxyUrl>/_plan/opencode-go/anthropic/v1/…` and `…/openai/v1/…`: it checks the job token (of a job with that plan), adds the user's key, and streams the request to `https://opencode.ai/inference/go/…` and the answer back, with only the harness's own headers (its user agent, session id, API version and betas; it adds `x-opencode-session` when there is none). It sends on no other header, so a header that the app's own gateway adds stays behind, and no other path. OpenCode's 401 makes the key `expired`, its 403 "OpenCode Go subscription required" `no-plan`. On its 429, the relay asks OpenCode's usage meter (`/v1/usage`, with the user's key) whether a limit is used up; if so, the job's error is `usage-limit` with that limit's `resetsAt`, and byoa keeps it (`usageLimit`); else it is `rate-limited`.

## Jobs

### run(user, options): Job

```ts
interface RunOptions {
  harness: 'claude' | 'codex' | 'grok' | 'fake'
  task: string | string[]     // several messages: one agent gets them all and decides the order
  setup?: { agentsMd?: string; skills?: { name: string; files: Record<string, string> }[] }  // files must have 'SKILL.md'
  plugins?: Plugin[]          // from readPlugin(readPluginDir(dir)); their skills and MCP servers are added
  mcp?: string[]              // the connected servers this job gets; default none
  model?: string              // Claude Code: an alias (opus, sonnet, ...) or a full name; Codex, Grok: a model name. Default: createAgents' models, else the CLI's
  effort?: string             // Claude Code --effort (low ... max); Codex model_reasoning_effort; Grok --reasoning-effort. Each model's own are in listModels
  onWait?: (w: { for: 'sandbox' | 'login'; ahead: number }) => void  // while the job waits in line
  sandboxKey?: string         // sandboxPer 'user': which of the user's kept sandboxes; default the user's one for the harness
  access?: 'full' | 'read-only'  // what the agent may do; default 'full'
  plan?: 'opencode-go'        // the user's OpenCode Go key (connectKey) in place of the lab login, with claude or codex
  conversation?: string       // the app's id of a conversation (1 to 128 characters): the job continues the harness's session of it
}

interface Job extends AsyncGenerator<AgentEvent> {
  send(message: string): Promise<boolean>  // one more message to the running agent; false once the job ended
}
```

- `conversation`: the job continues the harness's own session of the jobs before it with the same id, so the agent has their messages. The conversation has its own kept sandbox (the id is its `sandboxKey`; give no other one), and its job folder stays from job to job: byoa replaces only its own files there (the skills, AGENTS.md, the MCP config, the task). Claude Code: the first job gets `--session-id <a new UUID>`, the next ones `--resume <id>`. Codex: the first job starts a thread that is not ephemeral, which its app server names in `thread/started`; the next ones `thread/resume` it. Grok: `session/new` names the session; the next jobs `session/resume` it. Jobs of one conversation run one at a time, in the order they came. After each job byoa keeps the session id and, up to `transcriptBytes`, a copy of the session's files, encrypted in the store; when the provider lost the sandbox, the next job writes them into its new one (Claude Code and Grok keep sessions by the job folder's path, which is the same at one provider; Codex by date). When there is no copy, the job starts the conversation again and says so in an `error` with code `conversation`. With `sandboxPer: 'job'`, each job of a conversation has a new sandbox and a new job folder, and resumes only from the stored copy. Not with `session()`.
- `send` (steering): byoa runs each harness under a small driver script (`node .byoa/driver.mjs` in the job folder) that speaks the CLI's own protocol and gives it each message: Claude Code's stream-json input, Codex's app server (`codex app-server`) and Grok's Agent Client Protocol (`grok agent stdio`). Codex (`turn/steer`) and Grok (its `x.ai/interject` extension) take a message into the turn that runs, at the agent's next step; Claude Code takes it when that turn ends. A message that comes after a turn ended starts the next turn, in the same session. Each turn that is not the last gives a `turn` event; the job ends (`end`) after the turn that answers the last message. `send` returns false after the end, and with the fake harness.

- `plan`: the harness runs with the user's OpenCode Go plan, through the proxy's relay; the key never enters the sandbox. The job needs a model of the plan (`model`, else `models['opencode-go']` of createAgents; `listModels(user, 'opencode-go')` lists them), else `run` gives an `error` (code `sandbox`). Claude Code gets `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` (the relay), `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` (the job token), every model alias set to the job's model, and a `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` of its own with no Claude login; Codex gets `-c` overrides for a model provider `opencode-go` (`wire_api = "responses"`, `env_key = "BYOA_JOB_TOKEN"`) and a `CODEX_HOME` of its own. The user's jobs with a key need no lease, so jobs in different sandboxes run at the same time. With no key, `run` gives an `error` with code `signed-out`.
- `mcp`: names of the user's connected servers and of the app's own `tools`.
- `access`: `'full'`: every tool of the harness with no approval (Codex: the thread's sandbox `danger-full-access` with the approval policy `never`; Claude Code: `--permission-mode bypassPermissions`; Grok: `--always-approve`), for a sandbox that is the job's alone. `'read-only'`: the job's MCP tools, and reading files, so the harness reads its skills and AGENTS.md; no change to a file, and no network but the job's MCP servers. Codex: the thread's permission profile `byoa-read-only`, which extends Codex's `:read-only`, turns the network off and denies CODEX_HOME (its shell stays, because it reads a skill with `cat`; a command cannot write, open a connection or read the login), with the job's MCP tools approved in its `config.toml`. Claude Code: `--permission-mode dontAsk` with the tools `Read`, `Glob`, `Grep`, `Skill` and the job's MCP servers; each tool it refuses is a `permission` event. Grok: rules in the job's `.grok/config.toml` that deny `Bash`, `Write`, `Edit` and `WebFetch` and allow `MCPTool(*)` (a denied call is an error for the model, and the turn goes on; Grok reads files and loads skills with no prompt), and its web search only for a domain that does not exist (`GROK_CONFIG`, Grok's config overlay); a tool that Grok still asks for is refused (a `permission` event), and Grok then ends the turn. Apart from Codex's home folder, it does not hide files: the agent can read each file its user can read.
- Before the harness starts, byoa sends one MCP `initialize` from the sandbox to each of the job's servers, through the proxy. When no request reaches the proxy, the job does not start: an `error` event with code `mcp`, then `end` with `ok: false`. A server that does not answer gives an `error` event with code `mcp`, and the job runs.

Each run: the user's sandbox (resumed, or created for the first job; with `sandboxPer: 'job'`, a new one), the user's login, the pinned harness, the setup files in a new job folder (in a conversation, the conversation's folder), the task; then the login is taken out, a conversation's transcript is kept, and the sandbox is paused (or destroyed). Stop the loop (or call `return()`) to end a job early; byoa still cleans up.

### Events (one schema for every harness)

```ts
type AgentEvent =
  | { type: 'start'; harness: string; version: string; sandbox: string; conversation?: string; resumed?: boolean }
  | { type: 'text'; text: string }
  | { type: 'tool_call'; id: string; name: string; server?: string; input: unknown }   // server: the MCP server
  | { type: 'tool_result'; id: string; ok: boolean; output: string }
  | { type: 'permission'; tool: string; decision: 'denied'; input?: unknown }
```
