```ts
  | { type: 'error'; message: string; code?: 'signed-out' | 'expired' | 'no-plan' | 'usage-limit' | 'rate-limited' | 'harness' | 'sandbox' | 'mcp' | 'conversation'; resetsAt?: number }
  | { type: 'turn'; ok: boolean; result?: string; usage?: Usage }     // one turn of a job that has more messages (send)
  | { type: 'end'; ok: boolean; result?: string; usage?: Usage; session?: string }  // session: the harness's session id, in a conversation
// Usage: { input: number; output: number; cached?: number; costUsd?: number }
```

`run` does not throw for job failures: it yields `error` events and then exactly one `end`. `signed-out` / `expired`: ask the user to sign in again, or for a new key with `plan: 'opencode-go'` (`loginState` says the same). `no-plan`: the key's workspace has no OpenCode Go plan. `usage-limit`: the user's plan is used up (a 5-hour, weekly, monthly or other limit, or a spend cap); `resetsAt` (ms since 1970) is when it resets, when the tool said (Claude Code and Codex say it, and for OpenCode Go byoa asks OpenCode's usage meter; Grok Build does not), and `usageLimit` says the same until then; byoa reads each CLI's own code (Claude Code's `api_error`, Codex's `codexErrorInfo`, Grok Build's `error_kind`), and its words only when that is missing. `rate-limited`: the lab refused for now (too many requests, or overloaded); byoa keeps nothing. `mcp`: a server is not connected, its grant failed, it did not answer through the proxy, or the sandbox cannot reach the proxy (then the job did not start). `conversation`: the conversation's history is gone (the provider lost its sandbox, and its transcript was larger than `transcriptBytes`); the job runs, as the first of a new session. In `start`, `resumed` is true when the harness continued an earlier session of the conversation.

### listModels(user, h | 'opencode-go'): Promise<ModelInfo[]>

The models the user's plan can use with `h`, as the unmodified CLI lists them with the user's login (Claude Code: its `initialize` answer; Codex: its app server's `model/list`; Grok: the `initialize` answer of `grok agent stdio`), in a new sandbox that is destroyed after. `ModelInfo`: `{ id, name, description, isDefault, efforts, resolved? }`; `id` is what `model` takes, `efforts` what `effort` takes, `resolved` (Claude Code) the full model name of an alias. Each call starts a sandbox, so keep the list for a while. A Claude Code list waits for the user's running Claude Code jobs. Throws `LoginError` when `h` is not signed in.

With `h` `'opencode-go'`: the plan's chat models, from `https://opencode.ai/inference/go/v1/models` with the user's key, in the backend (no sandbox). The free models are left out: OpenCode serves them only to its own client. `efforts` are the model's own, as OpenCode lists them; Claude Code's `--effort` takes `low` to `max`. `isDefault` is false for each: a job names its model. Throws `LoginError` when the user has no key.

### session(user, { harness, setup?, plugins?, mcp?, sandboxKey?, access?, model?, effort?, onWait?, plan? }): Promise<Session>

For an app that runs its own program around the unmodified harness. It also takes `plan`, as `run` does; `args` then has the plan's flags. Throws `LoginError` when the harness is not signed in (or the user has no key of the plan), and `ProxyError` when the sandbox cannot reach the proxy. The app starts the harness itself, so `access` changes only the files byoa writes (Codex's MCP config).

```ts
const s = await agents.session(userId, { harness: 'claude', mcp: ['notion'] })
try {
  await s.sandbox.run(`my-server --claude ${s.bin}`, { cwd: s.work, env: s.env })
} finally { await s.close() }   // ends the job token, takes the login out, and pauses (or destroys) the sandbox
```

`Session`: `sandbox`, `work` (the job folder with byoa's files), `harness`, `bin` (the pinned binary), `version`, `args` (the harness flags for the job's model and effort, for the app's own command line), `env` (login folder, `BYOA_JOB_TOKEN`, and for Claude Code `MCP_TIMEOUT`; with a plan, the plan's settings above), `token`, `mcp` (`[{ name, url }]` at the proxy), `missing` (servers not connected), `failing` (`[{ name, message }]`: servers that did not answer through the proxy), `reportLogin('signed-in' | 'expired')`, `close()`.

### jobToken(user, { mcp?, ttlMs? }): Promise<JobToken>

A job token with no sandbox, for a harness outside byoa's sandboxes (such as on the user's own computer). `{ token, job, mcp, missing, close() }`. Send `token` as `Authorization: Bearer` to each `mcp[].url`.

## Store adapter

```ts
interface Entry { value: string; version: string }
interface Store {
  get(key: string): Promise<Entry | null>
  put(key: string, value: string): Promise<void>                        // writes whatever is there
  delete(key: string): Promise<void>
  cas(key: string, version: string | null, value: string): Promise<boolean>  // null: only if no entry; true if it wrote
}
```

The version must change on every write, and a key that is deleted and written again must never get an earlier version back. The one refresh owner of each grant depends on `cas`.

- Postgres: run `POSTGRES_SCHEMA` once (or `postgresSchema('my_table')`), then `postgresStore({ query: (sql, args) => pool.query(sql, args) })`.
- Convex: `convex/schema.ts` has `byoa: convexTable()`; `convex/byoa.ts` has `export const { get, put, remove, cas } = convexFunctions()`; in an action or HTTP action, `store: convexStore(ctx, internal.byoa)`. Call byoa only from actions and HTTP actions, and serve `agents.proxy` from an HTTP action.
- Tests: `memoryStore()` from `@madeyexz/byoa`.

## Sandbox adapter

```ts
interface SandboxProvider {
  readonly name: string
  readonly capabilities?: { volumes: boolean }  // optional; false: create refuses a volume, and createAgents refuses cliLogin
  create(opts?: { volumes?: { name: string; path: string }[]; labels?: Record<string, string>; timeoutMs?: number; keep?: boolean }): Promise<Sandbox>
  resume(id: string, opts?: { timeoutMs?: number }): Promise<Sandbox>  // starts a paused one; throws SandboxGoneError when it is gone
  destroy(id: string): Promise<void>                                   // by id, running or paused
  deleteVolume(name: string): Promise<void>
  keepAlive?(id: string, ms: number): Promise<void>  // optional: a sandbox that is not kept ends ms from now (the sign-in's check-ins)
}
interface Sandbox {
  readonly id: string
  readonly home: string
  run(cmd: string, opts?: { cwd?; env?; timeoutMs?; onStdout?; onStderr?; background? }): Promise<{ exitCode; stdout; stderr }>
  writeFile(path: string, data: string | Uint8Array): Promise<void>
  readFile?(path: string): Promise<Uint8Array | null>  // optional; null when it is not there
  pause(): Promise<void>      // keeps the files; resume starts it again
  setTimeout?(ms: number): Promise<void>  // optional: the provider's time again, ms from now (a kept one pauses then)
  destroy(): Promise<void>
}
```

- `keep: true`: a sandbox byoa keeps for the user. When it times out, the provider pauses it instead of deleting it.
- `run`: a command that exits with a non-zero code resolves; one that runs out of its `timeoutMs` resolves with exit code 137.
- `readFile`: byoa reads the user's login files and a conversation's transcript with it. Without it, byoa reads a file as base64 on a command's stdout, which a provider may keep in its command history. E2B, Daytona, Instabox, Sprites and the local provider have it.
- `setTimeout`: byoa calls it when a job has the user's AI login, so the time the job waited in line for the login does not count. E2B and Sprites have it, and Daytona for a sandbox of one job. Without it, a job that waited long for the login can reach the sandbox's time before its own ends.
- An adapter of the app's own can check itself with the conformance check in byoa's tests (`test/helpers/conformance.ts`).
- E2B: `pause` ends the sandbox's processes, then takes a full snapshot, with the memory: the next job's resume takes about 0.3 seconds, and node and the harness start warm. When E2B refuses it, because it still saves the sandbox's previous snapshot, byoa takes a snapshot of the files only; the next resume then boots the sandbox again and reads its disk cold, which can add 10 to 20 seconds. E2B keeps a paused sandbox with no time limit, and charges no compute for it.
- E2B: the default template is `byoa`; build it once per pin change with `buildE2BTemplate()`. Any template with Node 20 or later works (byoa installs the pinned harness when it is missing, more slowly).
- Daytona: `pause` stops the sandbox; `resume` starts it (also from archived, more slowly). A kept sandbox is not ephemeral and has no time to live; Daytona archives it after 7 days stopped.
- Daytona: with `cliLogin`, every user's login is a subpath of one shared volume (`byoa` by default). On Tier 1 and 2 a sandbox reaches only allowed domains, so serve the proxy on one (for example `*.convex.site`, `*.workers.dev`).
- Instabox: `pause` stops the sandbox; `resume` starts it, and a sandbox that paused itself (idle for 30 minutes, or at the plan's longest run) is booted again, so no process of an earlier job runs. A kept sandbox has no time limit, and Instabox keeps it until it is deleted; a sandbox for one job is deleted after it, and at the latest at its `timeoutMs`. The home folder is `/data/home`. A sandbox gets none of the account's Vault items or org Secrets, and no command is in Instabox's command history. Sandboxes reach every public domain. `create` with volumes throws. The free plan allows one sandbox at a time and three starts a minute; the adapter waits for a start when Instabox answers 429.
- Sprites: a Sprite sleeps by itself when nothing runs in it, so the adapter holds it awake until its time (the Tasks API in the Sprite); `setTimeout` and `keepAlive` set that time. At its time a kept Sprite sleeps with its files; one that is not kept ends its processes and deletes its home folder, and the next `create` deletes it. `pause` ends the job's processes and lets it sleep; `resume` after its time ends any old process. The home folder is `/home/sprite`. Each command runs with no Linux capabilities. Sprites reach every public domain. `create` with volumes throws. Labels become `key=value` labels of the Sprite.

## The fake harness

`harness: 'fake'` runs no model and needs no login. It reads the same MCP config Claude Code would. Each task line `call <server>.<tool> <json arguments>` is one MCP call through the real proxy; it shows the task's first line as one `text` event and skips the other lines. The last call's output is the `end` event's `result`. In a conversation it keeps each task in a session file and says, in a `text` event, how many earlier messages it remembers (`fake harness remembers 1 earlier messages: <first line>`), so an app tests its conversations with no model. Use it with `localSandbox()` and `memoryStore()` (or the app's own store) in tests.

---

Source: https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/SPEC.md

# byoa requirements, version 1

**Status:** draft, 2026-11-22. **Owner:** Ian Hsiao.

This document says what version 1 of byoa must do and how we check it. It does not say how to build it. "MUST" and "SHOULD" have their usual meanings (RFC 2119).

## Goal

A developer makes an app AI-native in one day, not in weeks. The app runs the user's own Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build in any sandbox. The user signs in to ChatGPT, Claude or Grok one time, or gives the key of their OpenCode Go plan one time, and connects each MCP tool one time.

## Users of this library

- **App developer.** Imports byoa into their own backend. Does not want to build login, MCP OAuth, skills loading, harness updates or sandbox code.
- **End user.** Uses the developer's app. Has a ChatGPT, Claude, Grok (SuperGrok, X Premium+) or OpenCode Go plan, and accounts in tools such as Notion, Gmail or Heptabase.

## Scope

In scope for version 1:

- Harnesses: Claude Code and Codex, both from the first version, and Grok Build (xAI), added on 2026-11-25.
- Plans: the user's Claude, ChatGPT or Grok plan, through the lab's own sign-in; and OpenCode Go, through a key that the user gives, with Claude Code or Codex (R1.8). OpenCode Go is a plan, not a harness.
- Sandbox providers: E2B, Daytona, Instabox and Sprites (Fly.io).
- Backends: Node, and Convex actions. Cloudflare Workers SHOULD work if it costs little.
- Store adapters: Convex and Postgres.

Out of scope for version 1:

- A hosted service. byoa never runs a server for other apps.
- Sharing one user's AI login between different apps.
- Harnesses other than Claude Code, Codex and Grok Build (OpenCode, Amp, Pi, Cursor). OpenCode Go runs in Claude Code and Codex (R1.8), not in OpenCode.
- A UI kit. The library gives data and events; the app draws its own UI.

## Requirements

### R1. AI login

- **R1.1** byoa MUST sign the user in to Claude Code by running the unmodified `claude` CLI login in the sandbox. The user completes sign-in on Anthropic's own page.
- **R1.2** byoa MUST sign the user in to Codex by running the unmodified `codex login --device-auth` in the sandbox, and to Grok Build by running the unmodified `grok login --device-auth`. The user enters the code on the lab's own page (OpenAI's, xAI's).
- **R1.3** byoa MUST give the app the sign-in URL and code as data, so the app can show them on any device (for example a phone).
- **R1.4** By default, byoa MUST keep the login (the CLI's own login files) in the app's own database, through the store adapter (R6), encrypted with a key that the app gives, for one user of one app. Each job MUST get a copy in its sandbox. After the job, byoa MUST save the files back when the CLI changed them (a token refresh), and MUST remove them from the sandbox, also from a sandbox that it keeps for the user's next job (R5.4). So between jobs the store is the only copy. byoa MUST NOT let two sandboxes refresh one user's login at the same time, so that two token refreshes do not revoke each other. The login is shared by default (`parallel`), for every harness, so that one user's jobs run at the same time: while the login is not due for a refresh before a job's time runs out, the jobs of one user each hold a copy; when it is due, one job MUST hold it alone, after the other jobs end. The app MAY turn sharing off. To know when a login is due, byoa MAY read the time its access token ends from the login files. byoa MUST NOT use a token, and MUST NOT call the lab's token endpoints itself; the CLI is the only client that uses the tokens.
  A backend can die during a job, so that the job never closes. byoa MUST then lose little: during the job it MUST save what the CLI changed about every minute; the next job in a kept sandbox that a dead job left MUST save the login that job's CLI refreshed, under the lease, before it writes the stored copy, unless the stored login changed since; and byoa MUST remove the files from the sandbox before the provider pauses or ends it, also with no backend. byoa MUST save files from a sandbox only when they are of the same account as the stored login and not older (the agent of a job can change any file), and MAY read the account and the refresh time from them for this.
- **R1.5** The login part MUST be replaceable, with no change to R2 to R5. byoa MUST also ship a login that stays in a volume of that one user of that one app, mounted through the sandbox adapter (R5.3), which the app's database never holds.
- **R1.6** byoa MUST report login state: `signed-in`, `signed-out`, `expired`; and for the key of a plan (R1.8), also `no-plan`. A plan that is used up (R1.9) is still `signed-in`.
- **R1.7** A sign-in that the user leaves MUST NOT keep its sandbox: the app MUST be able to end it at once (`cancelLogin`, also at sign-out), and with no word from the app, the sign-in sandbox MUST end within a few minutes after the app's last check-in (`finishLogin`), on every provider that can change a sandbox's time. A sign-in lasts 15 minutes at most, as long as Codex's device code.
- **R1.8** (beta: V20 has not run with a real Go key yet) byoa MUST also run Claude Code and Codex on the user's OpenCode Go plan, with a Console API key of the user (`oc_sk_…`) that the app gives (`connectKey`), instead of a lab login. byoa MUST check the key with OpenCode and keep it through the store adapter (R6), encrypted with a key that the app gives, for one user of one app. The key MUST NOT be in the sandbox's environment, files or processes at any time: the harness sends its model requests with the job token to a relay in the app's proxy (R3), which adds the key and sends them on to OpenCode, with the harness's own user agent and session headers, and refuses the job token after the job (R3.4). The relay MUST send on only the model APIs (`anthropic/v1/…`, `openai/v1/…`), and only for a job that has the plan. When OpenCode answers 401 (a wrong, revoked or expired key), the key is `expired`; when it answers 403 "OpenCode Go subscription required", it is `no-plan`. A key does not rotate, so one user's jobs with it MUST run at the same time, with no lease. byoa MUST use only OpenCode's documented API and its documented settings for each harness (Claude Code: `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`; Codex: a model provider with the Responses API, for the job only), with a config folder of the job's own that has no lab login. Unlike a lab login (R1.4), the key is used by byoa itself, in the app's backend.

- **R1.9** byoa MUST tell the app when the user's plan is used up (its 5-hour, weekly or other limit, or a spend cap), apart from every other failure: an `error` event with code `usage-limit`, and `resetsAt` when the tool says when the plan resets. byoa MUST read it from each CLI's own output, its structured code first, and its text only when that is missing: Claude Code's API error on its assistant message (`api_error` `usage_limit_reached`, with `rate_limit_info.resetsAt`) and its `rate_limit_event`; Codex's `codexErrorInfo` (`usageLimitExceeded`) and the used-up window of its `account/rateLimits/updated`; Grok Build's words and the `error_kind` of its `turn_completed` (Grok says no reset time). For a plan with a key (R1.8), the relay MUST read it from OpenCode's 429 and its documented usage meter (`/v1/usage`). A refusal for now (too many requests, a lab that is overloaded) MUST be `rate-limited`, and a login that the CLI's own code says does not work (Codex's `unauthorized`) MUST be `expired`. After a job ends with `usage-limit`, byoa MUST keep that in the store, for the user and harness (for a plan, the user and plan), until `resetsAt`, or for 15 minutes when the tool did not say. Until then, a job of that user and harness MUST end at once with the same error and start no sandbox, and the app MUST be able to read it with no sandbox (`usageLimit`). A new sign-in, a new key, a sign-out and a job that works end it.

### R2. MCP connections

- **R2.1** byoa MUST connect a remote MCP server for one user with MCP authorization (OAuth 2.1 with PKCE). It MUST use Client ID Metadata Documents when the server supports them, and Dynamic Client Registration only when it does not.
- **R2.2** byoa MUST also accept a bearer token that the user pastes.
- **R2.3** Each grant MUST have exactly one refresh owner: the app's backend. Two jobs that need a refresh at the same time MUST cause one refresh request.
- **R2.4** byoa MUST store grants through the store adapter (R6), in the app's own database, encrypted with a key that the app gives.
- **R2.5** byoa MUST let the app choose which MCP servers each job gets. (Bookish gives MCP servers only to jobs that the user asked for.)
- **R2.6** byoa MUST let the app's backend send a request with a user's grant to an API of the same service that is not MCP (for example an export). By default, the token goes only to the origin of the grant's MCP server. The app's backend MAY name more origins for the grants of one MCP server origin, as exact origins (https, no path, no wildcard), in its own configuration; the MCP server, the sandbox and the user MUST NOT be able to add one. byoa MUST add the token only for those origins, MUST NOT follow redirects, and MUST NOT give the token to the app. (Margins' MCP server is on `margin.rippling.computer`, and its export is on `helpful-tern-930.convex.site`.)
- **R2.7** byoa MUST let the app give its own tools as functions in its backend. The proxy (R3) MUST serve them as the tools of an MCP server, only to a job that the app gave them (R2.5), and MUST give each call the user of the job. The app writes no MCP server, and no user connects anything for them.

### R3. MCP proxy: real tokens stay outside the sandbox

- **R3.1** The `mcp.json` in the sandbox MUST point to the app's proxy, with a short-lived token for one job and one user.
- **R3.2** The proxy MUST add the real token to each request and send it to the MCP server.
- **R3.3** No real MCP token MUST be in the sandbox's environment, files or processes at any time.
- **R3.4** The proxy MUST refuse a job token after the job ends.
- **R3.5** Before the harness starts, byoa MUST check from the job's sandbox that each MCP server of the job answers through the proxy. When the sandbox cannot reach the proxy, the job MUST NOT start, and MUST end with an error. A server that does not answer MUST give an error event. (A harness that cannot reach a server leaves its tools out and still ends well.)

### R4. Skills, AGENTS.md and config

- **R4.1** byoa MUST write skills in the Agent Skills format where each harness reads them (for example `.claude/skills/`, `.agents/skills/`).
- **R4.2** byoa MUST write AGENTS.md, and CLAUDE.md for Claude Code, from one source.
- **R4.3** byoa MUST write MCP config in each harness's own format: JSON for Claude Code, TOML for Codex and Grok Build.
- **R4.4** byoa SHOULD read an Agent Plugins 1.0 package (`plugin.json`, `skills/`, `mcp.json`).

### R5. Harness and sandbox

- **R5.1** byoa MUST install a pinned version of each harness in each sandbox, or use a provider template with that version.
- **R5.2** A new harness version MUST reach every user at their next job. (Bookish had to copy a new core into old sandboxes, because a template reaches only new sandboxes.)
- **R5.3** Each sandbox provider MUST be one adapter with one interface: create, resume, run a command, write a file, read a file, mount a volume, pause, destroy. A command that runs out of its time MUST end with exit code 137 on every provider, not throw. Reading a file is optional: without it, byoa reads a file as base64 on a command's output. Setting a running sandbox's time again is optional too: byoa does it when a job has the AI login, so the job's wait in line for the login does not count. A provider says what it can do (`capabilities`): a provider with no volumes (Instabox, Sprites) refuses a volume, so the volume login of R1.5 does not work on it and createAgents refuses it; the stored login of R1.4 does. One conformance check (`test/helpers/conformance.ts`) MUST pass for each adapter.
- **R5.4** The lifecycle MUST be the app's choice, with the same app code on every provider:
  - **One kept sandbox per user (the default).** Each user has one sandbox of the app for each harness. The first job creates it. After each job, byoa pauses it (E2B: pause; Daytona and Instabox: stop; Sprites: sleep), and the next job resumes it, with a new job folder. One job of a user and harness runs at a time; the others wait in line (R5.8). When the provider no longer has the sandbox (it was deleted, or it expired), the next job creates a new one. A sandbox that times out during a job (a crash, a lost network) is paused, not deleted, and no process of that job runs when it resumes. byoa MUST delete the user's sandbox at sign-out, and MUST give the app a way to delete it, such as when it deletes the user.
  - **Many kept sandboxes per user (a `sandboxKey` for each job).** The same, but each key that the app gives a job (such as a project), and each conversation (R5.9), has its own sandbox and its own lease, so jobs with different keys run at the same time. With the stored login of R1.4, jobs share the login by default, for every harness. The app MUST be able to delete the sandbox of one key, or all of the user's.
  - **One sandbox per job (`sandboxPer: 'job'`).** Create a sandbox, load the user's setup, run the job, destroy the sandbox.

  In all three, the user's AI login (R1.4) and grants (R2) stay in the app's database, and the security properties of R1.4 and R3 do not depend on the choice: no real MCP token goes into the sandbox, a job token is refused after its job, and no copy of the AI login stays in the sandbox between jobs.
- **R5.5** `agents.run` MUST stream events (text, tool calls, permission requests, errors, turns, end) in one schema for every harness.
- **R5.6** byoa MUST let the app limit what the agent of a job may do, with each CLI's own options only (Lab rules). With `access: 'read-only'`, the agent MUST be able to call the job's MCP tools and to read files, so that the harness can read its skills and AGENTS.md; it MUST NOT be able to change a file, or to reach the network by itself. With Codex, its commands MUST NOT be able to read its home folder (CODEX_HOME), which holds the login. The default (`full`) is every tool of the harness with no approval, for a sandbox that is the job's alone.
- **R5.7** byoa MUST let the app choose the model and effort of each job, and of each harness by default, with each CLI's own flags only, and MUST list the models a user's plan can use, as each CLI lists them with that user's login. For a plan with a key (R1.8), byoa MUST list the plan's models from its API with the user's key, with no sandbox, and a job MUST name one of them (or get the app's default for the plan).
- **R5.8** One user's many agents MUST be the app's choice, in three patterns that work together: jobs of one sandbox wait in line and run in the order they came, with no time limit unless the app sets one; one job MAY carry several messages to one agent, which decides their order; and jobs with different sandboxes run at the same time (R5.4, R1.4).
- **R5.9** A job MAY name a conversation (the app's id, such as a chat thread). Then the job MUST continue the harness's own session of the earlier jobs of that conversation, with each CLI's own flags only (Lab rules): Claude Code `--session-id`, then `--resume`; Codex's app server, a thread that is not ephemeral, its id from the `thread/started` notification, then `thread/resume`; Grok Build's ACP, the session that `session/new` names, then `session/resume`. A conversation MUST have its own kept sandbox (R5.4), whose job folder stays from job to job, except the files byoa writes (R4), which each job gets new. Its jobs run one at a time. The `start` event MUST say whether the job resumed, and the `end` event MUST name the harness's session. After each job, byoa MUST keep the session id and, when it is not larger than the app's limit, a copy of the session's files, encrypted in the store; when the provider lost the sandbox, the next job MUST write that copy into its new sandbox. When there is no copy, the job MUST say so (an `error` with code `conversation`) and start a new session. The app MUST be able to delete a conversation, with its copy and its sandbox.
- **R5.10** A running job MUST take more messages from the app (steering), in each CLI's own protocol, through a small driver script that byoa runs in the sandbox beside the unmodified CLI: Claude Code's stream-json input (a message waits for the turn that runs); Codex's app server (`codex app-server`), whose `turn/steer` puts a message into the turn that runs; Grok Build's Agent Client Protocol (`grok agent stdio`), whose `x.ai/interject` extension does the same. A message that comes after a turn ended starts the next turn. Each turn before the last gives a `turn` event, and the job ends after the turn that answers the last message.

### R6. Store adapter

- **R6.1** The store adapter MUST be a small interface (get, put, delete, compare-and-set) that an app can write for its own database.
- **R6.2** Compare-and-set is needed for R2.3.

### R7. Developer experience

- **R7.1** A new app MUST reach its first agent run in under 50 lines of its own code.
- **R7.2** byoa MUST include a fake harness for tests, so apps can test without a plan or a sandbox.
- **R7.3** byoa SHOULD ship an agent skill in the Agent Skills format (`skills/byoa/`) that teaches a coding agent to add byoa to an app, in the npm package and with the package's version as its `metadata.version`, and its site SHOULD serve the docs for LLMs as `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt`. Both MUST name only the API that byoa has.

## Lab rules

byoa follows the labs' published rules as read on 2026-11-22:

- Anthropic ([legal and compliance](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/legal-and-compliance)) allows an end user to sign in to the unmodified Claude Code binary with their own plan, including where a platform hosts Claude Code. It forbids third parties to "collect, store, or intermediate Claude.ai credentials or session tokens", unless Anthropic agrees otherwise.
- OpenAI ([Sign in with ChatGPT Terms](https://openai.com/policies/sign-in-with-chatgpt-terms/), effective 2026-11-04) requires that "any persistent storage of Authentication Tokens must be local and under the user's control, not in a remote or managed environment", and that the plan is used "only for the application they connected". Paid or remotely hosted apps must [apply](https://openai.com/form/sign-in-with-chatgpt-interest/) to be partners.
- OpenCode ([Terms of Use](https://opencode.ai/legal/terms-of-service), effective 2026-11-08, read on 2026-11-25) says that the user "will only use the Services for your own internal use, and not on behalf of or for the benefit of any third party", and forbids using "multiple accounts to circumvent usage limits". Its [Go docs](https://opencode.ai/docs/console/go) say Go "is designed for OpenCode and other coding agents that produce similar types of requests", and ask each client to send "its own user agent" and "a stable session ID". OpenCode documents a Go key in Claude Code and in Codex. Whether an app may run a user's key for that user's own tasks is arguable, not clearly allowed: the work is the user's own, but the app gains from it too. Ian Hsiao accepted this for version 1 on 2026-11-25. There is no "Sign in with OpenCode" for apps; the user creates the key in OpenCode's Console.
- xAI (read on 2026-11-25) publishes Grok Build (`@xai-official/grok`, Apache-2.0) for SuperGrok and X Premium+ subscribers, with a device-code sign-in and a headless mode for scripts. Its [terms of service](https://x.ai/legal/terms-of-service) (2026-10-27) say "You may not share your account credentials or make your account available to anyone else", and its [acceptable use policy](https://x.ai/legal/acceptable-use-policy) forbids "Accessing the Services through unauthorized automated or non-human means". Neither says anything about an app that runs Grok Build for its own users, or that stores their login. Ian Hsiao accepted this when he added Grok Build to version 1; we have not asked xAI.

So byoa MUST:

- run only unmodified `claude`, `codex` and `grok` binaries, and never pretend to be another client (Codex's app server names byoa as its client: `clientInfo.name` is `byoa`);
- send the user to the lab's own sign-in page;
- not share one AI login between apps;
- for OpenCode Go, use only the user's own key, with OpenCode's documented API and the harness's own user agent, and never OpenCode's Console CLI sign-in, which has OpenCode's own client ID.

The labs' terms above restrict where these tokens may be stored. byoa keeps the AI login in the app's database by default (R1.4), and ships a per-user volume as an option (R1.5). Each app checks the labs' terms for its own use.

Each app is responsible for its own agreements with the labs. An app that offers OpenCode Go asks OpenCode (help@anoma.ly) before it ships it. We plan to sign agreements for our own apps when they have traction.

Our hosted mail demo (https://byoa.rippling.computer/demo, `examples/mail/convex`) is a hosted service for strangers: it keeps each visitor's Claude, ChatGPT or Grok login, encrypted, in its Convex deployment, for at most one hour after the visitor's last request, and then signs it out with the CLI and deletes it; sooner when the visitor clicks Sign out or Delete my data. That is the storage that Anthropic's and OpenAI's terms above restrict. Ian Hsiao accepted this on 2026-11-26, before we have an agreement with Anthropic or OpenAI. The demo's page tells visitors that the job uses their own plan and how long their login stays.

Our help agent, the chat in the corner of each page of https://byoa.rippling.computer (`site/help.html`, backend in [madeyexz/byoa-help](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa-help)), is the one place where we do not follow "each user uses their own plan": every visitor's question runs on Ian Hsiao's own ChatGPT plan, in Codex, signed in once with `codex login --device-auth` and kept, encrypted, in its Convex deployment. OpenAI's [Codex app-server docs](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/app-server) say "App-server authentication has never been permitted for commercial or hosted services", and its Terms of Use forbid making an account "available to anyone else". Ian Hsiao accepted that risk to his own account on 2026-11-26. The chat says that it runs on the maintainer's plan, and limits keep its use small. An app on byoa must not do this.

## Verification

Version 1 is done when every check below passes. Each check names the requirement it proves.

| # | Check | How | Proves |
|---|---|---|---|
| V1 | Bookish uses byoa | Replace `site/agent/login.ts`, `site/agent/sandbox.ts` and `src/core/connectors.ts` in Bookish with byoa. Bookish's existing e2e tests pass. | R1, R2, R5 |
| V2 | A second app uses byoa | A second app (the to-do example in `examples/todo`, Margins, or the mail app) runs its first agent job with byoa, on a real sandbox provider and a real plan, with no code copied from Bookish. Count the app's own lines. | R7.1 |
| V3 | Every harness | One test user runs the same task with Claude Code, with Codex and with Grok Build. Each run uses that user's own plan. | R1.1, R1.2, R5.5 |
| V4 | Two providers | The same user runs a job on E2B, then on Daytona or Instabox. The second job uses the same MCP grants and skills with no new MCP sign-in. | R5.3, R2 |
| V5 | Tokens stay out | After a job with an MCP call, a test searches the sandbox's environment, every file, and `/proc/*/cmdline` and `/proc/*/environ` for each real token. It finds none. | R3.3 |
| V6 | Old job tokens fail | A job token is used after its job ends. The proxy refuses it. | R3.4 |
| V7 | One refresh | Two jobs start at the same time with an expired access token (with `sandboxPer: 'job'`, so that they run at the same time). The MCP server's token endpoint gets one refresh request, and both jobs succeed. | R2.3, R6.2 |
| V8 | Sandbox lifecycle | By default, a user's second job runs in the first job's sandbox, which was paused between them, and jobs with two sandbox keys run in two more sandboxes, of which deleting one key removes only that one. When the provider no longer has a sandbox, the next job works in a new one with no new sign-in, and deleting the user's sandbox removes it at the provider. With `sandboxPer: 'job'`, after a job its sandbox no longer exists at the provider. | R5.4 |
| V9 | Harness update | Change the pinned version of a harness (Claude Code, Grok Build). The next job for an existing user runs the new version. | R5.2 |
| V10 | Config formats | For a sample plugin, the files byoa writes match the expected files for each harness, byte for byte. | R4 |
| V11 | Unmodified binaries | The test checks the hash of the installed `claude`, `codex` and `grok` binaries against the published packages. Grok's own postinstall unpacks its binary from the published `grok.br`: the test unpacks that file too. | Lab rules |
| V12 | The docs match the API | A test checks that every `agents.*` method, and every name imported from byoa, in the README, the docs (`docs/`) and the agent skill exists in byoa, that the package ships the skill, and that the skill's `metadata.version` and the pinned skill install in the README and in Getting started are the package's version. It also checks that the README's price table and its task have the numbers that the FAQ's cost tables give, as the home page's price bars do. | R7.3 |
| V13 | The app's own tools | A job with a real harness calls a tool that the app gave as a function. The function runs in the backend for the job's user. The app has no MCP server, and the user has no grant. | R2.7 |
| V14 | A proxy that is down | A job starts while its sandbox cannot reach the proxy. The harness does not start, and the job ends with an `mcp` error and `ok: false`. | R3.5 |
| V15 | Read-only access | A job with a real harness and `access: 'read-only'` reads its skill and calls an MCP tool. A command that writes a file fails, and a command that opens a network connection fails. With Codex, a command that reads CODEX_HOME fails. | R5.6 |
| V16 | Jobs at the same time | One user starts three Codex jobs with three sandbox keys. They run at the same time with one sign-in, and the login works after them. | R1.4, R5.4, R5.8 |
| V17 | A backend that dies | A job's CLI refreshes its login, and the backend dies before the job closes. The next job in that sandbox uses the refreshed login, and a job after a new sign-in uses the new login. A real check also finds no login file in the sandbox once the provider paused it. | R1.4 |
| V18 | A sign-in that is left | A sign-in that the app cancels has no sandbox at the provider right after. A sign-in with no check-in for a few minutes has none either. | R1.7 |
| V19 | Models | `listModels` returns, for a real login of each harness, what the CLI lists; a job with a model and effort from that list runs with them. | R5.7 |
| V20 | OpenCode Go (beta: not run yet) | One test user with a real Go key runs the same task with Claude Code and with Codex on E2B, through the relay. Three jobs of that user run at the same time; a job gets the model it names; a key that OpenCode refuses is `expired`, and one of a workspace with no Go plan is `no-plan`. A search of each sandbox's environment, files and `/proc/*/cmdline` finds no key. | R1.8, R1.6, R5.7, R5.8 |
| V21 | Conversations | With a real login of each harness on E2B, one user's conversation has three jobs. The second job knows what the first was told and finds the file the first wrote in the job folder. The third job runs after the conversation's sandbox was deleted at the provider, and still knows it, from the stored copy. A job of each harness takes a second message while it runs and answers it before it ends. | R5.9, R5.10 |
| V22 | Protocol models | TLC checks TLA+ models (`spec/tla/`) of the job lifecycle and the slot's lease, the shared login's lease and its refresh, crash recovery, the sign-in sandbox and sign-out, the store indexes, each store adapter's guarantees (lost answers, retries, stale reads), steering, the MCP grant's refresh, job tokens, plan keys, the usage-limit hold, and the hosted demo and help agent, with backends that die, leases that run out and clocks that differ, and liveness under stated fairness. Each model says what TLC must find (no error, or the counterexample of a known issue) and whether it is in the fast set. | R1.4, R1.6, R1.7, R1.8, R1.9, R2.3, R3.4, R5.4, R5.8, R5.9, R5.10, R6 |
| V23 | A used-up plan | With output of each pinned CLI for a used-up plan, in the shape that its binary writes, and a stand-in for OpenCode's 429 and usage meter: the job ends with `usage-limit` and the reset that the tool said; the next job of that user and harness ends at once, with no sandbox and no request to OpenCode; after the reset, a job runs. A refusal for now is `rate-limited`, and Codex's `unauthorized` is `expired`. | R1.9 |

V1 to V9 and V13 to V21 run against real providers and real plans, so they cost money. They run before each release, not on every commit. V10, V11, V12 and the fake-harness tests run on every commit; these include V13, V14, V16, V17, V18, V19, V20 and V21 with the fake harness, a stand-in CLI and, for V20, a stand-in for OpenCode's API. V23 runs only so (`test/login.test.ts`, `test/plan.test.ts`): no real check runs a plan out, so the stand-ins' output comes from the pinned binaries (Claude Code's stream-json schema, Codex's `generate-json-schema` and source of 0.171.0, Grok Build's strings) and from OpenCode's docs, not from a plan that ran out. In this repository: `npm test` runs V10, V12 and the fake-harness tests, `npm run test:v11` runs V11, `spec/tla/check.sh` runs V22 by hand, when a protocol or its model changes (`TLA_SET=fast` for the fast set; no CI runs it, because the models do not read the code: each finding's test in `npm test` guards the code), and the job `example-todo` runs the to-do example's fake-harness tests (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`). `npm test` starts no paid sandbox, also when the providers' keys are set: each paid check needs its own flag. `npm run test:v4` runs V4 (`test/v4.test.ts`) with `E2B_API_KEY` and `DAYTONA_API_KEY`; `BYOA_V4_PROVIDERS=e2b,instabox` runs it on E2B and Instabox. `npm run test:e2b` runs V8 on E2B (`test/e2b.test.ts`), `npm run test:daytona` runs V8 on Daytona (`test/daytona.test.ts`), `npm run test:instabox` runs V8 on Instabox (`test/instabox.test.ts`), and `npm run test:sprites` runs V8 on Sprites (`test/sprites.test.ts`). `npm run test:v20` runs V20 on E2B (`test/v20.test.ts`), with `OPENCODE_GO_API_KEY` and `E2B_API_KEY` set. V20 has not run yet, so OpenCode Go (R1.8) is in beta: its tests use a stand-in for OpenCode's API, and the real Claude Code and Codex were checked only against that stand-in, locally and on E2B. `node scripts/v21.ts` runs V21 on E2B in steps (`login <harness>`, `check`, `cleanup`), because it needs a person to sign in. On an Instabox plan that allows fewer than three sandboxes (the free plan allows one), V8 there checks one sandbox key alone, not two at the same time.

## Open questions

- Does the first version support Cloudflare Workers, or only Node and Convex?
- How does a Claude login move from one sandbox provider to another without the app holding it? Today the user signs in again.
- Do Anthropic, OpenAI and xAI accept the default stored login (R1.4) for apps that run their unmodified CLIs, or does an app need an agreement with them? We will ask them.
- Does OpenCode accept an app that runs a user's Go key for that user's own tasks (R1.8), given "only for your own internal use"? We will ask them.
- The shared login (R1.4) is the default for every harness. The CLIs also refresh their login when the lab answers 401 to a token that has not run out. Two sandboxes that get that answer at the same time both refresh, and one refresh fails. How often does that occur?
- `access: 'read-only'` (R5.6) does not hide files: the agent can read each file that its user can read, also Claude Code's and Grok Build's own login files (Codex's are denied to its commands). Does byoa need a level that lets the agent read only its job folder, for apps that run on the user's own computer?
- How long does a user's paused sandbox stay? Today byoa deletes it only at sign-out and when the app calls `deleteSandbox`. E2B and Instabox keep a paused or stopped sandbox with no time limit; Daytona archives a stopped one after 7 days, and the next job restores it more slowly. Does byoa need a limit for users who stop using an app?
- Do we write a spec for credential references as an extension of Agent Plugins, and send it to the Agentic AI Foundation?

Source: https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/skills/byoa/SKILL.md

---
name: byoa
description: Adds byoa to an app, so the app runs each user's own Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build in a sandbox (E2B, Daytona, Instabox, Sprites or local), on the user's own Claude, ChatGPT, Grok or OpenCode Go plan, with the user's MCP connections. Use when you add AI agent jobs to an app's backend with byoa, write its sign-in, MCP connect, proxy or callback routes, stream agents.run events to a UI, write a byoa store adapter, or test with byoa's fake harness.
metadata:
  version: "1.1.0"
---

# Add byoa to an app

byoa is a library. It runs inside the app's own backend (Node, Bun or Convex actions). It is not a hosted service. The app gives it a sandbox adapter and a store adapter. byoa then signs each user in to their own plan, keeps their MCP grants, and runs each job in that user's sandbox (or, as an option, a new sandbox for each job).

The reference app is the to-do example: https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/tree/main/examples/todo. Its `app.ts` holds all of its byoa code: the sign-in, the app's own tools (`tools`), a chat (`conversation`), more messages while a job runs (`job.send`) and `access: 'read-only'`. Its `todos.ts` holds the tools and a SQLite store. Read both before you write the app's code, and copy their patterns.

The full API, with every option and event, is in [reference/api.md](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/skills/byoa/reference/api.md). The rules every app must follow are in "Lab rules" below. Do not skip them.

## 1. Install

Install byoa from npm:

```sh
npm install @madeyexz/byoa
bun add @madeyexz/byoa
```

Also install the sandbox SDK that the app uses: `e2b` for E2B, `@daytona/sdk` for Daytona; Instabox and Sprites need none. byoa needs Node 22.18 or later, or Bun. The package is `@madeyexz/byoa`: do not write `npm install byoa` or `import ... from 'byoa'`, and do not install `byoa-sdk`, an unrelated package.

`metadata.version` above is the `version` in the package.json next to this skill. The npm package has this skill in it (from 1.1.0), so `npx skills experimental_sync -y` after the install links `node_modules/@madeyexz/byoa/skills/byoa` into the app's skills, and the skill always matches the installed byoa. When the installed version is not `metadata.version`, believe the installed version's types.

When a name in this skill is a type error, the installed byoa is older than this skill: update it (`npm install @madeyexz/byoa@latest`), or use only what the installed version's types have. Do not write around the missing types.

## 2. One createAgents

Make one `agents` object in the backend. Do it once per process (or once per Convex action).

```ts
import { createAgents } from '@madeyexz/byoa'
import { e2b } from '@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/e2b'           // or: daytona from '@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/daytona', instabox from '@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/instabox', sprites from '@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/sprites'
import { postgresStore } from '@madeyexz/byoa/store/postgres' // or: convexStore, or the app's own Store

const agents = createAgents({
  app: 'myapp',                                     // lower-case letters, digits, -; at most 24
  sandbox: e2b({ apiKey: process.env.E2B_API_KEY }),
  store: postgresStore({ query: (sql, args) => pool.query(sql, args) }),
  encryptionKey: process.env.BYOA_KEY!,             // openssl rand -base64 32; keep it the same between restarts
  proxyUrl: 'https://myapp.example.com/byoa/mcp',   // public HTTPS; serve agents.proxy here and below
  oauth: { redirectUrl: 'https://myapp.example.com/byoa/callback' },
  tools: { todos: todoTools },                      // the app's own tools, as functions: see section 5
})
```

- **Store.** `postgresStore` needs its table once: run `POSTGRES_SCHEMA` (from `@madeyexz/byoa/store/postgres`). For Convex, see reference/api.md. For another database, write a `Store` with four methods: `get`, `put`, `delete`, `cas` (compare-and-set). The example's `sqliteStore` in `examples/todo/todos.ts` is one in 19 lines. A new version on every write is required, and a deleted and rewritten key must never get an old version back.
- **Sandbox.** `e2b()`, `daytona()` and `instabox()` read their API key from `E2B_API_KEY` / `DAYTONA_API_KEY` / `INSTABOX_API_KEY` when you give none, and `sprites()` its token from `SPRITES_TOKEN`. Instabox and Sprites have no volumes, so use the default `storedLogin()` there, not `cliLogin`. The default E2B template is named `byoa`, and a new E2B account does not have it: the first job then fails with `404: template 'byoa' not found`. Build it one time with `buildE2BTemplate()` from `@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/e2b`, or pass `e2b({ template: 'base' })`: byoa then installs the pinned harness in each new sandbox (about 10 seconds). `localSandbox()` from `@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/local` is a folder on this computer. It isolates nothing: use it only for development and tests.
- **The sandbox must reach `proxyUrl`.** With E2B, Daytona, Instabox or Sprites it must be a public HTTPS URL (in development, a tunnel such as `cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:3000`). On Daytona Tier 1 and 2, only allowed domains work, such as `*.convex.site` or `*.workers.dev`.

## 3. Routes the app must serve

The app serves two byoa routes, and its own API routes that call `agents.*`. All handlers are fetch handlers (`Request` → `Response`). On Node, wrap the app's handler with `toNodeListener` from `@madeyexz/byoa/node`.

```ts
if (url.pathname.startsWith('/byoa/mcp/')) return agents.proxy(req)  // the MCP proxy: no app session check here
if (url.pathname === '/byoa/callback') {                               // the MCP server's sign-in page sends the browser here
  const p = url.searchParams
  await agents.finishMcp({ state: p.get('state') ?? '', code: p.get('code') ?? undefined, error: p.get('error') ?? undefined })
  return Response.redirect(`${publicUrl}/`, 302)
}
```

- The proxy checks the job token itself. Do not put the app's own sign-in check in front of it, because the harness in the sandbox has no app session.
- `finishMcp` returns `{ user, name }`. It finds the user from the stored `state`, so the callback needs no session either.
- Every other route reads the user from the app's own session. The `userId` you pass to byoa is the app's stable user id. Never take it from a header or a body that the browser controls (the example's `x-user` header is a stand-in only).

## 4. Sign the user in to their plan

The sign-in runs the unmodified CLI in a sandbox. The user signs in on the lab's own page. byoa gives the app only that page's URL (and, for Codex and Grok Build, a code).

```ts
// Claude: show the URL; the user signs in and pastes the code that Anthropic's page shows
const { url } = await agents.connectLogin(userId, 'claude')
const r = await agents.finishLogin(userId, 'claude', { code })            // r.state: 'signed-in' or an error

// ChatGPT (Codex): show the URL and the code; the user enters the code on OpenAI's page
const { url, code } = await agents.connectLogin(userId, 'codex')
const r = await agents.finishLogin(userId, 'codex', { waitMs: 20_000 })  // call again while r.state === 'pending'

// Grok (Grok Build, for SuperGrok and X Premium+): the same as Codex, on xAI's page
const { url, code } = await agents.connectLogin(userId, 'grok')
const r = await agents.finishLogin(userId, 'grok', { waitMs: 20_000 })

await agents.cancelLogin(userId, 'codex')  // the user closed the sign-in: its sandbox ends now
await agents.loginState(userId, 'claude')  // 'signed-in' | 'signed-out' | 'expired'
await agents.signOut(userId, 'claude')
```

Show `url` as a link or a QR code, so the user can sign in on another device. Keep each request short (for example `waitMs: 20_000`) and let the page call `finishLogin` again while the state is `pending`. This also works from short-lived backends such as Convex actions. The sign-in's sandbox lives only while the page checks in: each `finishLogin` keeps it 2 more minutes. For Claude, have the page call `finishLogin(userId, 'claude')` with no code every 30 seconds while the user is on Anthropic's page. When the user closes the sign-in, call `cancelLogin`. Copy the example's `page.html`.

**Where the login stays.** With no `login` option, byoa keeps the CLI's own login files encrypted in the app's store (`storedLogin()`, the default). Each job gets a copy in its sandbox; after the job, byoa saves it back when the CLI refreshed it and removes it from the sandbox. A user's jobs in different sandboxes share the login, for every harness. Options:

- `login: storedLogin({ store: loginStore, encryptionKey: loginKey })`: a table and a key of their own.
- `login: cliLogin`: a volume of that user, behind the sandbox adapter. The app's database never holds the login. It needs a provider with volumes (E2B volumes must be turned on for the team).

Tell the developer that the labs' terms restrict where these tokens may be stored (see Lab rules), and let them choose. Do not choose for them in silence.

**OpenCode Go (beta; a key, not a sign-in).** No real Go key has run it yet: tell the developer it is in beta. A user with an OpenCode Go plan runs Claude Code or Codex on it with an API key that they create in OpenCode's Console (`oc_sk_…`). The app takes the key one time (a password field; never in a URL or a log) and gives it to byoa:

```ts
const r = await agents.connectKey(userId, 'opencode-go', key)  // r.state: 'signed-in', or 'no-plan' (no Go plan yet); with r.error when OpenCode refused it
await agents.loginState(userId, 'opencode-go')                // 'signed-in' | 'signed-out' | 'expired' | 'no-plan'
await agents.signOut(userId, 'opencode-go')                   // deletes the key
```

byoa keeps the key encrypted in the store. It never goes into the sandbox: `agents.proxy` relays the harness's model requests to OpenCode and adds the key there, so the same proxy route serves it (do not filter paths below `proxyUrl`). Jobs pass `plan: 'opencode-go'` and a `model` (section 6). Tell the developer that OpenCode's terms do not clearly allow an app to run a user's key for them (see Lab rules), and let them choose.

## 5. Connect MCP tools, one time per user

```ts
// A server with its own sign-in (MCP authorization, OAuth 2.1 with PKCE)
const c = await agents.connectMcp(userId, 'https://mcp.notion.com/mcp', { name: 'notion' })
if (!c.connected) return Response.json({ signInUrl: c.signInUrl })  // send the browser there; it comes back to /byoa/callback

// A server that takes a token the user pasted (or the app's own server, with this user's token)
await agents.connectMcp(userId, 'https://myapp.example.com/mcp', { name: 'todos', bearer: token })

await agents.listMcp(userId)            // [{ name, url }]
await agents.removeMcp(userId, 'notion')
```

- `name`: lower-case letters, digits and -, at most 32. The job asks for servers by this name.
- The URL must be `https://` (or `http://` on localhost). With `bearer`, byoa checks the token with one MCP `initialize` and throws if the server refuses it.
- A sign-in that is not finished in 15 minutes runs out; call `connectMcp` again.
- byoa refreshes each grant itself, with one refresh owner. Do not refresh or read the tokens in app code. To call a non-MCP API of the same service (for example an export), use `agents.fetchWithGrant(userId, name, url)`.

**The app's own tools.** Do not write an MCP server for the app's own data. Give the tools to `createAgents` as functions, and name the group in the job's `mcp`:

```ts
const todoTools = {
  add_todo: {
    description: 'Add one to-do.',
    input: { type: 'object', properties: { title: { type: 'string' } }, required: ['title'] },  // JSON Schema of the arguments
    run: ({ title }, { user }) => db.addTodo(user, String(title)),                             // in the backend, for the job's user
  },
  list_todos: { description: "List the user's to-dos.", run: (_args, { user }) => db.todos(user) },
}
const agents = createAgents({ ...options, tools: { todos: todoTools } })
agents.run(userId, { harness, task, mcp: ['todos'] })
```

- `agents.proxy` serves them at `<proxyUrl>/todos` and checks the job token. `user` is the user of the job; never take the user from the arguments.
- What `run` returns goes to the agent: a string as it is, other values as JSON. When it throws, the agent gets the message as a failed call. byoa does not check the arguments against `input`: check them in `run`.
- No user connects anything for them, and `listMcp` does not list them. `connectMcp` refuses their names.

## 6. Run a job and stream its events

```ts
for await (const ev of agents.run(userId, {
  harness: 'claude',                   // 'claude' | 'codex' | 'grok' | 'fake'
  task,                                // the user's request
  mcp: ['notion'],                     // the servers this job gets; default none
  setup: { agentsMd, skills },         // AGENTS.md (and CLAUDE.md for Claude Code); skills: [{ name, files: { 'SKILL.md': '...' } }]
  access: 'read-only',                 // what the agent may do; default 'full'
  model: 'opus', effort: 'high',       // optional; default createAgents({ models }), else the CLI's own
  // plan: 'opencode-go',              // optional: the user's OpenCode Go key in place of the lab login; then model is a Go model
})) {
  // ev.type: 'start' | 'text' | 'tool_call' | 'tool_result' | 'permission' | 'error' | 'turn' | 'end'
}
```

- The events are the same for every harness. The full schema is in reference/api.md.
- `run` never throws for job failures. It yields `error` events (`code`: `signed-out`, `expired`, `no-plan`, `usage-limit`, `rate-limited`, `harness`, `sandbox`, `mcp` or `conversation`) and always ends with one `end` event (`ok`, `result`, `usage`). On `signed-out` or `expired`, show the sign-in again (for `plan: 'opencode-go'`, ask for a new key); on `no-plan`, tell the user that the key's workspace has no Go plan.
- **A used-up plan.** `usage-limit`: the user's plan is used up (a 5-hour, weekly or other limit); `resetsAt` (ms since 1970) is when it resets, when the tool said (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode Go; not Grok Build). Show it to the user. byoa keeps it until then (15 minutes when the tool gave no time): a job of that user and harness ends at once with the same error and starts no sandbox. `agents.usageLimit(userId, harness)` (or `'opencode-go'`) says so before a job, with no sandbox: check it before you show a chat input or start a job. A new sign-in, a new key or a sign-out ends it. `rate-limited`: the lab refused for now (too many requests, overloaded); try again in a moment. Do not match the error's text: use the code.
- A server in `mcp` that the user has not connected gives an `error` with code `mcp`, and the job runs without it.
- **The proxy check.** Before the harness starts, byoa checks from the sandbox that each of the job's servers answers through the proxy. When the sandbox cannot reach the proxy, the job does not start: an `error` with code `mcp`, then `end` with `ok: false` (`session` throws `ProxyError`). A server that does not answer gives an `error` with code `mcp`, and the job runs. Show these errors: they mean a wrong `proxyUrl`, a tunnel that ended, or a server that is down.
- **What the agent may do (`access`).** With `'full'` (the default), the agent has every tool of its harness with no approval: a shell, file changes and the network. That is for coding agents in a sandbox that is the job's alone. With `'read-only'`, the agent calls the job's MCP tools and reads files (the harness reads its skills this way: do not forbid the shell in AGENTS.md, because Codex reads a skill with `cat`); it cannot change a file or reach the network by itself. Use `'read-only'` when the agent needs only its MCP tools (a to-do list, a mail client), and always with `localSandbox()` on a user's own computer. Apart from Codex's home folder (its login), it does not hide files: the agent can read each file its user can read. Ask the developer which one each kind of job needs.
- **The sandbox.** By default (`sandboxPer: 'user'`), each user has one sandbox of the app for each harness: the first job creates it, byoa pauses it after each job and resumes it for the next, with a new job folder. One job of a user and harness runs at a time; the others wait in line, in the order they came, with no limit unless `waitMs` sets one (set it on short-lived backends such as Convex actions). A sandbox the provider lost is replaced by a new one. When one user has many workspaces (projects, conversations), pass `sandboxKey` in `run` or `session`: each key gets its own kept sandbox and lease. `sandboxPer: 'job'` gives each job a new sandbox and destroys it after the job; use it when nothing may stay between jobs.
- **Conversations.** For a chat, pass the chat's id as `conversation` in each `run` of it (one harness per conversation). The job continues the harness's own session of the earlier jobs, in the conversation's own kept sandbox, whose `~/work` stays; `start` says `resumed`, `end` names the `session`. byoa keeps the transcript encrypted in the store (up to `transcriptBytes`), so a lost sandbox does not lose the conversation; when it is too large, the next job gives an `error` with code `conversation` and starts again. Call `agents.deleteConversation(userId, chatId)` when the user deletes the chat. A job with no `conversation` remembers nothing of earlier jobs, and its `~/work` is new.
- **More messages to a running job (steering).** `run` returns a `Job`; `job.send(text)` gives the running agent one more message, with every harness. Codex and Grok Build take it into the turn that runs; Claude Code after that turn. Each turn before the last gives a `turn` event, and `send` returns false once the job ended: then send it as the next job of the conversation. The recipe below puts both together.
- **Many agents of one user.** Three ways, which an app can mix; ask the developer which they want:
  1. A queue: jobs of one sandbox run one after the other. `onWait: ({ for, ahead })` tells the app how many are ahead.
  2. Several messages to one agent: `task: ['first', 'second']`. The agent reads them all and decides the order.
  3. Several sandboxes at once: a `sandboxKey` for each agent, or `sandboxPer: 'job'`. The jobs share the user's login and run at the same time, for every harness. Tell the developer the risk that stays with a shared login (reference/api.md, `storedLogin`); `storedLogin({ parallel: false })` turns sharing off.
- **Models.** `agents.listModels(userId, harness)` lists what the user's plan can use (`id`, `efforts`); pass `model` and `effort` in `run`, or defaults in `createAgents({ models })`. Each call starts a sandbox, so keep the list for a while. With `plan: 'opencode-go'`, a job needs a model of the plan: `agents.listModels(userId, 'opencode-go')` lists them from OpenCode's API with no sandbox, and `createAgents({ models: { 'opencode-go': { model } } })` sets the default.
- `agents.signOut` deletes the user's sandbox for that harness. When the app deletes a user, call `agents.deleteSandbox(userId)` too; when it deletes a project that had a key, `agents.deleteSandbox(userId, { sandboxKey })`.
- If the client goes away, stop the loop (or call `return()` on the generator): byoa then closes the job token and pauses (or destroys) the sandbox. The example's `ndjson()` in `app.ts` streams the events as JSON lines and does this on `cancel`.
- To run the app's own program around the unmodified harness, use `agents.session(userId, { harness, mcp })` and call `s.close()` in a `finally`. See reference/api.md.

### A chat with the agent

A chat is the most common feature: each message of the user is one job of one `conversation`, and a message that comes while a job runs goes to that job. The routes, as in the example's `app.ts`:

```ts
const running = new Map<string, Job>()          // the jobs that run now; import { type Job } from '@madeyexz/byoa'

// POST /api/ask { chat, task }: one message of the user. The page makes the chat id one time (crypto.randomUUID())
const job = agents.run(userId, { harness, task, conversation: chat, mcp: ['todos'], setup: { agentsMd }, access: 'read-only' })
const id = crypto.randomUUID()
running.set(`${userId}/${id}`, job)
// stream the events to the page with the job's id (the example's ndjson(), with an `x-job` header), and remove the
// job from `running` when the stream ends or the browser goes away

// POST /api/ask/send { job, text }: a message while the agent works
const j = running.get(`${userId}/${body.job}`)
return Response.json({ sent: j ? await j.send(body.text) : false })   // false: the job ended; send it as a new /api/ask

// POST /api/chat/delete { chat }: the user deletes the chat or starts a new one
await agents.deleteConversation(userId, chat)
```

What the page does with each event:

| Event | The page |
| --- | --- |
| `start` with `resumed: false` | A new session. When the chat had earlier messages, its history is gone (the provider lost the sandbox, and the transcript was larger than `transcriptBytes`): an `error` with code `conversation` comes first. Say so. |
| `text`, `tool_call`, `tool_result` | Show them as they come. Refresh the app's data after a `tool_result` that changed it. |
| `turn` | One answer ended, and the agent goes on with the message the user sent while it worked. Keep the input open. |
| `end` | The job ended. `ok: false` follows an `error`. Close the input for `send`, so the next message is a new job. |
| `error` `signed-out` or `expired` | Show the sign-in again (for `plan: 'opencode-go'`, ask for a new key). |
| `error` `usage-limit` | The user's plan is used up. Show when it resets (`resetsAt`, else the message), and keep the input closed until then (`agents.usageLimit`). |
| `error` `rate-limited` | The lab refused for now. Say so, and let the user try again in a moment. |
| `error` `harness` | The CLI failed. Show the message. |

- Key `running` by the user too, and read the user from the session, so one user cannot send to another user's job.
- `running` is in this process's memory. With more than one backend process, `send` must reach the process that runs the job (sticky sessions, or one process for jobs).
- One conversation is one harness's session. When the user changes the harness, start a new chat id.

## 7. Test without a plan or a sandbox

Use `harness: 'fake'`, `localSandbox()` from `@madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/local` and `memoryStore()` from `@madeyexz/byoa`. The fake harness runs no model. Each task line `call <server>.<tool> <json>` is one MCP call through the real proxy, so a test proves the app's routes, grants and proxy end to end. With the local sandbox, `proxyUrl` can be `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/byoa/mcp`. Copy `examples/todo/todo.test.ts`. A conversation works with the fake harness: in each job of one, it says `fake harness remembers N earlier messages`, so a test can check that a chat goes on and that a deleted chat starts again. Steering does not: the fake harness takes no message while it runs, so `job.send` returns false. Do not write a test that expects `send` to work with `fake`. Do not offer `fake` to end users in production.

## Lab rules

Every app on byoa must follow these rules. If a request breaks one, stop and tell the developer.

- Run only the unmodified `claude`, `codex` and `grok` binaries that byoa installs (pinned, and checked in byoa's own tests). Do not patch them, wrap them to change what they send, or set headers or a user agent to pretend to be another client.
- Send the user to the lab's own sign-in page, from `connectLogin`. Do not embed, proxy or copy that page, and never ask the user for a password or an API key in place of it. The one key byoa takes is an OpenCode Go key, with `connectKey`, which OpenCode's Console makes for this.
- For OpenCode Go, never use OpenCode's Console CLI sign-in (`npx @opencode/console`): it has OpenCode's own client ID. OpenCode's terms say "only for your own internal use, and not on behalf of or for the benefit of any third party", so it is not clearly allowed for an app: tell the developer to ask OpenCode (help@anoma.ly) first.
- Never read, export or call the labs' APIs with the user's AI tokens. The CLI is the only client that uses them. Do not call the labs' token endpoints.
- One app's AI login is only for that app. Give each app its own `app` name and its own store. Never share a login between apps.
- Real MCP tokens never go into the sandbox. Give a job its servers with `mcp: [...]`. Never put a grant's token in `setup`, the task, environment variables or files.
- The labs' terms restrict where AI logins may be stored. Anthropic says third parties may not "collect, store, or intermediate Claude.ai credentials or session tokens" without its agreement. OpenAI says stored tokens must be "local and under the user's control", and paid or hosted apps must apply to be partners. xAI's terms forbid sharing an account and "unauthorized automated" access, and say nothing about an app that runs Grok Build for its users. byoa's default keeps the login in the app's database; `cliLogin` keeps it in a per-user volume. Each app checks the terms and makes its own agreements: https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/SPEC.md#lab-rules

## Check your work

- The app's byoa code is small: the example's backend, a chat with sign-in, tools and steering, uses byoa in 49 lines. If you write sign-in, OAuth, token refresh or sandbox code yourself, you are rebuilding byoa: use its API.
- Run the app's tests with the fake harness and the local sandbox.
- Every API name you use is in reference/api.md. If a name is not there, read the source (`src/agents.ts` and `src/job.ts` in https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa) before you use it.

---

Source: https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/examples/todo/README.md

# AI-native to-do list: an example app on byoa

A small to-do app. The user signs in with their own Claude, ChatGPT or Grok (SuperGrok, X Premium+) plan (or saves the key of their OpenCode Go plan), and then chats with the agent about their to-dos ("add buy milk, and mark the oldest one done", then "now the same for tomorrow"). Each message is one job of the chat: byoa resumes the chat's sandbox (or creates it for the first job), continues the user's own, unmodified Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build session in it, and pauses the sandbox after the job. While the agent works, the user can send it one more message.

The app has no code from Bookish. It is the second app for check V2 in [SPEC.md](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/SPEC.md#verification).

## The files

| File | What it does | Lines of code |
|---|---|---|
| [app.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/examples/todo/app.ts) | The backend, as one fetch handler. All of the app's byoa code is here. | 100 |
| [todos.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/examples/todo/todos.ts) | The app's own data (SQLite), its four to-do tools, and byoa's store adapter for SQLite. | 65 |
| [main.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/examples/todo/main.ts) | Starts the server on Node and selects the sandbox provider. | 24 |
| [page.html](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/examples/todo/page.html) | The page: sign in, the chat, the list and more tools, styled after shadcn/ui, with no build step. | 365 |
| [todo.test.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/examples/todo/todo.test.ts) | Tests with byoa's fake harness. | 108 |

"Lines of code" does not count empty lines and comments. Of the backend's 189 lines, 49 in app.ts use byoa: `createAgents`, the routes that call `agents.*`, the chat and its messages while a job runs, the MCP callback, and the stream of events to the page. The SQLite store adapter is 19 more; with byoa's own Postgres or Convex adapter, it is one line. The rest is the to-do app itself.

## How the app uses byoa

1. **One `createAgents`** ([app.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/examples/todo/app.ts)). The app gives byoa its sandbox provider, its own database (through `sqliteStore`, 19 lines in [todos.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/examples/todo/todos.ts)), an encryption key, and the URLs where it serves byoa's MCP proxy and the MCP sign-in callback. The app gives no `login` option, so byoa keeps each user's plan login (the CLI's own login files) encrypted in the app's database, and writes a copy into each job's sandbox. After the job, byoa saves the files back when the CLI refreshed them, and removes them from the sandbox. No sandbox volumes are needed. With `login: cliLogin`, the login stays in a volume of the user instead, and the app's database never holds it. The labs' terms restrict where these tokens may be stored: see [SPEC.md](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/SPEC.md#lab-rules), and check them for your own app.
2. **Sign in to the plan.** `agents.connectLogin(user, 'claude')` runs the real `claude auth login` in a sandbox and gives the URL of Anthropic's own sign-in page. The user signs in there and pastes the code that page shows; `agents.finishLogin` types it into the CLI. For ChatGPT, `codex login --device-auth` gives OpenAI's page and a code to enter there; for Grok, `grok login --device-auth` gives xAI's page and a code. For OpenCode Go, the user makes an API key in OpenCode's Console and saves it on the page: `agents.connectKey(user, 'opencode-go', key)` checks it with OpenCode and keeps it encrypted, and a job with `plan: 'opencode-go'` and a model from `agents.listModels(user, 'opencode-go')` runs Claude Code or Codex on it. The key never goes into the sandbox.
3. **The app's own tools.** The four to-do tools are functions in [todos.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/examples/todo/todos.ts), given to `createAgents({ tools: { todos } })`. `agents.proxy` serves them at `<proxyUrl>/todos` to each job that names `todos` in `mcp`, and gives each tool the user of the job, from the job token. So the app writes no MCP server, keeps no token for it, and the user connects nothing. The user can also connect any remote MCP server (for example Notion) with its own sign-in page: `agents.connectMcp`, then byoa does the OAuth and calls `/byoa/callback`.
4. **Chat.** `agents.run(user, { harness, task, mcp, setup: { agentsMd }, access: 'read-only', conversation: chat })` gives a stream of events (`start`, `text`, `tool_call`, `tool_result`, `error`, `turn`, `end`) in one schema for every harness. The app sends them to the page as they come, one JSON object for each line. `conversation` is the page's id of the chat, so each job continues the harness's own session of the chat (`start` says `resumed`). **New chat** calls `agents.deleteConversation`. `access: 'read-only'`: the agent calls its tools and reads files, and cannot change a file or reach the network by itself.
5. **One more message while the agent works.** `run` returns a `Job`. The app keeps the running jobs by an id that it sends to the page (the `x-job` header), and `POST /api/ask/send` calls `job.send(text)`. A turn that is not the last gives a `turn` event. `send` returns false when the job ended, or with the fake harness, which takes no message while it runs.
6. **The proxy.** The harness in the sandbox gets only a job token. Its MCP calls go to `agents.proxy`, which runs the app's tools, or adds the user's real token and sends the call to the MCP server. The real token never goes into the sandbox.

## Run it

You need Node 22.18 or later. From the root of this repository:

```sh
npm ci                                  # installs and builds byoa
cd examples/todo && npm install
BYOA_KEY=$(openssl rand -base64 32) FAKE=1 npm start
```

Open http://127.0.0.1:3000, type a name, select **Fake harness**, and ask with lines such as `call todos.add_todo {"title":"Buy milk"}`. The fake harness runs no model: each line `call <server>.<tool> <json>` is one MCP call through the real proxy. Ask again in the same chat, and it says how many earlier messages it remembers.

In your own app, install byoa with `npm install @madeyexz/byoa` instead.

### Settings

| Variable | Default | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `BYOA_KEY` | (required) | 32 random bytes as base64. byoa encrypts the MCP grants, the plan logins and the chats' transcripts with it. Keep it the same between restarts. |
| `SANDBOX` | `local` | `local`, `e2b` (needs `E2B_API_KEY`) or `daytona` (needs `DAYTONA_API_KEY`). |
| `PUBLIC_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:$PORT` | Where browsers and sandboxes reach the app. |
| `PORT` | `3000` | |
| `DB` | `.data/todo.db` | The SQLite file. |
| `FAKE` | off | `1` lets jobs use the fake harness. |

The local sandbox is a folder on your computer. It isolates nothing, so use it only on your own computer. With Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build in it, the harness runs on your computer with your login.

With E2B or Daytona, the sandbox must reach the proxy, so `PUBLIC_URL` must be a public HTTPS URL, for example from `cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:3000`. On Daytona Tier 1 and Tier 2, a sandbox reaches only [allowed domains](https://www.daytona.io/docs/en/network-limits).

## Test it

```sh
npm test         # the fake harness and the local sandbox: no plan, no sandbox provider (steering needs a real harness)
npm run typecheck
```

CI runs both on every commit (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`, job `example-todo`).

## What a real app changes

- **The user.** The page sends the user's name in an `x-user` header. That is a stand-in, not a sign-in: anyone can type any name. A real app reads the user from its own session.
- **The database.** SQLite in one process is enough for one server. For more servers, use byoa's Postgres or Convex store adapter, or write one for your database (four operations: get, put, delete, compare-and-set).

Source: https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/examples/todo/app.ts
